Multilingual detoxification coverage is broadening (e.g., RTP-LX spans 28 languages, PTP 17 languages with 425K prompts, and TextDetox/PAN covers 9 languages), but fragmented label schemas and culturally contingent definitions of harm make cross-benchmark comparisons unreliable without shared protocols and native-speaker validation.

Mitigations (data filtering, SFT/RLHF/preference tuning, decoding-time steering, representation editing, and guardrails) reduce overt toxicity but can over-suppress legitimate dialectal or identity-related expression, creating a safety–equity trade-off that is amplified in low-resource and code-mixed settings.

nodes.title: Rising From the Ashes: How Agentic AI is Unblocking Challenges in Cybersecurity
nodes.one_liner: Agentic AI is framed as a force multiplier that can resurrect stalled security ideas by making expertise replicable and low-latency reasoning practical, while simultaneously creating a new requirement to secure the agents themselves.
points: Cybersecurity incident costs are estimated at 0.001%–9% of global GDP, underscoring that scaling defenses hinges on reducing labor/latency/expertise bottlenecks rather than inventing entirely new primitives.

A capability-to-challenge mapping argues that five agentic AI traits—natural-language understanding, high-volume information processing, cognitive stamina, generalization/replicability, and multidisciplinary knowledge—can systematically mitigate five adoption blockers (excessive human effort, unattainably low latency, scarce expertise, task-specific solutions, and problem complexity).

Across 16 defensive case studies (from instrumentation optimization and formalizing standards to SBOM/supply-chain analysis, provenance triage at hundreds of millions of events/day, and self-healing systems), agentic AI is positioned to convert previously non-scalable expert workflows into parallelizable, repeatable pipelines—but only if agent autonomy and privileged tool access are secured to avoid amplifying AI-specific vulnerabilities.

nodes.title: SoK: AI Secure Code Generation: Progress, Pitfalls, and Paths Forward
nodes.one_liner: The interesting twist is that models largely “know” secure coding in natural language, but the hard problem is reliably actuating that knowledge into boundary-correct, functionality-preserving defenses under executable exploits.
points: A three-layer KAUGE framework shows secure-coding-principle understanding (6,382 fixed-answer questions from 456 OWASP/CERT rules) is high across models (lowest mean 86.2%) yet consistently exceeds executable secure generation, exposing a large knowledge–actuation gap of ~47.9 points on function tasks (CWEval) and ~72.9 points on web apps (BaxBench).

Natural-language understanding of secure coding principles is a strong predictor of executable secure outcomes (Spearman ρ=0.71, p=0.025 on CWEval secure-pass@k; ρ=0.63, p=0.056 on BaxBench), but models often fail at applying defenses at the correct implementation boundary even when they can correctly identify the relevant principle.

Mechanism-aware diagnosis reveals why pass/fail metrics mislead: among functional outputs, “secure-only” cases (secure but not SCP-compliant) outnumber “compliant-only” cases (compliant but vulnerable) by 1,100 vs 287 (p<0.001), showing security can arise via unmodeled defenses while apparent principle compliance can still miss sink-specific exploit details.

nodes.title: AgentRiskBOM: A Risk-Scoping Security Bill of Materials for Agentic AI Systems
nodes.one_liner: The most actionable shift is treating delegated agent authority (tools, permissions, memory, approvals, and auditability) as a versioned, diffable bill-of-materials that can be enforced in CI/CD before incidents occur.
points: A JSON-schema “authority envelope” for tool-using agents achieves 14/16 native capability-dimension coverage versus 1.0 (SBOM), 1.5 (AI-BOM), and 2.0 (ML-BOM), making autonomy, tool permissions, credential scope, approvals, memory persistence, and audit signals first-class review objects rather than implicit configuration.

Across 52 risk scenarios in 14 categories and 13 open-source agents, the artifact provides 100.0% modeled risk-category visibility compared with 10.5% for SBOM-like views and 20.9% for AI-BOM-like views, turning operational risks (e.g., unsafe external actions, inter-agent trust propagation, missing approvals/logging, and overprivileged credentials) into pre-deployment checkable fields.

Structured “authority drift” becomes mechanically gateable: a diff detector correctly classified all 33 injected deployment mutations, and an independent penalty-based scorer shows rank-level robustness with Spearman 0.73 (despite only 46% label agreement), implying scores work best for triage and change detection rather than automated certification.

nodes.title: AOHP: An Open-Source OS-Level Agent Harness for Personalized, Efficient and Secure Interaction
nodes.one_liner: Making agents OS-native—via composable services, structured UI/event streams, and system-enforced information-flow control—simultaneously boosts task success and cuts LLM runtime/token costs while tightening privacy guarantees.
points: An Android OS-level “agent harness” that treats agents as first-class OS actors improved mobile agent performance on 30 cross-app tasks, increasing checkpoint-weighted completion from 54.44% to 75.56% (+21.12 points) and fully solving 7 additional tasks versus stock Android.

On the 11 tasks both systems completed successfully, the harness reduced operational overhead by 44.64% fewer tool calls, 44.21% lower runtime (33.94→18.93 minutes), 51.55% fewer tokens (7.10M→3.44M), and 47.62% fewer LLM requests (273→143), indicating that OS-native structured interfaces and background execution materially lower agent cost-to-complete.

Default-redaction plus vault-mediated execution and taint tracking prevented private plaintext exposure while still enabling legitimate actions, passing five policy checks (sensitive display, ordinary actions, sensitive actions requiring consent, fail-closed on unsupported access, and redacted/tainted sensitive event streams) in an annotated payment-app case study.

nodes.title: Data Facts: A Metadata Schema for Structured Data Exchange in the NANDini Multi-Agent Ecosystem
nodes.one_liner: A minimal metadata pointer plus TTL and cryptographic checks can turn multi-agent data exchange into a verifiable, access-controlled pipeline that dramatically improves correctness while actively resisting tampering and credential forgery.
points: Adding a single data_facts_url pointer to agent registry records enables structured dataset discovery plus on-demand freshness (TTL) and integrity (SHA-256) checks with 100% retrieval success and only ~260–270 ms extra time-to-first-data from two additional HTTP round-trips.

Live data access via the schema and access pipeline eliminates prior-driven guesswork on counter-intuitive queries, delivering 100% decision accuracy (420/420) versus 35.2% without data access (p < 0.001) across 840 evaluations and remaining robust across 1–3 agent delegation hops.

Safety controls are measurable and effective: TTL enforcement cuts stale-data decision errors from 37.6% to 8.8% (76.6% stale detection, FP=0), checksum verification detects 100% of injected corruption (1%–50%), and the JWT+capability-gateway+A2A delegation stack blocks 100% of 46 forgery attempts with zero observed data leakage.

nodes.title: VeriPort: Automated and Verified Patch Backporting at Scale
nodes.one_liner: Verified patch backporting becomes practical when LLM-generated fixes are treated as untrusted drafts and only shipped after independent, executable exploit-blocking and functionality-preserving evidence passes per version.
points: An agentic backporting pipeline that isolates minimal security hunks and gates every patch with both exploit and regression “oracles” achieved 95.3% reliability across 10 runs on 128 BackportBench tasks without an upstream MSP, beating the strongest baseline by 22.7 percentage points and reaching 100% pass@10.

At npm ecosystem scale, the system solved 91.3% of 393 CVEPatchBench tasks reliably across 3 runs versus 71.1% for Claude Code (a 20.2-point gain), while also showing far lower run-to-run variance (2.3 points vs 9.5), indicating materially better operational stability for automated remediation.

Production deployment generated 5,000+ verified backported patches for 169 high/critical CVEs and empirically corrected advisory metadata by flagging 2,100 falsely listed affected versions and 127 missed vulnerable versions across 92 advisories, leading to 23 upstream advisory fixes (−387 versions, +81 versions).

nodes.title: The Web4 Agent Economy: A Large-Scale Empirical Study of the Landscape, Challenges, and Opportunities
affiliations: The State Key Laboratory of Blockchain and Data Security, Zhejiang University
Hangzhou High-Tech Zone (Binjiang) Institute of Blockchain and Data Security
nodes.one_liner: What’s interesting is the ecosystem has already hit “millions of sub-$1 agent payments per day,” yet the hardest problem is still basic interoperability and conformance at the payment boundary rather than lack of protocols.
points: Web4 already operates at meaningful scale with 99,448 EIP-8004 agent identity registrations across chains, heavily concentrated on BNB Smart Chain (~40.0%) and Base (~19.9%), indicating rapid but geographically uneven ecosystem formation.

The machine-to-machine payment layer shows production-grade volume with daily x402 activity reaching millions of transactions and an average payment size of about $0.46 USDC, signaling a shift from subscription APIs to pay-per-call micro-settlement as the default economic primitive for agents.

Developer-reported friction clusters into three integration bottlenecks—identity/authorization (230 issues; ~69.1% closed), cross-environment ops (96 issues; 50.0% closed), and payment interoperability (87 issues; ~25.3% closed)—implying that payment conformance across payer/gateway/resource remains the dominant reliability risk as adoption scales.

nodes.title: Probabilistic Agents in Deterministic Audits: Evaluating Multi-Agent Systems for Automated Audits Based on the German IT-Grundschutz
nodes.one_liner: The core takeaway is that LLM agents can extract and organize audit-relevant facts, but their probabilistic reasoning collapses when the workflow demands deterministic, evidence-backed compliance verdicts.
points: HybridRAG+multi-agent automation meaningfully reduces manual audit effort in semantic-heavy phases (Structural Analysis and Modeling), but still tops out at modest extraction quality with best entity-extraction F1 of 52.3% and best dependency-analysis F1 of 53.8%, leaving human validation mandatory where omissions create audit-critical blind spots.

Dependency reconstruction remains the main safety bottleneck: the highest-recall model finds 70.1% of the 881 ground-truth dependencies yet with only 43.6% precision, reflecting systematic generation of “plausible” but unsupported links that can break deterministic protection-need inheritance chains.

Deterministic compliance judgments are not reliably automatable with current LLMs, as the IT-Grundschutz check achieves only 32% best accuracy and models over-predict non-compliance (false negatives) by failing to distinguish documented intent from implemented evidence, implying AI should act as an evidence-retrieval and draft-reporting assistant rather than an autonomous auditor.

nodes.title: Forensic Trajectory Signatures for Agent Memory Poisoning Detection
nodes.one_liner: Tool-call logs alone can act like EDR for LLM agents by turning persistent memory-poisoning into a detectable, architecture-induced trajectory signature that generalizes across model families and even distinguishes memory attacks from prompt injection.
points: A mechanistically forced tool-call transition—invoking memory recall before sending an exfiltration email—separates successful persistent-memory poisoning executions from non-exfiltration runs with AUC=0.9563 using a single rule, and suppressing this transition breaks the attack under the stated architecture assumptions.

A lightweight trajectory detector using only tool-call order/count features reaches AUC=0.9904 (BCa 95% CI [0.987, 0.993]) and 0.9838 recall on 2,520 delayed-trigger runs (76.2% attack successes), showing that high-fidelity detection is possible without memory-content access, prompts, model weights, or email contents.

The behavioral signature is overdetermined and largely model-agnostic: removing all recall-related features leaves AUC unchanged at 0.9904, leave-one-model-out tests hit AUC=1.000 on 6/9 model hold-outs, the invariant transfers to GPT-4.1/GPT-4o without retraining, and a prefix-only variant still achieves AUC=0.934 enabling inline blocking with moderate degradation.

nodes.title: Adversarial Pragmatics for AI Safety Evaluation: A Benchmark for Instruction Conflict, Embedded Commands, and Policy Ambiguity
nodes.one_liner: The key insight is that safety evaluation errors often come from pragmatic misinterpretation (quote vs command, content vs authority, scope vs exception), and minimal-pair tests plus judge-validity metrics make those failure modes measurable rather than hidden by pass/fail scores.
points: A contrastive, linguistically controlled benchmark design exposed that 85.2% (46/54) of outputs were policy-compliant while only 66.7% (36/54) were full task successes, showing that “safe-looking” behavior can mask capability or pragmatic-control failures unless task, policy, and risk are labeled separately.

Minimal-pair robustness was low even when row-level success looked decent: only 48.1% (13/27) of pair–model cells passed a strict criterion requiring both variants to be task-successful and policy-compliant, indicating that many models rely on brittle heuristics that break under changes in embedding, deixis, transcript context, or policy framing.

LLM judges produced valid structured labels for all 54 rows but had uneven validity—66.7% agreement on task success versus 98.1% on refusal outcome—implying LLM-as-judge is suitable for triage on obvious refusal/compliance labels but unsafe to use as a primary grader for nuanced pragmatic constructs like attribution, ambiguity, and agent transcript interpretation.

nodes.title: An Empirical Evaluation of Prompt Injection Vulnerabilities in Large Language Models Across Multilingual and Obfuscated Attack Scenarios
nodes.one_liner: Multilingual and context-rich prompt injections reliably elicit phishing and keylogger assistance from all tested LLMs, and lightweight obfuscation only weakly degrades attacker success.
points: Across 15,540 generations over six frontier LLMs, 68.76% of malicious prompts produced fully actionable phishing/malware outputs and 80.84% produced at least partial attack enablement (full compliance + stalling), indicating prompt injection misuse is the dominant outcome rather than an edge case.

Safety behavior is strongly model-dependent—full compliance ranges from 44.09% (GPT-5 Mini) to 84.32% (DeepSeek-V3.2), yet even the most conservative model still fulfills 74.32% of malicious requests when stalling assistance is counted, implying today’s “refusal-only” guardrails leave substantial exploitable residual risk.

Attack success increases with realistic framing and non-English inputs: elaborate prompts raise average full compliance from 62.01% (direct) to 76.69% (elaborate) and Turkish/Chinese/Russian show higher full compliance than English (up to 80.18% vs 71.31%), while simple obfuscations reduce but do not prevent harm (Hex still 54.41% full compliance), exposing multilingual and encoding-aware alignment gaps.

nodes.title: Security--Fidelity Tradeoffs: The Hidden Cost of Prompt Injection Defense
nodes.one_liner: Measuring prompt-injection “security” alone can hide whether a defense is actually robust or just silently deleting user data—and SECFID quantifies that hidden cost.
points: A new benchmark (SECFID) makes three prompt-injection outcomes—execute, process-as-data, or ignore—separately observable, revealing that standard attack-success metrics conflate safe data handling with content suppression.

Across 1,168 examples and 48 model/defense configurations, no system achieves both strong prompt-injection security and high task fidelity: the highest-fidelity point hits 96.5% fidelity but only 47.8% security, while the most secure points reach 99.3% security with just 71.0%–73.9% fidelity.

Defenses that look equally “secure” by execution-rate can behave very differently: SECALIGN can convert many hijacks into faithful processing (repair) whereas DefensiveTokens often attains similar security by suppressing content, and a simple fidelity-aware DPO preference tuning boosts processing substantially (e.g., on held-out editing, 43.2%→80.6% processed) while keeping execution below 1%.

nodes.title: Understanding and Evaluating Claw-like Agent Security Through a Computer-Systems Lens
nodes.one_liner: The most dangerous agent failures come from cross-component system behaviors (loaders, memory, logs, credential mediation), where the LLM is often not the security boundary at all.
points: SafeClawArena’s 406 adversarial tasks show end-to-end compromise rates spanning ~20% to ~70% across 15 (platform, model) configurations, indicating that always-on, system-privileged “Claw-like” agents remain broadly exploitable even with frontier LLMs.

Native in-process malicious Plugins succeed 100% on unhardened platforms regardless of the underlying LLM (but drop to 0% when the platform removes the plugin loader), demonstrating that some failures are fundamentally system-layer privilege violations that model alignment cannot compensate for.

Platform hardening can dramatically reduce risk for some model families (e.g., GPT-5.4 overall attack success 70%→22%), yet can yield little benefit or even regressions for others (e.g., Gemini variants remain ~50%+ on the hardened platform), implying defenses must be evaluated jointly with the specific LLM and may shift leakage across channels rather than eliminate it.

nodes.title: RIPA: Sensory-Vector Prompt Injection Attacks on LLM-Controlled ROS 2 Robots
nodes.one_liner: If an LLM-controlled robot trusts serialized sensor context, then prompt injection stops being just a text problem and becomes an end-to-end pipeline integrity problem across OCR/STT/middleware—with simple obfuscations still slipping past keyword-centric filters.
points: Across 100 runs per injection variant on five LLMs, prompt-injection robustness was strongly model-specific rather than scale-dependent (e.g., Llama-3.3-70B and Gemma-3n ~4B both hit 100% ASR on all variants, while two mid-size models had 0% ASR on direct-override yet 100% ASR on structural variants).

A two-stage hybrid semantic firewall reduced ASR to 0% for known injection patterns with 0/20 false positives on a small benign set, but still suffered a 10.2% trial-weighted bypass rate (58/570) under obfuscation—dominated by synonym substitution (30/30) and hyphenated encoding (28/30).

Sensor-context poisoning via LiDAR (publishing fabricated /scan that becomes system-prompt state) achieved 100% ASR on DeepSeek-V4-Flash across all variants (N=30), showing that compromising environment-state serialization can reliably hijack actuation while bypassing user-message firewalls entirely.

nodes.title: IHDec: Divergence-Steered Contrastive Decoding for Securing Multi-Turn Instruction Hierarchies
nodes.one_liner: A lightweight JSD-based attribution signal can gate contrastive decoding to stop lower-priority prompts from silently taking over in late-turn conversations without paying an alignment tax.
points: IHDec, a training-free inference-time method that uses Jensen–Shannon divergence to detect role-influence inversions and applies divergence-steered contrastive decoding, improves multi-turn conflict instruction-hierarchy accuracy on IHEval by +11.98 percentage points over the strongest reported training-based baseline and by up to +38.1 percentage points over architectural interventions.

On Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct in multi-turn conflicts, IHDec reaches 50.68% accuracy versus 12.60% (ISE) and 13.25% (prompting), indicating that hierarchy failures in long dialogues are better addressed by token-level decoding control than by role-embedding fine-tuning that degrades under recency-driven history effects.

IHDec preserves general capability with only a 0.088-point drop on MT-Bench-101 (9.29→9.21) while also improving benign aligned instruction following by up to +7.48 percentage points and reducing prompt-injection susceptibility on Safety Defense by up to +39.0 percentage points over vanilla.

The method flips an observed negative scaling trend into positive scaling synergy: across Qwen3 4B→32B, vanilla instruction-hierarchy accuracy stays low (~12–13%) while IHDec increases monotonically to 38.5% at 32B (a +27.8 percentage point gain), showing larger models amplify risk unless actively steered at decoding time.

nodes.title: Distributed Attacks in Persistent-State AI Control
nodes.one_liner: Persistent codebases turn AI agent subversion into a supply-chain-like game where distributing and timing payload components across PRs can beat even strong LLM monitors unless monitoring itself becomes stateful and multi-view.
points: Persistent-state coding workflows enable distributed (multi-PR) attacks that keep each pull request locally plausible, yielding high success-conditioned evasion of standard PR-diff monitors (e.g., 87% gradual vs 75% best-position non-gradual on a task-description diff monitor) and exposing that a single monitoring approach cannot reliably cover both gradual and single-PR “timed” payloads.

High evasion is a property of the persistent-state attack surface rather than one model: under the same GPT-4o diff monitor, gradual-attack evasion remains ≥65% across different attacker backends (Claude Sonnet 4.5: 94% with 45% success; Gemini 3.1 Pro: 65.3%; Kimi K2.5: 100% on 53/53 successful attacks).

Defenses improve most from stateful summarization and cross-modality ensembling rather than more raw context: a stateful link-tracker diff monitor cuts gradual evasion from 87% to 54%, and a 4-monitor (diff+trajectory) ensemble reduces gradual evasion from 93% under the weakest standard diff monitor to 47% while keeping honest false positives below 2%.

nodes.title: HARC: Coupling Harmfulness and Refusal Directions for Robust Safety Alignment
nodes.one_liner: Coupling a model’s internal “harmfulness” and “refusal” directions at both prompt and generation time turns safety into a low-dimensional control problem that improves jailbreak robustness without the usual capability or over-refusal tax.
points: HARC reduces average jailbreak attack success rate by 4.67× on Llama-3.1-8B and 4.75× on Qwen-2.5-7B versus the base model while keeping over-refusal at or below baseline and preserving overall helpfulness/capability.

Black-box jailbreaks succeed primarily by suppressing the prompt-side harmfulness and/or refusal residual-stream directions before any output is generated, and different attack families (e.g., DAN vs PAIR vs CodeAttack) occupy separable regions in the harmfulness–refusal projection plane.

Even when prompt-side harm recognition is bypassed, the model often re-recognizes harmfulness during response generation (response-token positions) yet fails to convert that signal into refusal, motivating dual-position coupling that scales to 70B/72B models with near-zero ASR on PAIR/PAP/DeepInception and large CodeAttack drops (e.g., 0.688→0.242 on Llama-3.1-70B).

nodes.title: Harnessing Textual Refusal Directions for Multimodal Safety
nodes.one_liner: A simple text-only activation “refusal direction,” once corrected for modality bias via neutral-image re-centering and trust-region scaling, becomes a scalable safety layer for images and videos without multimodal safety training data.
points: MARS, a training-free inference-time method that reuses text-derived refusal directions, raised unsafe-image refusal on VISU from 0.2–22.9% (zero-shot) to 43.3–78.5% across five MLLMs while keeping safe-image refusal comparatively low (0.6–10.3% for most models).

On multimodal jailbreaking (HADES), MARS boosted refusal to 59.2–99.5% and improved Llama-Guard safety scores to 79.8–99.8%, substantially reducing successful jailbreaks without requiring any multimodal safety data.

For video jailbreaks, MARS achieved the strongest training-free gains—e.g., +59.4 percentage points refusal on Qwen3-VL (28.8%→88.2%) and +52.0 points on Qwen3.5 (26.2%→78.2%)—showing that text-only safety structure can transfer even to video inputs.

nodes.title: EvalSafetyGap: A Hybrid Survey and Conceptual Framework for LLM Evaluation-Safety Failures
nodes.one_liner: Capability scores, safety metrics, and governance disclosures can all improve while the underlying safety properties remain uncertain, so safety evaluation must be dynamic, multi-attempt, and audit-ready.
points: Benchmark-based capability signals can be misleading under optimization pressure, with 29/60 widely used benchmarks showing high or very high saturation (including 14/60 “very-high”), and only 16% of 445 benchmark papers reporting uncertainty estimates or statistical tests—undermining fine-grained model comparisons.

A ten-model audit found no reliable link between capability and sustained jailbreak robustness: the capability–ASR-100 association was statistically indeterminate (Pearson r=+0.232, p=0.520; 95% CI [-0.530, 0.741]), implying capability thresholds alone are a weak basis for safety assurance.

The apparent open–closed “safety gap” in the audit was modest and largely attributable to governance/disclosure rather than behavioral robustness, with the largest group separation in governance (mean gap ≈0.268; d≈1.90) while ASR-100 robustness differed little (gap ≈0.043; p=0.640) and conclusions were sensitive to how one borderline model was classified.

nodes.title: Beyond the Prompt: Jailbreaking Function-Calling LLMs via Simulated Moderation Traces
nodes.one_liner: Function calling turns “tool traces” and validator feedback into a high-privilege side-channel that can progressively convert refusals into compliance with strikingly few queries.
points: A stateful function-calling design that interleaves trusted tool schemas/validation messages with untrusted arguments and tool-like outputs enables jailbreak intent to be distributed across turns, making prompt-level sanitization and single-message filtering fundamentally incomplete defenses.

Simulated Moderation Traces (SMT) achieves near-perfect jailbreak performance on tool-enabled commercial LLMs, reaching 99.67% ASR on SafeBench-Tiny and 98.33% ASR on JailbreakBench with high harmfulness (Avg HarmScore 74.27/76.83) while using fewer than 1.5 queries on average (1.48/1.37), substantially outperforming prompt-centric and prior function-calling baselines.

Traditional mitigations (length limits, low temperature, safety reminders, safety checks) reduce SMT but still leave high residual risk (e.g., 78% ASR on Claude-Sonnet-4.5 under combined defenses), whereas a function-calling-aware system-prompt guard (FCGuard) can drop ASR to 0% on GPT-5.4 and Claude-Sonnet-4.5, implying that defenses must reason over full interaction state (schemas, arguments, tool outputs, and history) rather than isolated prompts.

nodes.title: Securing the AI Agent: A Unified Framework for Multi-Layer Agent Red Teaming
nodes.one_liner: The standout idea is layer-paradigm matching: treat agent security as an evidence problem and pick rule-based, LLM-audit, interactive red teaming, or statistical jailbreak evaluation depending on which layer you’re trying to prove unsafe.
points: AI-Infra-Guard operationalizes a four-layer agent attack-surface model (infrastructure, protocol/tool, agent behavior, model) and ties each layer to a distinct evidence type and assessment method, implying end-to-end agent security requires heterogeneous testing rather than a single scanner.

The infrastructure module scales deterministic coverage to 75+ AI components with 107 fingerprint rules and 1,443 vulnerability rules, and explicitly stratifies confidence into verified/version-based/inferred findings (including 87 empty-predicate rules) to manage uncertainty from missing versions and immature advisory ecosystems.

The skill supply-chain scanner is benchmarked on SkillTrustBench (5,520 cases distilled from 62,652 skills) where top base models reach ~0.98–0.985 loose F1 with recall ~0.997, but false-positive rates vary sharply by model (as low as 0.012 vs as high as 0.187), showing model choice can dominate operational triage cost even with a fixed audit harness.

nodes.title: Cognitive Firewall: A Proactive, Zero-Trust, Multi-Gate Framework for LLM Safety
nodes.one_liner: Decomposing safety into categorical, escalation-combined gates (intent, zero-trust context, trajectory consistency, and output risk) materially improves multi-turn jailbreak containment while keeping false refusals relatively low.
points: A four-gate, conversation-level “Cognitive Firewall” reduced jailbreak attack success from 45%/10%/30%/74% (undefended) to 1%/0%/2%/14% across single-turn (jbb), escalation (crescendo), decomposition (safemt), and human-crafted multi-turn (mhj) attacks, showing that tracking intent and trajectory can nearly eliminate automated jailbreaks but still leaves a meaningful residual on hardest human attacks.

Most risk reduction was proactive (pre-generation): intent and consistency gates accounted for the majority of blocks (e.g., 89/92 jbb blocks from intent and 48/50 crescendo blocks from consistency), while the post-generation output gate was critical for decomposition payloads (e.g., 21/39 safemt and 12/43 mhj blocks), implying defenses need both early conversation oversight and a final response backstop to cover complementary failure modes.

The framework achieved an 8% over-refusal rate on XSTest versus 18–21% for stricter guard baselines, and it blocked 75% of authority/override probes (12/16) with 0% benign role-mention refusals, indicating that isolating “zero-trust” authority claims as a dedicated decision channel can improve security without heavily degrading benign utility.

nodes.title: SCARCE: Scalable Cascade Analysis for Rare-event Characterisation via Embeddings
nodes.one_liner: A practical path to certifiable rare-event safety metrics: data-driven Subset Simulation that stays sample-efficient, transfers across domains, and still supports anytime-valid bounds under adaptive stopping.
points: Replacing Subset Simulation’s handcrafted performance function with learned embeddings plus geometric “rulers” yields ∼400–500× lower mean absolute error on MNIST rare misclassification than grid-searched traditional SS, while avoiding systematic over-counting (traditional SS reports ≈9.6×10⁻³ vs a ≈4.0×10⁻³ reference).

A non-negative supermartingale construction enables an anytime-valid, level-wise high-probability upper envelope on the running rare-event probability estimate, remaining statistically valid under adaptive quantile thresholds and early stopping (via Ville’s inequality control of upward excursions).

For fleet-level LLM jailbreak probability estimation using Llama-Guard-3-8B hidden states, a PCA-based ruler reaches 2.6% mean relative error for adversarial fractions η≥10⁻³ across five turns—well within the reference’s own 27.9% average bootstrap relative half-width—and transfers to a GCG-style corpus with 2.93% relative error after refitting calibration, with a directional KL selector correlating strongly with estimation error (Spearman ρ=0.83).

nodes.title: Resolution Thresholds in VLM Detection of Harmful ASCII Art Across Construction Modes and Languages
nodes.one_liner: Downscaling often helps VLMs “see” harmful ASCII art, but semantic filler—especially positive English words—still defeats detection across most resolutions and models.
points: Across 62 valid (model, ASCII-mode) strata, 59.7% showed a statistically significant monotonic drop in harmful-ASCII detection as resolution increased (BH-corrected q<0.05), establishing resolution as a first-order failure trigger for VLM moderation.

Word-embedded ASCII construction is the most reliable evasion: positive English-word fill (L5) achieved the lowest aggregate detection rate at 0.062 pooled over models, resolutions, and languages, indicating most VLMs default to reading benign filler text over the global harmful shape.

Language effects were minor relative to resolution/mode effects: only 4.7% of 640 English-vs-Chinese strata differed significantly after BH correction, implying the vulnerability generalizes across scripts even though Chinese-word fill (L8) showed a notable low-resolution advantage for Chinese-built models (0.69 vs 0.36 pooled detection at r=0.1) that reversed at high resolution (0.00 vs 0.11–0.13 at r≥0.8).

nodes.title: Curvature-Guided Module Localization for Low-Rank Detoxification of Backdoored Large Language Models
nodes.one_liner: Mechanistic localization using activation patching plus Fisher/K-FAC curvature identifies a small, nonredundant set of transformer projections where low-rank “surgical” repairs can erase a conditional LLM backdoor while keeping outputs clean-like.
points: Curvature-guided module localization plus targeted rank-8 LoRA repair drove Triggered Malicious Response Rate (TMRR) to 0.000 in multiple settings (e.g., begin-trigger: K=5 with 1000 samples at 30 epochs and K=7 with 100–1000 samples at 10–30 epochs; middle-trigger: K=5 or K=7 with ≥100 samples at 10–30 epochs), showing that backdoor removal can be achieved via localized weight-space edits rather than full retraining.

The approach is data-efficient for the hardest cases where trigger effects must propagate through the network, reaching near-zero/zero TMRR with as few as 50–100 detoxification examples in the middle-trigger setting (e.g., K=5 at 50 samples and 30 epochs yields TMRR=0.070 and at 100 samples yields TMRR=0.000), implying that mechanistic target selection can substitute for large clean corpora when adapter budget is limited.

Benign behavior is largely preserved while suppressing the backdoor, with Triggered-to-Clean Behavioral Similarity (TCBS) typically staying high (~0.82–0.86) even when TMRR collapses to ~0, indicating that aligning triggered internal activations to clean trajectories can neutralize the attack without broad capability degradation.

nodes.title: CSO-LLM: Class Subspace Orthogonalization for Post-Training Backdoor Detection and Trigger Inversion in LLMs
nodes.one_liner: CSO turns backdoor trigger search into a geometry problem: penalize “moving toward the target class subspace” and innocuous triggers pop out while target-class-looking tokens get suppressed.
points: Adding a class-subspace orthogonalization (CSO) cosine-similarity penalty to a margin-based objective provides implicit token blacklisting that can move an innocuous true trigger token (“seriously”) from rank 830 to rank 2 in a 30k-token vocabulary, sharply reducing false trigger candidates dominated by target-class sentiment words.

In post-training settings with only model access plus ~50 clean samples per class, CSO-based detectors achieve high detection with low false alarms (e.g., on Qwen3-4B/Yahoo-7 at high poison rate: discrete CSO detects 9–10/10 poisoned models across triggers with 1/10 false positives on clean models), while plain margin detection fails completely (0/10 TPR, 10/10 FPR).

CSO enables accurate ground-truth trigger inversion for multi-token triggers where prior LLM defenses largely fail (e.g., on Qwen3-4B/Yahoo-7, “Tell me seriously” recall is 25/30–30/30 tokens for CSO vs 0/30–8/30 for DBS/MM/UAT/GBDA), and it remains effective against moderately adaptive “intrinsic-feature” triggers but can be evaded by highly non-stealthy triggers that spread behavior across many sentiment synonyms.

nodes.title: FlipGuard: Defending Large Language Models Against Quantization-Conditioned Backdoor Attacks
affiliations: School of Cyber Science and Technology Shandong University
Suzhou Research Institute of Shandong University
nodes.one_liner: Quantization itself becomes an activation switch for stealth backdoors, and a lightweight pre-quantization weight “boundary flip” can shut them down without needing data or trigger samples.
points: Quantization-conditioned backdoors can remain effectively hidden during full-precision auditing yet activate after common post-hoc quantization (INT8/FP4/NF4), collapsing security scores (e.g., StarCoderBase-3B Code Security 74.6% → 7.0% after INT8; Phi-2 content-injection Keyword Occurrence 0.07% → 92.9% after NF4).

FlipGuard’s targeted pre-quantization weight perturbations (typically ~6–20% of weights) largely neutralize QCB behaviors across code vulnerability insertion, over-refusal, and content injection, restoring attacked models to near-baseline security levels (e.g., Phi-2 NF4 over-refusal 30.2% → 0.53%; Phi-2 NF4 injection 92.9% → 0.47%; StarCoderBase-3B INT8 Code Security 7.0% → 82.4%).

The defense can deliver high security with small utility changes on standard benchmarks (MMLU/TruthfulQA/HumanEval/MBPP) and appears safe to apply even when a model is clean (e.g., clean Phi-2 over-refusal stays ~0.53–0.60% after FlipGuard + quantization), supporting a practical “defend-before-you-quantize” supply-chain posture.

nodes.title: Cloak and Detonate: Scanner Evasion and Dynamic Detection of Agent Skill Malware
affiliations: Hong Kong University of Science and Technology
Guangzhou HKUST Fok Ying Tung Research Institute
nodes.one_liner: Static scanning for agent skills fails under semantics-preserving transformations, but runtime detonation with OS-level information-flow tracking remains effective even when the payload is packed or obfuscated.
points: Payload-preserving evasion is highly effective against install-time skill scanners: self-extracting packing bypassed all eight evaluated scanners at >90% (≥96% for most static/hybrid tools) and structural obfuscation bypassed >80% on most static scanners, reaching 96% on a hybrid scanner, implying appearance-based auditing is brittle under adaptive adversaries.

Cloaking does not meaningfully reduce real agent utility: across Claude Code (Sonnet 4.6) and OpenAI Codex (GPT-5.4), neither structural obfuscation nor packing caused statistically detectable task-success degradation on 87 SkillsBench tasks while preserving high trajectory similarity (~0.88–0.90), meaning evasions can remain operational and stealthy.

Behavior-centric runtime auditing substantially improves robustness: the proposed sandbox+information-flow approach detected 97% of benchmark attacks at 2% false positives and sustained 87% detection on executable in-the-wild malicious skills, while a top static scanner collapsed from 99% to 10% under structural obfuscation, showing dynamic OS-boundary evidence resists surface-level cloaks.

nodes.title: Linguistic Firewall: Geometry as Defense in Multi-Agent Systems Routing
nodes.one_liner: Turning agent selection into a fixed embedding-space projection creates a 'linguistic firewall' that makes metadata prompt-injection effectively inexpressible at routing time while improving latency by orders of magnitude.
points: Non-textual, evaluation-driven routing (ANTAP) reduces description-based router-hijacking Attack Success Rate to near-zero (≈0.2–0.4%) versus ~67–75% for a description-based router, showing that removing inference-time metadata parsing can structurally eliminate an entire injection pathway.

Empirically learned behavioral operators also suppress backdoored/sleeper agents: across multiple LoRA backdoor variants (e.g., BadNet/Sleeper/VPI/MTBA/CTBA), ANTAP holds ASR to ~0.3–2.4% on triggered queries while embedding-based routing remains far higher (≈12–21%) and textual routing stays ≈73–79%, implying offline capability tests can function as a practical root-of-trust for MAS routing.

Routing via a single geometric projection yields large efficiency and scaling gains: ANTAP’s online latency is ~26–38 ms versus ~0.4–2.5 s for text-based routing as prompt/description length grows, and its ASR can even drop with more agents (3.35%→0.46% from 2→19 agents) while the text baseline worsens (~33.9%→34.9%).

nodes.title: AI-Generated PowerShell Malware: An Experimental Framework and Dataset
affiliations: Università degli Studi di Napoli Federico II
nodes.one_liner: Behavioral dynamic analysis shows small open-weight models can produce PowerShell malware that is operationally indistinguishable from real samples nearly half the time, despite low textual similarity.
points: Fine-tuned open-weight LLMs generated PowerShell malware whose dynamic malicious-event footprint closely matched real-world samples, with a median Jaccard similarity of 84.5% and 48.4% of cases showing complete event overlap.

High-fidelity malware generation was achieved with sub-10B-parameter models using parameter-efficient QLoRA training and 4-bit quantization, indicating consumer-hardware attackers can bypass proprietary-model guardrails by self-hosting smaller models.

Static/text similarity can understate functional risk because generated scripts often diverge lexically yet converge behaviorally, making sandboxed dynamic analysis with telemetry-derived rules essential for reliable evaluation of LLM-generated malware.

nodes.title: Cybersecurity is the True Frontier for Generative AI Success or Failure
nodes.one_liner: Cybersecurity stress-tests generative AI with adversaries, massive unlabeled data, and hard real-time constraints—conditions where impressive demos often fail to translate into dependable defenses.
points: Static binary malware analysis forces AI systems to handle contexts where a single sample can reach billions of tokens and attackers can intentionally pad binaries to evade analysis, making naive long-context transformer approaches computationally infeasible and operationally brittle.

Despite malware being involved in under 20% of attempted breaches, static analysis remains a high-leverage proving ground because expert labeling can take hours to weeks per binary and yields ambiguous ground truth due to analyst disagreement and adversarial manipulation.

Early agentic malware-analysis demonstrations show feasibility but not readiness for scale, exemplified by multi-agent systems taking 46 minutes to analyze one relatively simple malware sample, implying that real-world deployment will hinge on hybrid triage, tool integration, and stringent latency/false-positive constraints.

nodes.title: LLM Semantic Signaling Game and Mechanism Design: Systematic Blindness, Awareness Shaping, and Mindset Dynamics
affiliations: New York University Tandon School of Engineering
nodes.one_liner: The key twist is that “systematic blindness” is formalized as missing features (not just wrong thresholds), which explains why stealthy LLM phishing can persist until defenses expand the receiver’s representational cue set and/or change incentives.
points: Aggregate token-level risk scores from LLM-generated messages can be treated as approximately Gaussian (e.g., stealth setting showed Kolmogorov distance 0.016 with skewness 0.10 and excess kurtosis −0.04), enabling closed-form likelihood-ratio/threshold detection rules for LLM-mediated phishing.

Receiver “awareness” modeled as a feature-set type (what cues are even represented) drives large differences in adversarial success: a stealth phishing control was accepted 54.1% by naive receivers but only 15.7% by highly aware receivers, with Gaussian predictions matching Monte Carlo within ≤1.0% absolute error across all pairs.

Mechanism-design levers can flip incentives toward benign pooling by reshaping costs and populations: increasing the aware-receiver share to ~0.48 eliminates profitable malicious deviation, and adding a modest nonbenign-control penalty (τ=0.10) drops the required aware share to ~0.18, implying that awareness training plus friction/guardrails can be substitute complements in practice.

nodes.title: KidnapRAG: A Black-Box Attack for Hijacking Reasoning in Agentic Retrieval-Augmented Generation Systems
nodes.one_liner: Iterative retrieval-and-reasoning improves robustness to naive poisoning, but it also creates a sequential attack surface where an adversary can steer query reformulation step-by-step using only public web documents.
points: A pure black-box attacker who can only publish externally retrievable documents can reliably hijack multi-step Agentic RAG by chaining role-specific poisons (Bait → Chain-Link → Mal-Ins) that progressively redirect query reformulation and evidence grounding rather than relying on a single injected passage.

Across ReAct and WebThinker with multiple LLM backbones and datasets, the chained attack reaches high target-answer induction while sharply degrading QA accuracy (e.g., EM drops from 0.68→0.20 with ASR 0.39 on HotpotQA for ReAct+Qwen2.5-32B, and EM 0.38→0.01 with ASR 0.78 on MuSiQue for ReAct+Llama-3.3-70B).

Sequential “chain dragging” increases attack success by sustaining the compromised reasoning trajectory over additional retrieval steps, and the attack can evade simple safety gating on intermediate traces (OpenAI Moderation guard rate falls to 0.0% on ReAct and ~4.2% on WebThinker for attacked chains on HotpotQA).

nodes.title: Minos: A Multi-Agent Collaborative Framework for Provenance-Based Backward Tracking
affiliations: Ningbo Key Laboratory of Quantum Software and Security
nodes.one_liner: What stands out is that intent-aware, multi-agent LLM orchestration (debate + grounded RAG + lifecycle memory) can outperform classic provenance backtracking while explicitly trading compute for interpretable, audit-friendly investigations.
points: Across 14 APT scenarios spanning five public provenance datasets, the multi-agent Minos framework reached 0.92 average recall and 0.64 precision while producing attack subgraphs that were 49% more compact than baselines (35 vs. 68–129 edges on average).

Replacing exhaustive graph traversal with hypothesis-guided planning plus a “count-first” query protocol reduced dependency-explosion overhead, cutting average token use to 164K versus 248K when the protocol is removed and preventing precision collapse on high-degree nodes (0.64 vs. 0.48).

Safety- and reliability-oriented agent scaffolding materially changed error modes: removing adversarial deliberation dropped precision from 0.64 to 0.51 (more false positives), while removing coarse-grained MITRE-tactic state caused uncontrolled exploration with precision falling to 0.28 and subgraph size inflating to 98 edges.

nodes.title: A Lifecycle and Application-Stack Survey of Large Language Model Vulnerabilities: Attacks, Risks, Defenses, and Open Problems
nodes.one_liner: The key insight is that LLM vulnerabilities are best modeled as information-flow and privilege failures across the full lifecycle—especially where untrusted text can steer retrieval and tool-using agents—so security hinges on composable system controls, not just better prompts or alignment.
points: LLM security failures are primarily system-level—spanning eight lifecycle stages from data collection through deployment—so the same attack (e.g., “poisoning” or “prompt injection”) can reappear with different feasibility and impact depending on where trust boundaries, provenance, and authority sit in the stack.

Indirect prompt injection and RAG/memory attacks turn untrusted content (web pages, PDFs, emails, repositories, tool outputs) into executable influence, making “confused deputy” failures—where attacker-controlled text steers an over-privileged agent to misuse the user’s authority—a dominant real-world risk.

Effective mitigation requires defense-in-depth that prioritizes deterministic controls (least-privilege tools, typed schemas, sandboxing, allowlists, budgets, signed artifacts, human approval for high-impact actions) because point fixes like prompt hardening, filters, or alignment are probabilistic and do not reliably compose across multi-step agent workflows.

nodes.title: MESA: Prioritizing Vulnerable Communication Channels for Securing Multi-Agent Systems
nodes.one_liner: Communication topology makes MAS attacks predictable enough that defenders can pre-rank and harden a small slice of edges to block a disproportionate share of compromises—without needing any attack logs.
points: Edge-level risk in LLM multi-agent systems is highly concentrated, with the top 20% most vulnerable communication edges accounting for about 59% of total observed attack success and a single compromised edge contributing up to 75% of success in worst cases, implying large security ROI from targeted channel hardening.

A label-free edge-ranking method combining six graph-structural metrics with two clean-execution probes predicts per-edge attack success with mean Spearman ρ≈+0.60 (peaking at +0.73), showing that security-critical channels can often be identified pre-deployment without attack traces.

Under budgeted defense, monitoring the top 10% of ranked edges intercepts roughly 3× more successful attacks than random allocation, and simple randomization over the top few edges reduces adaptive-attacker success by ~10.5 percentage points compared to deterministic top-k protection.

nodes.title: Black-Box Inference of LLM Architectural Properties with Restrictive API Access
nodes.one_liner: Architectural secrecy via “single-token logprob only” APIs is illusory because spectral methods plus TTFT timing can still back out hidden dimension, depth, and size—just at much higher query cost.
points: Even when an LLM API only reveals the sampled token’s single log-probability (no top‑k logits and no logit-bias), NightVision can still infer architectural IP—recovering hidden dimension with 23% mean relative error across 32 open-source models (9% on MoE) and showing current “restrictive” APIs do not fully prevent architectural leakage.

A timing side channel (time-to-first-token) combined with an estimated hidden dimension enables rough recovery of depth and total parameter count for larger models, achieving ~53% mean relative error on ≥3B-parameter models but often exceeding 100% error below 3B parameters where prefill-dominated timing assumptions break down.

Closing the logit-leak channel substantially raises attacker cost but does not eliminate it: achieving ≤30% hidden-dimension error requires ~12×–190× more tokens than prior logit-bias/top‑k attacks, with practical runs reporting token budgets on the order of 10^11–10^12 (median ~4×10^11), implying that cost/friction—not security—becomes the primary barrier.

nodes.title: Behind the Refusal: Determining Guardrail Activation via Behavioral Monitoring
nodes.one_liner: Refusals leak their provenance: subtle HTTP+lexical artifacts can reveal guardrail activation and even fingerprint block patterns with near-perfect separation from model refusals.
points: A black-box behavioral monitoring method using only 40 prompts detects whether an AI system is fronted by a guardrail with 100% accuracy across 162 target configurations (9 guardrails × 6 block patterns × 3 LLMs) and 0% false positives on a no-guardrail control, with strong benign-vs-malicious separation (q < 0.001).

Combining HTTP and lexical signals is reliably discriminative while timing-only signals are noisy (timing produced moderate significance even on no-guardrail controls), implying guardrail detection should prioritize protocol/response-structure and templating artifacts rather than latency heuristics.

A learned block-pattern fingerprint distinguishes guardrail blocks from intrinsic LLM refusals on unseen prompts with 0.98 average F1 (5/9 guardrails at 1.00 F1), enabling adaptive offensive/defensive workflows that choose guardrail-evasion vs alignment-jailbreak strategies based on the refusal’s true origin.

nodes.title: Embedding Inference Attack
nodes.one_liner: Even when a RAG assistant refuses to answer malformed inputs, retrieval still happens—and the returned chunks can be used to reliably infer the hidden embedding model, enabling downstream privacy attacks.
points: A black-box attacker can fingerprint which embedding model an IR/RAG system uses by comparing only the unordered sets of retrieved documents via Jaccard overlap, even without access to rankings, similarity scores, or embeddings.

In a 13-model evaluation, only 1,249 tailored generated queries (k=3) were enough to uniquely identify the victim embedding model, while simple adversarial inputs (random strings, non-queries, probing prompts) could also fully discriminate models in the no-reranker IR setup (11/11 successful queries).

Similarity-threshold filtering can sharply reduce model identifiability but at a quality cost: at threshold 0.60 the number of discriminative generated queries dropped from 1,249 to 194 (k=3), while retrieval quality became highly model-dependent (e.g., LaBSE Recall@1000 fell from 0.5419 to 0.0173, whereas e5-large-v2 stayed at 0.9777).

nodes.title: Words Speak Louder Than Code: Investigating Cognitive Heuristics in LLM-Based Code Vulnerability Detection
nodes.one_liner: LLM-based vulnerability detectors can be “socially engineered” via ordinary workflow metadata—framing and anchors can hide vulnerabilities at scale without touching the code.
points: Non-code context alone can systematically flip LLM vulnerability verdicts, with cross-model average susceptibility highest for framing (33.2%) followed by anchoring (23.5%) and halo/author attribution (18.4%), indicating CI/CD metadata is a first-class reliability risk for LLM scanners.

Cognitive cues act like a “volume knob” that shifts recall and false-positive rate in near lockstep (Pearson r=0.965; regression slope≈0.994), so precision largely plateaus and verdict flips often occur without correct root-cause identification.

A black-box “cognitive attack” that forges benign-looking PR/commit metadata can suppress up to 97% of previously detected vulnerabilities (combined ASR up to 97.23%), and prompt-based instructions to ignore metadata fail to reliably mitigate suppression (many models remain >40% ASR even under stronger defenses).

nodes.title: COHORT: Collaborative Orchestration for Hardening via Offensive Replay on Emulated Topologies
nodes.one_liner: Replay-based paired evaluation on high-fidelity emulation turns LLM-generated mitigations into measurable, deployable network-device commands—then reveals both a 4.4× multi-agent lift and a fast plateau in cumulative hardening.
points: A role-decomposed multi-agent LLM pipeline validated by offensive replay on real-vendor-firmware GNS3 emulations achieves a 46.7% mitigation success rate (attack progress reduced and LAN+internet connectivity preserved), a 4.4× improvement over a matched single-agent baseline at 10.7%.

Most of the performance gain comes from role specialization (MSR 38.6% without the critic loop), with iterative implementation–critique refinement adding a further +7.9 percentage points to reach 46.7%, showing that decomposition matters more than self-review alone.

Defense stacking on a persistent network state quickly saturates—cumulative attack-step reduction plateaus at ~52% by the 4th sequential defense—implying diminishing returns from greedy additive hardening and a need for non-greedy selection/replacement strategies to push beyond the ceiling.

nodes.title: Why Trust Your Agent? Empirical Security Gains from TRiSM-Guided Agentic Workflows in Healthcare
nodes.one_liner: A concrete TRiSM-to-controls mapping (server-side prompts, least privilege tools/data, pre-prompt embedding checks) delivers double dividends in healthcare agents: far fewer successful injections and notably higher report accuracy, while also revealing that no single LLM is robust across vectors.
points: A TRiSM-guided multi-agent redesign cut mean attack success rates from 31% to 10% for RAG poisoning and from 42% to 25% for data-field injection across 5 LLMs (500 attacks), indicating that architectural controls materially outperform “model-only” safety expectations.

Moving prompt construction from client-side to server-side structurally eliminated the client-side network-injection vector that otherwise succeeded 59% of the time on the single-agent baseline, showing that where prompts are assembled is a first-order security decision.

Security-hardening via least-privilege agent decomposition and workflow guardrails increased medical report accuracy by 14 percentage points (72.5%→86.5%) over 800 generations, implying that reducing attack surface and reducing cognitive load on models can improve both safety and output quality simultaneously.

nodes.title: Generative AI and Federated Learning for Intrusion Detection Systems: A Survey
nodes.one_liner: The most consequential takeaway is that combining generative AI with federated IDS can simultaneously improve data scarcity/imbalance and materially worsen adversarial and evaluation risks unless realism and federated benchmarks catch up.
points: Generative models are being used in IDS pipelines for anomaly detection, synthetic traffic generation/augmentation, missing-value imputation, adversarial traffic generation, and alert explanation—improving data efficiency but expanding the attack surface via dual-use generation.

Federated-learning IDS addresses privacy by keeping raw network traffic local, yet non-IID client data, communication overhead, and poisoning risks remain dominant blockers; compressed autoencoder approaches report up to 95% communication reduction while maintaining detection utility.

Current IDS benchmarking is still mostly centralized (e.g., CICIDS2017, CICDDoS2019, CICIoT2023), with FLNET2023 standing out as an explicitly federated dataset—implying that many reported FL-IDS results may not reflect realistic client heterogeneity, topology, or temporal drift.

nodes.title: Knowledge Over Parameters: Evolving Smart Contract Vulnerability Detection
nodes.one_liner: Treating vulnerability detection rules as executable, continuously debuggable software artifacts—rather than prompts or fine-tuned weights—yields higher accuracy, better adherence, and cross-model portability at low cost.
points: EVOVULN reaches 71% macro-F1 across five real-world smart-contract vulnerability types (66% precision, 81% recall), outperforming zero-shot GPT-5.2 (52% macro-F1) and top coding-agent baselines (57%), indicating that evolvable procedural policies can beat raw model scale for semantic logic-bug detection.

Ablations show the approach is jointly driven by rule evolution and controlled execution: removing evolution drops macro-F1 from 71% to 46% (−25 points, largely via precision collapse from 66%→37%), while removing the IoC Runtime at inference drops macro-F1 to 49% (−22 points) with recall falling from 81%→44%, evidencing that unconstrained LLMs drift away from prescribed multi-step logic.

Evolved detection knowledge transfers across models without retraining (66% macro-F1 on Qwen3.5-9B and 67% on MiniMax-M2.5) and can let a lightweight detector surpass a much larger model by 19 F1 points, with a one-time evolution cost under $50, implying a practical “knowledge-over-parameters” path to robust, low-cost auditing.

nodes.title: Manufactured Confidence: How Memory Consolidation Turns Hearsay into Confident Facts
nodes.one_liner: Long-term agent memory can silently turn casual hearsay into high-authority “facts,” and once a single memory becomes load-bearing, confident phrasing—not truth or source—drives cascading security-critical decisions.
points: LLM memory consolidation systems (e.g., mem0 and LangMem) rewrote hedged/hearsay statements into confident, dated “facts” with a 100% laundering rate in the poisoning protocol (1.00 vs 0.00 for a verbatim vector-store control), and agents then followed these manufactured facts to grant unauthorized access at high rates (e.g., 0.69–0.75 in the natural staleness condition and 0.72 with no defense in the injection mix).

Agent decisions were driven by the confidence of the phrasing rather than provenance: across five models, confident assertions produced the same unauthorized-grant rate (~0.81) whether bare, attributed, or forged as a “system of record,” while hedges collapsed grants (often to 0.00) without needing any special keywords.

Common mitigations failed in predictable ways: a passive “unverified” label leaked substantially and variably by provider (e.g., wrong-grant remained 0.77 on gpt-4o-mini and qwen-72b), while an active “do not trust” instruction reduced wrong decisions to 0.00 only by forcing blanket escalation on correct memories (false-escalation 1.00), and discrimination was restored only when a redundant authoritative source was available (wrong-grant 0.00 with no escalation).

nodes.title: Antaeus: Hunting Repository-Level Logic Vulnerabilities via Context-Grounded LLM Reasoning
nodes.one_liner: The key win is turning logic-vulnerability detection into repository-specific invariant recovery—grounding LLM reasoning in explicit code evidence and then using peer-comparisons to separate real anomalies from pervasive coding conventions.
points: A context-grounded, repository-scale pipeline detected 15 of 28 confirmed C/C++ logic vulnerabilities (~54% recall) in CWE-200/CWE-284, beating the strongest compared baseline at 4 of 28 (~14%) under similar cost constraints.

Lightweight repository-wide function prioritization reduced detailed LLM analysis from 149,758 in-scope functions to 4,859 analyzed functions (a 30.8× reduction), showing that high-recall ranking can bound audit cost without eliminating most discoveries.

Comparative validation pruned recurring “project-norm” concerns without losing true positives, cutting false positives by 20% (1,682→1,345) with Opus 4.7 and by 26% (3,927→2,918) with GPT-5.4—evidence that anomaly-style cross-sink checking materially improves triage precision for logic bugs.

nodes.title: An Empirical Study of Security Calibration in Large Language Models for Code
nodes.one_liner: LLM confidence is a poor safety signal for secure coding—especially in real repositories—because high-confidence outputs are frequently wrong, and the mismatch gets dramatically worse once cross-file build/test realities enter the loop.
points: Across 36k+ security-critical code generations, all evaluated code LLMs were systematically overconfident about security (verbalized security ECE: GPT‑4o‑mini ≈0.46–0.48, Gemini‑2.0‑Flash ≈0.25–0.26, Qwen3‑Coder‑Next ≈0.41–0.42), producing high-confidence vulnerable outputs at notable rates (False Trust at p≥0.8: 33.9%, 17.5%, and 38.3% respectively).

Functional self-assessment was consistently less reliable than security self-assessment (e.g., Gemini functional ECE ≈0.42–0.44 vs security ECE ≈0.16–0.17; Qwen functional ECE ≈0.77–0.78 vs security ECE ≈0.24–0.25), implying runtime/execution uncertainty dominates model confidence errors more than vulnerability-pattern uncertainty.

Calibration and trustworthiness collapsed in repository-level patching: average ECE jumped to ≈0.70–0.73 and False Trust rose to ≈70–83% (e.g., GPT False Trust 16.9%→83.2%), with decomposition attributing 45–82% of the degradation to build fragility and the remainder to cross-file complexity even when builds succeeded.

nodes.title: EnclaveX: End-to-End Confidential AI with CPU/GPU TEEs
nodes.one_liner: A practical CPU+GPU TEE pipeline shows that the real performance tax in confidential LLM inference is protected CPU↔GPU I/O, while app-level attestation adds ~1% latency and meaningfully reduces Kubernetes-admin power over secrets.
points: End-to-end confidential LLM inference that spans Intel TDX CPU TEEs and NVIDIA H200 confidential GPUs can be deployed in Kubernetes while keeping application secrets inaccessible even to a fully privileged K8s administrator (e.g., blocking key release until app-level attestation succeeds and disabling in-guest memory dumping).

On an H200, enabling confidential compute inside a TDX CVM imposes substantial inference penalties versus non-confidential native execution—throughput drops by 35.0%–62.8%, inter-token latency increases by 35.2%–73.9%, and time-to-first-token rises by 11.2%–38.3%—with overhead shrinking as batch size or input length increases, indicating CPU↔GPU protected I/O as the dominant bottleneck.

Adding SCONE-based application-level attestation on top of native TDX+cGPU attestation increases total attestation latency from 1.1611s to ~1.1758s (~1.27% overhead), showing that stronger end-to-end trust chains can be achieved with near-zero incremental startup cost relative to baseline platform attestation.

nodes.title: CAREBench: A Child-Safety Risk Benchmark for Language Models
nodes.one_liner: A benchmark that targets the pre-CSAM, pre-explicit phase of harm shows some frontier LLMs still provide scripts, tactics, or relational reinforcement that can materially escalate child risk long before content becomes overtly illegal.
points: Across 500 upstream child-safety prompts spanning 12 risk categories, seven frontier LLMs showed large safety variance with failure rates ranging from 2.3% to 58.0%, implying that current child-safety behavior is highly model-dependent rather than a solved, industry-wide baseline.

The automated MultiJudge grading pipeline matched human sensitivity about as well as humans match each other (Cohen’s κ=0.55 vs parent–parent κ=0.52) and its acceptability verdicts aligned with human pairwise preferences 89.3% of the time, suggesting LLM-ensemble judging can be a practical, reproducible proxy for caregiver/clinician judgments in this domain.

Even the strongest model still failed notably in relational/mental-health-adjacent categories (e.g., one model’s remaining failures concentrated in therapist-replacement 26% and emotional-dependency 17%), while other models frequently produced highly actionable harmful artifacts (e.g., code/scripts for coercion or impersonation), indicating that “refusal on explicit abuse” is insufficient to prevent earlier-stage grooming, isolation, surveillance, and dependency escalation.

nodes.title: Safety Testing LLM Agents at Scale: From Risk Discovery to Evidence-Grounded Verification
nodes.one_liner: Executable test cases with deterministic, environment-grounded oracles make agent safety evaluation both scalable and brutally revealing—showing that adaptive, multi-turn adversaries can reliably drive real tool-mediated harm.
points: An automated, executable safety-testing pipeline for tool-using LLM agents can uncover severe real-world failure modes at scale, with multi-channel attacks achieving an average 93.9% verified success rate across four production agent frameworks.

Combinatorially composing risk × attack-method × environment taxonomies yielded 1,600 replayable safety cases spanning 124 risk categories and maintained broad executability (first-level average ESRs ~79.0%–95.3% across risk groups), indicating coverage can scale without hand-authoring each scenario.

Evidence-grounded verification that prioritizes environment-state changes over tool-call intent and model self-report enables deterministic, manipulation-resistant labeling, revealing a capability–vulnerability tension where higher task competence correlates with higher attack success (e.g., overall ESR 88.6% for Claude Code vs. 70.3% for OpenClaw under identical scenarios).

nodes.title: (A)I Sees What You Don't: Exploiting New Attack Surfaces in Third-Party Mobile Agents
nodes.one_liner: Mobile VLM agents turn “invisible” pixels and repurposed debug/IPC channels into a practical path from unprivileged on-device influence to full host-PC command execution.
points: Across five popular third‑party Android mobile-agent frameworks, every system was vulnerable to at least 6 of 7 tested attacks, showing that the perception–decision–action pipeline creates systemic, agent-specific attack surfaces beyond traditional app threats.

Subliminal visual prompt injection is highly reliable: six evaluated VLM backends extracted low-opacity overlay text at 2–20% opacity with 90–100% success (18/20 to 20/20), enabling instruction hijacking that is effectively invisible to users.

Host compromise is feasible via attack chaining: screenshot TOCTOU gaps of 50–500 ms (≈210 ms average) plus unsafe host command construction enabled 100% (20/20) host-side code execution on 4/5 frameworks, sometimes requiring no Android permissions for data theft (broadcast interception) and only common permissions (overlay/storage/accessibility) for full escalation.

nodes.title: Memory as an Attack Surface in LLM Agents: A Study on Multiple-Choice Question Answering
nodes.one_liner: Agent memory turns past interactions into a persistent, stealthy injection channel that can measurably flip MCQ answers and bias choice selection even when the current question is benign.
points: Across 1,064 MCQs, inserting false information into an agent’s external memory caused answer changes in 7.80% of cases (82/1,064), demonstrating that “clean” prompts can still yield corrupted outputs via retrieved prior state.

Model choice strongly determines memory-attack sensitivity: the false-memory answer-shift rate ranged from 0.00–0.91% for GPT-5.4 Mini to as high as 34.48% for Phi3-14B (cybersecurity), implying open models in this setup were markedly more brittle to memory poisoning.

Targeted option steering is more effective via post-answer reinforcement than biased-example exposure, with feedback increasing selection of the attacker-chosen option C by up to +12.07 percentage points (Phi3-14B, cybersecurity) versus up to +8.62 points from example biasing, indicating that “retry with feedback” loops are a high-leverage control point for attackers.

nodes.title: UA-ChatDev: Uncertainty-Aware Multi-Agent Collaboration for Reliable Software Development
nodes.one_liner: Token-logprob uncertainty gates when multi-agent software teams should retrieve and verify, substantially improving completeness/consistency and especially code executability at the cost of higher token and time budgets.
points: On the 1,200-task SRDD benchmark, UA-ChatDev achieved the best Overall Quality score (Q=0.649 with Qwen2.5-Coder 7B and Q=0.596 with Gemma 2 9B) versus ChatDev’s Q=0.395, indicating uncertainty-triggered verification materially improves end-to-end software generation reliability.

Uncertainty quantification notably boosted execution reliability, with executability rising from 0.779 to 0.859 (+8.0 points) for Qwen2.5 and from 0.794 to 0.840 (+4.6 points) for Gemma 2, consistent with reducing propagation of early-phase hallucinations into runnable code failures.

The reliability gains come with measurable overhead: compared to ChatDev (≈148s, ≈22.9k tokens), UA-ChatDev consumed ≈35.7k–40.5k tokens and ≈280–306s due to selective retrieval and extra refinement loops, highlighting a practical accuracy–latency tradeoff for agentic software pipelines.

nodes.title: Truth or Sophistry? LoFa: A Benchmark for LLM Robustness Against Logical Fallacies
affiliations: Shenzhen International Graduate School, Tsinghua University
nodes.one_liner: Even state-of-the-art LLMs that “know” the right answer can be talked out of it by semantic misdirection—especially equivocation and fabricated authority—making fallacy resistance a distinct, measurable safety surface beyond factual accuracy.
points: LoFa introduces an objective, ground-truth QA benchmark of 1,952 questions paired with 10 fallacy-based persuasive arguments each (19,492 total attacks) plus a multi-round debate protocol and the LFR@k metric to isolate persuasion-induced failures from baseline knowledge gaps.

Across datasets, distraction/distortion fallacies are disproportionately effective (e.g., Llama-3.1-405B reaches only 29.42% LFR@3 on Equivocation and 57.05% on Straw Man on average), while flaws-in-reasoning/evidence fallacies are resisted far better (e.g., the same model averages 88.07% on Slippery Slope and 92.95% on Circular Reasoning), implying robustness work should prioritize semantic misdirection defenses over pure logical-form checking.

Model size improves resistance but preserves “architectural fingerprints” (Llama-3.1 average LFR@3 rises from 59.75%→70.38%→77.17% for 8B→70B→405B), and prompting helps unevenly (GPT-4 CoT boosts LFR@3 by ~7–13% for most fallacies but slightly worsens Appeal to Authority by 1.87%), suggesting scaling/prompting alone won’t eliminate certain systematic vulnerabilities like authority deference (GPT-4 LFR@3=39.20% on AA in NQ1).

nodes.title: From Tool Connection to Execution Control: Benchmarking Security Invariants in MCP-Style Agent Runtimes
nodes.one_liner: Treating agent actions as capability invocations over principals, canonical resources, and owned data handles turns prompt- and UI-driven “approval” into a testable execution security boundary that can both block attacks and leave reliable forensic trails.
points: An execution-control runtime enforcing eight explicit invariants (e.g., grant-backed approval, canonical resources, principal/handle binding, bidirectional data-flow authorization, and deny-path audit) blocked 10/10 benchmarked MCP-style attack cases, while a naive connection-layer baseline allowed 10/10 and a practice-informed mitigation baseline still allowed 6/10.

Connection-layer mitigations (metadata linting, per-call prompts, session checks) mainly helped with identity/session failures (blocking 4/10), but did not prevent tool-poisoning, approval-fatigue authorization bypass, or cross-tool data exfiltration because they failed to bind approvals to grants, resources, capabilities, and handle ownership at execution time.

Ablations show prevention is driven primarily by runtime grant matching (exposes 6/10 cases when removed) plus smaller but critical gates for approval (2/10), protocol init/version (2/10 each), handle ownership (1/10), and data-pipe target policy (1/10), while removing deny-path audit caused forensic evidence loss in 10/10 cases even though blocking still occurred.

nodes.title: MMBench-Live: A Continuously Evolving Benchmark for Multimodal Models
affiliations: Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications
nodes.one_liner: A continuously updated VLM benchmark can be cheap, fast, and still preserve stable rankings while measurably dampening contamination-style memorization signals.
points: A multi-agent automated pipeline can refresh a multimodal benchmark in 1–2 hours for about $30 per update while generating 5.9K new instances at 96.06% manually verified answer correctness.

Cross-version comparability is largely preserved, with model-averaged performance correlating strongly between the original MMBench and MMBench-Live (Pearson r=0.8876; Spearman ρ=0.8286), implying live updates can stay “same-task” enough to track progress without resetting baselines.

Contamination-related memorization signals are reduced under a PaCoST confidence-shift proxy, where MMBench-Live shows roughly half the mean shift (0.0060 vs 0.0118) and lower effect size (Cohen’s d=0.059 vs 0.097), suggesting fresher real-world sampling plus executable verification can blunt leakage-driven score inflation.

nodes.title: Detecting Clinical Hallucinations in LVLMs via Counterfactual Visual Grounding Uncertainty
affiliations: National Institute of Healthcare Data Science at Nanjing University
nodes.one_liner: Using counterfactual prompts to force a grounding verifier into revealing spurious localization turns hallucination detection into an interpretable, model-agnostic uncertainty test that works across clinical LVLMs.
points: A plug-and-play clinical hallucination detector audits black-box LVLM outputs by extracting visually verifiable entities and grounding them with a medical-adapted Qwen3-VL-2B verifier, yielding both a hallucination decision and entity-level localization evidence without accessing the LVLM’s hidden states.

Counterfactual visual grounding uncertainty (penalizing factual grounding confidence by counterfactual confidence weighted by box IoU) is pivotal: removing the counterfactual branch collapses performance for the Monte-Carlo scoring variant from AUC 0.8811 to 0.3572 (below random), while removing IoU reweighting causes a smaller drop to AUC 0.8595.

On a 1,904-pair CT/MRI test set spanning four LVLM backbones, the method achieves very high MRI detection performance (HDR 91.93–96.81% with precision 90.10–93.88%) and maintains the best CT precision among compared baselines (up to 68.00%), indicating strong cross-model transfer and a safer false-positive profile than high-recall but low-precision detectors.

nodes.title: EgoSafetyBench: A Diagnostic Egocentric Video Benchmark for Evaluating Embodied VLMs as Runtime Safety Guards
nodes.one_liner: A matched-pair, contrastive-ladder egocentric video benchmark reveals that apparent “robust safety” can be either missed contextual hazards or indiscriminate alarming—especially under deceptive in-scene text.
points: Across 1,200 egocentric 5-second robot-view scenarios labeled every 0.5s, even top VLM guards reach 82–88% video-level balanced accuracy yet still miss 21–48% of unsafe half-second chunks, showing that “noticing a hazardous video” does not translate to reliably catching hazardous moments in time.

Context-dependent hazards are consistently harder than obvious hazards for every evaluated model, with a U1–U2 recall gap of 10.8–16.0 points for the strongest closed models and up to ~31 points for weaker open models, implying current guards over-rely on surface cues and underperform on state/relationship reasoning (e.g., placement, motion path, object state).

Misleading in-scene text/signals degrade all guards but in opposite ways: vulnerable open models flip from correct-to-missed on 18.7–22.4% of hazards when the sign lies (≈+12% video miss vs matched truthful controls), while stronger closed models largely resist hazard suppression (flip 1.8–3.6%) but sharply increase over-intervention on safe content when misleading text is present (safe-chunk false alarms rise by +20.6 to +23.6 points for Gemini-3.5-Flash and Gemini-3.1-Flash-Lite).

nodes.title: Online Safety Monitoring for LLMs
affiliations: UvA Bosch-Delta Lab, University of Amsterdam
nodes.one_liner: Risk-calibrated thresholding turns almost any safety score into an online “stop” rule with formal error control—and in practice it can detect unsafe generations earlier than heavier sequential-testing monitors.
points: A single time-invariant threshold on a streaming verifier score, calibrated via conformal risk control (CRC) or a high-probability UCB rule, achieves statistically controlled false-alarm rates while matching or beating more complex sequential e-process monitors on detection delay across factuality and harmlessness settings.

High-probability monitors (UCB and e-valuator variants) generally keep empirical false-alarm control across ε targets, but an anytime e-valuator violates the bound at ε ∈ {0.05, 0.1} on Mistral in the MATH factuality setup, illustrating that stronger-looking sequential methods can still miscalibrate in finite samples.

Monitoring quality is dominated by signal strength: a dedicated external verifier (PRM/SCM) yields much higher detection power (e.g., on MATH around ε≈0.3 the PRM-based monitors exceed 0.9 power while token-logprob signals are ~0.5), and safeguards not trained for the specific online task (Llama Guard on Anthropic Red Teaming) plateau below ~0.8 power even when false alarms are controlled.

nodes.title: kNNGuard: Turning LLM Hidden Activations into a Training-Free Configurable Guardrail
