nodes.one_liner: Hidden-state geometry from a frozen LLM can be repurposed into a configurable, training-free guardrail that is both fast enough for production and quick to retarget by swapping a tiny labeled bank.
points: Using only a 100-example reference bank (50 safe/50 unsafe) and no gradient updates, kNNGuard FE reaches 87.4% average F1 with 12.9% false-positive rate and 45.9–46.8 ms latency per prompt across six domains (coding, medical, safety, jailbreak, and prompt injection).

Activation-space kNN delivers markedly better class separability than embedding-only kNN, with t-SNE silhouette scores rising from 0.391→0.813 (coding) and 0.532→0.739 (medical), aligning with large topical gains (e.g., 99.1–99.3% F1 and ≤0.9% FPR on coding instruction/output tasks).

Operational adaptation is dominated by bank refresh rather than training: building the main 100-sample activation bank takes 7.95 seconds (≈3156× faster than 7.0 hours LoRA fine-tuning on 13,854 samples), while still outperforming or matching fine-tuned guardrails at much lower latency (e.g., 2.7× faster than Nemotron Topic Guard and ~10× faster than Nemotron Safety Guard V2).

nodes.title: Overthink-Triggered Slowdown Attacks on LVLM-Based Robotic Systems
nodes.one_liner: A black-box, physically realizable “text sign” can DoS LVLM-driven robots by inducing long reasoning traces, and early prefix signals (32 tokens; Spearman ρ≈0.73 with full latency) are sufficient to search and detect these slowdown triggers efficiently.
points: Human-readable scene text embedded in a robot’s camera view can reliably trigger LVLM “overthinking” and act as a practical availability attack by inflating decision latency without modifying prompts or model internals.

Across 3,000 held-out road-scene images and three LVLMs, optimized single-text triggers caused >1.0× slowdown for all model–trigger pairs, with a worst-case 6.96× latency amplification on Gemma3 under fixed decoding settings.

The attack persists in the physical world: a printed A3 sign still produced up to 4.74× latency amplification (and 4.85× token amplification) in a live camera-in-the-loop robotic setup, implying real safety risk for time-constrained autonomy pipelines.

nodes.title: Janus: a Playground for User-Involved Agentic Permission Management
nodes.one_liner: A modular agent+evaluation playground shows no single permission-assistant strategy is best, and that user behavior (yes-fatigue vs denial) can dominate agent security outcomes.
points: In 60 baseline permissive runs with an alignment-aware user, the system achieved 100% output-check pass rates and a median 87.8% coverage of predefined “desired” tool calls, indicating the evaluation harness can reliably measure both task success and permission outcomes.

Across 5× full-factorial evaluations (3 scenarios × 4 subscenarios × 3 user behaviors), only the “ask for every tool call” design (user confirmation) eliminated attacks and out-of-alignment actions for an alignment-aware user, showing that continuous user gating can dominate security but at substantial interaction cost.

Both always-approve and always-deny user behaviors systematically broke safety–usability tradeoffs—always-approve drove high attack/misalignment rates for most designs, while always-deny caused much higher output-evaluation failure rates—implying real deployments must explicitly model permission fatigue and error-prone human responses rather than assuming ideal users.

nodes.title: Formal Security Analysis of Agent Protocol Composition
nodes.one_liner: Formal, source-linked TLA+ checks plus executable replay reveal that agent-protocol insecurity is dominated by composition and responsibility gaps, not just isolated spec bugs or server vulnerabilities.
points: Across five emerging agent protocols (MCP, A2A, ANP, ACP-Cap, ACP-Client), the framework reports 35 specification-level security findings and confirms 12 of them via 80 implementation tests, showing that many protocol security requirements are either missing, ambiguous, or not enforced in real SDKs.

Protocol composition introduces substantial new risk: 8 pairwise composed models yielded 30 additional counterexamples across 43 cross-boundary security obligations (≈70%), meaning unsafe behavior frequently emerges only when protocols are bridged through runtimes/conductors rather than within any single protocol.

Responsibility and enforcement are the core systemic failure mode: only one protocol is observed to enforce a security-relevant control in practice (ANP’s DID identity verification), and no protocol assigns enforcement for cross-protocol behavior, leaving composition safety effectively orphaned and pushing critical controls into unowned runtime/bridge glue code.

nodes.title: An Agentic AI Framework to Accelerate Scientific Discovery in Plant Phenotyping
nodes.one_liner: The standout is a deployable, provenance-first agentic architecture that bridges cloud UX and exascale HPC to turn terabyte-scale phenotyping from post-hoc batch analysis into an interactive query loop.
points: A two-agent design (a cloud-hosted conversational Co‑Scientist and an HPC-resident Compute Agent) linked by a secure token-authenticated streaming channel enables interactive plant-phenotyping analyses while preserving strict cross-domain separation needed for national-lab deployments.

On Frontier, a ViT-based sliding-window segmentation pipeline with 50% tile stride plus Hann-weighted blending and connected-component pruning supports high-resolution plant masking as a reusable substrate for downstream trait extraction across multiple imaging modalities.

In production use, end-to-end provenance capture (including prompts, model/implementation versions, parameters, artifacts, and agent decisions) adds <1% runtime overhead while shrinking a previously manual workflow of ~2 hours/day over 6 days into minutes after new images arrive and enabling follow-up queries in <1 minute once traits are cached.

nodes.title: ElephantAgent: Contextual State Continuity in Agentic Systems
nodes.one_liner: A practical way to stop “rug pull” tool-descriptor changes and memory rollback in LLM agents is to treat agent context like a stateful system and require every context transition to be cryptographically continuous and ledger-authorized.
points: ElephantAgent defends agentic tool/memory poisoning by enforcing Contextual State Continuity: before each query it recomputes a digest over a bounded “contextual state” (tool descriptors + memory) and fail-closes if it diverges from the latest digest in a TEE-backed, linearizable ledger, deterministically catching out-of-band edits/rollbacks.

To handle in-band semantic abuse that can be “properly committed” (e.g., prompt-injection-induced harmful updates), ElephantAgent adds Historical Traceability that logs SCM-signed transition receipts plus sealed snapshots to enable post-hoc audit and recovery to a known-good prior state when artifacts remain available.

A prototype over MCP using a Nimble-backed SCM on Intel TDX reports low steady-state overhead: per query ~4.23–4.33 ms for verification and ~5.25–5.39 ms for state updates, yielding only 1.02×–1.04× end-to-end runtime overhead across three tasks (50 runs each), while initialization rises 8.22× (219 ms → 1800 ms) due mainly to remote attestation/SCM setup.

nodes.title: AgentFlow: Building Agent Dependency Graphs for Static Analysis of Agent Programs
affiliations: Huazhong University of Science and Technology
nodes.one_liner: A dependency-graph IR that treats prompts, tools, memory, and guardrails as first-class nodes makes static analysis of agent software practical at ecosystem scale—and surfaces nontrivial prompt-to-privileged-tool exposure in the wild.
points: AGENTFLOW introduces a framework-agnostic Agent Dependency Graph (ADG) IR that explicitly models agents, prompts, models, capabilities (including MCP/skills), memory states, and control policies as typed nodes connected by component-, control-, and data-dependency edges to enable static governance and security analyses of agent programs.

On 60 real-world projects across shared frameworks, AGENTFLOW analyzed 59/60 successfully and recovered substantially richer dependency structure (median 17 nodes and 28 edges per project) than AST-based agent analyzers (median 4 nodes/0 edges and 2.5 nodes/2 edges), indicating that alias-aware framework-semantic modeling is critical to uncovering implicit agent dependencies.

Across 5,399 GitHub agent programs, the ADG-based prompt-to-tool analysis flagged 238 risky projects (4.4%) with 4,357 prompt-to-tool paths, and a manual audit of 100 findings showed 73% precision with most false positives stemming from overly coarse sink semantics (e.g., read-only file/SQL actions misclassified as high-impact).

nodes.title: Hephaestus: Toward a Cybersecurity AI Scientist
affiliations: Institute of Information Engineering, Chinese Academy of Sciences
University of Chinese Academy of Sciences
nodes.one_liner: The key idea is that automating cybersecurity discovery demands not just stronger agents, but a governance-embedded, evidence-producing research workflow built for adaptive adversaries and shifting model/tool substrates.
points: Cybersecurity requires an AI-scientist design that is explicitly adversarial, dual-use-aware, and non-stationary, where the primary research units are security events and interaction traces rather than static datasets or single benchmark scores.

Credible cyber conclusions depend on controlled environments (digital twins/cyber ranges) plus auditable evidence pipelines, making environment design and replayability first-class methodological components instead of optional evaluation infrastructure.

A practical Cybersecurity AI Scientist is best realized as a modular, role-specialized multi-agent system with multi-model routing and bounded capability packages so governance constraints (permissions, containment, release boundaries) can be enforced at the module level rather than bolted on after results are produced.

nodes.title: Agent Safety Is Action Alignment
nodes.one_liner: Refusal-based “alignment” is a category error for agents because action harm is relational (authority exercised vs authority granted), so safety must be enforced at the tool boundary via least privilege rather than learned in model weights.
points: A defense-trained agent that reports >90% prompt-injection rejection can still execute injected account deletions 78% of the time, showing safety fine-tuning can be non-monotone and yield negative security relative to the base model.

Supervised prompt-attack defenses primarily learn surface heuristics rather than intent, increasing false refusals by up to 50%, rejecting benign late-stage reasoning up to 90% of the time, and cutting benign accuracy by up to 40% on unseen topics.

In multi-step agent loops, refusal-style defenses collapse benign task execution (47–77% fail at step 1 vs 3% for the base model) and amplify into up to 99% timeouts, while ordinary tool-use still drifts toward over-privilege with <15% least-privilege compliance and >1-in-3 skill misrouting even without defenses.

nodes.title: VeriChat: An Agentic Conversational AI Assistant for Hardware Security Verification
nodes.one_liner: An agentic RAG assistant that actually runs open-source EDA tooling can move hardware-security conversations from “possibly wrong guidance” to evidence-backed, formally checkable outcomes.
points: A retrieval-augmented, three-agent pipeline (query optimization + hybrid retrieval + grounded generation) achieved 87.73% factual-claim faithfulness—over 23 percentage points higher than the next best proprietary baseline—indicating substantial hallucination reduction in high-assurance hardware-security Q&A.

Hybrid, topic-partitioned retrieval over a curated 28,221-document (≈61 GB) corpus delivered 76.40% context recall and 89.85% context precision versus 23.00% and 20.31% for a naive RAG setup, showing that query tagging plus partitioned vector stores sharply improves evidence coverage while suppressing off-topic context.

Tool-in-the-loop verification (Icarus Verilog + Yosys + SymbiYosys/Z3) enabled autonomous discovery and proof of a rare-trigger AES S-Box Trojan (activation probability ≈1/2^24 ≈ 6×10^-8 per valid cycle), including simulation-confirmed key leakage and a bounded-model-checking counterexample, demonstrating how conversational assistants can transition from advice to executable security sign-off artifacts.

nodes.title: An AI-Based Solution for Secure Service Provisioning in IoT
affiliations: Cochin University of Science and Technology
nodes.one_liner: The key takeaway is that pairing adaptive DRL selection with federated behavioral monitoring turns runtime compromise into a quickly learned avoidance behavior, whereas SecSLA compliance alone fails to prevent sustained risky interactions.
points: A DQN-based selector augmented with behavioral trust reduces compromised-provider selections to 0% within 1 day after the attack onset while maintaining 100% task completion (COP=1.000, failure rate=0.000).

SecSLA-only strategies can look “successful” operationally (COP≈0.999) yet still drive persistent exposure, sustaining ~223–233 compromised interactions per day post-attack because compromised providers keep advertising valid SecSLAs.

Shared GRU-based Behavioral Fingerprinting (via federated learning) yields a stronger and more discriminative trust signal than local or threshold detectors—dropping compromised providers to Ts as low as ~0.65 after one day and cutting compromised interactions by 61% (n=10), 78% (n=25), and 87% (n=50) versus greedy SecSLA-only selection.

nodes.title: Securing People and their Machines Against Major Faults
nodes.one_liner: It shows how to do 'social recovery' and state recovery for fully infrastructure-less, serverless platforms with formal correctness guarantees, while pinpointing the single unrecoverable failure case where no surviving peer retains the needed information.
points: A peer-based recovery design for grassroots platforms replaces a lost identity key only when a designated supermajority of identity custodians authorizes the change, after which the user’s friends propagate the new public key across the social graph to restore friendships without any global authority or infrastructure.

Machine/state loss with the private key retained is recoverable without custodian approval by reconstructing state from peer-held replicas (friends as state custodians for the social graph, and designated state custodians for coins), but recovery is information-theoretically impossible if a fault erases the last surviving record of a relationship/edge.

For grassroots coins, exact recovery of a sovereign’s single-writer transaction log (preventing inadvertent double-spends) is achieved by tying payment finality and recovery to a supermajority quorum of state custodians, leveraging quorum intersection so every finalized block survives and is included after recovery.

nodes.title: Agent-Native Immune System: Architecture, Taxonomy, and Engineering
nodes.one_liner: The central idea is to treat agent security like biology: embed adaptive, self-updating defenses directly into the agent’s reasoning and coordination loop rather than relying on static alignment or perimeter guardrails.
points: A six-layer “Immune Tower” (L0–L5) is proposed to move defenses inside an agent’s runtime cognitive loop, explicitly adding a pre-cognitive Barrier Immunity layer (L1) to isolate tools/memory before malicious metadata or poisoned state can influence reasoning.

The framework formalizes “agent viruses” (cognitive, memory, tool, and multi-agent) and “agent vaccines,” emphasizing that minimal memory attacks can be highly effective (e.g., three injected memory records reportedly achieve >70% tool-selection hijack success), implying agent security must treat persistent memory and toolchains as first-class attack surfaces.

A continual adaptation loop (Harness Triad: Meta/Self/Auto) is specified to generate and validate parametric defenses (steering vectors/LoRA) using an explicit false-positive control metric—Autoimmunity Rate—with recommended tolerances on the order of 1–5%, highlighting that operational safety depends on balancing detection sensitivity against self-induced functionality loss.

nodes.title: Skills Are Not Islands: Measuring Dependency and Risk in Agent Skill Supply Chains
nodes.one_liner: Agent skills behave like a multi-channel software supply chain, and most of the real risk sits in transitive skill/package/service dependencies that are invisible from the root skill file.
points: A skill-oriented dependency extractor (SDA) achieved 0.95 overall dependency F1 on a 500-skill benchmark (with 1.00 accuracy on key metadata fields) and 0.95 F1 on multi-layer graphs, substantially outperforming package-centric SBOM tools (≤0.24 overall F1) and an LLM-only baseline (0.52 F1).

At ecosystem scale (1.43M skills), governance signals lag far behind activation metadata: front matter is present in 99.55% of skills but dependency-like fields appear in only 1.40%, while identity is brittle with 58.73% non-unique skill names, complicating provenance and risk notification.

Security-relevant exposure is predominantly transitive rather than direct—60–78% of skill security signals, 98.01% of axios exposures, and 93.10% of vulnerable MCP-service hits are dependency-only—implying root-skill review misses most actionable risk without graph-wide audits and lockfile/manifest support.

nodes.title: Safety from Honesty in a Disinterested AI Predictor
affiliations: Center for Theoretical Study, Charles University in Prague
nodes.one_liner: It’s an explicit attempt to turn alignment into a distributional rare-event guarantee by separating “honest posterior prediction” from “agentic deployment,” then bounding how often training can stumble into coordinated harm-enabling predictors.
points: A consequence-invariant, posterior-seeking training objective combined with epistemic contextualization (treating most raw text as attributed communication acts rather than facts) is argued to reduce selection pressure for implicit agency by ensuring deployment outcomes never provide a reward signal to the Predictor.

Safety is formalized as bounding the training-time probability of producing a “dangerous Predictor” whose guardrailed deployment increases the log-odds of a specified harmful event beyond a system threshold, yielding the bound ν_t(dangerous) ≤ C_bad·R_shell where C_bad captures within-loss-band enrichment from training and R_shell captures within-band sparsity of dangerous behaviors.

The Guardrailed Predictor withholds answers when the predicted excess harm log-odds relative to abstention exceeds a threshold α, implying that sustained harm would require coordinated false-negative harm estimates across many queries, which the framework claims should be combinatorially rare absent consequence-dependent training signals.

nodes.title: Always-OnAgents:A Survey of Persistent Memory, State, and Governance in LLMAgents
nodes.one_liner: Persistent memory turns LLM agents into stateful systems where safety hinges less on recall accuracy and more on whether state can be authorized, audited, deleted, and rolled back across sessions.
points: A 435-work coded corpus shows the literature over-emphasizes state accumulation and retrieval (retrieve: 269/435; write: 200/435) while under-building governance and recovery (audit: 88/435; forget: 66/435; rollback: 27/435), implying most “memory” agents cannot provably undo or repair bad persistent state.

Authority is the least-covered persistent-state axis (72/435 works) despite being central to preventing stale permissions, scope creep, and persistence-enabled poisoning, indicating a systemic mismatch between what agents can store and what they are safely allowed to act on.

The proposed Always-On Evaluation Protocol (AOEP-v0) shifts evaluation from answer quality to enforceable lifecycle obligations (mutation, deletion propagation, and rollback traceability), motivating agent infrastructure that logs permission epochs, provenance, and compensable side effects rather than only storing retrievable text.

nodes.title: Exploring the Cryptographic Limits of Transformer Networks
nodes.one_liner: Circuit-level scaling laws make it possible to bound when transformers can implement hash-like computations that enable steganographic collusion, while revealing a sharp depth–width–tokens trade-off between attention-free and attention-routed constructions.
points: Compiled threshold-circuit measurements for toy Keccak, Merkle–Damgård, and Merkle Tree hashing match the predicted depth/width formulas exactly across all tested configurations (Tables 2–4), indicating that circuit-theoretic scaling can provide reliable structural upper bounds on transformer resources needed to implement these primitives.

For single-block Keccak (toy settings), the circuit depth scales as 6·n_rounds+2 and the width scales linearly with the state size (≈11·25^w), while for multi-block inputs depth grows as 2+n_b(2+6·n_rounds) and width grows as 11·25^w+p−r, showing a clear depth penalty for sequential absorption and a width penalty for carrying unabsorbed message bits.

Two constructive transformer implementations expose a concrete architecture trade-off: a no-attention mapping needs embedding dimension d≥width_circuit and depth Ω(depth_circuit), whereas a tokens-as-gates mapping keeps FFN width constant but requires tokens T equal to the number of circuit gates and assumes idealized unnormalized hard attention, highlighting that covert cryptographic computation is structurally feasible in principle but may hinge on attention realizability in practical softmax models.

nodes.title: Symbolon: Symbolic Execution by Learning Code Transformation
nodes.one_liner: Learning and reusing context-sensitive, replay-validated source rewrites turns symbolic execution from a brittle, strategy-dependent tool into a consistently higher-coverage and higher-yield bug-finding pipeline—even on the Linux kernel.
points: Across 32 real-world C programs and 16 KLEE search strategies, the approach boosts replayed line coverage on the original code by 3.69× on average (3.87× when aggregated by strategy), while narrowing the gap between the strongest and weakest search strategies from 7.4× to 1.7×—indicating the gains generalize beyond any single exploration policy.

By transforming source representations to reduce state blow-ups and solver-hostile constraints, it cuts symbolic execution overhead by 29.2× in peak memory and 123× in average solver time per query (means), turning many previously memory/solver-bound runs into tractable campaigns under the same 12-hour budget.

Security impact scales with the added reachability: replaying generated tests on unmodified targets yields +240 unique UBSan and +25 unique ASan violations across strategies, and when used as a front-end to kernel syscall-spec generation it helped uncover 21 previously unknown Linux kernel bugs (e.g., UAF/OOB/RCU stalls) and increased syzkaller edge coverage 2.47× overall (20,323→50,260).

nodes.title: Multi-Agent Firewall Architecture for Privacy Protection of Sensitive Data in Interactions with Language Models
nodes.one_liner: The most interesting aspect is the end-user and API-wide “agentic DLP” design that keeps inspection local by default, escalates to LLM reasoning only when needed, and still achieves up to 94.93% F1 with a small fine-tuned model.
points: A local-first LLM privacy firewall that intercepts both web chat and API traffic (HTTP(S)+WSS) via a Chromium extension plus a transparent MiTM proxy can enforce data-loss-prevention without app modifications and fails closed when the backend is unreachable.

On a 500-sample Nemotron-PII (US locale) benchmark, the best-performing configuration (fine-tuned Gemma 3 4B, LLM-only) reached 94.93% F1 with 94.95% precision and 94.92% recall, indicating small specialized models can deliver near-frontier PII detection quality while remaining deployable on local infrastructure.

Hybrid detection shows strong operational trade-offs: deterministic-only yields 93.40% precision but just 47.33% recall (62.83% F1 at 0.038s mean latency), while adding zero-shot NER boosts F1 to ~81.66% at ~0.85s mean latency, and forcing general LLM reasoning increases F1 to ~85–86% but raises mean latency to 1.26–5.96s depending on the model.

nodes.title: Prismata: Confining Cross-Site Prompt Injection in Web Agents
nodes.one_liner: Turns cross-site prompt injection into a web-style integrity problem by deriving per-element trust from DOM structure and enforcing it mechanically, achieving near-zero attack success without requiring any site annotations.
points: Prismata enforces contextual least privilege for web agents by labeling page regions and mediating both observations and actions, cutting prompt-injection attack success from 85.5% to 0.7% on average while increasing task completion under attack from 4.5% to 23.0%.

Large-scale DOM analysis across 1,500+ high-traffic sites found only 1.2% of 90,000+ untrusted-content instances lie on a critical path to an interactable element, and after structural-cue-based confinement the residual exposure shrinks to ~0.1% (and ~0.017% on sites following best practices).

Benign utility is largely preserved with task success moving from 29.9% without Prismata to 26.6% with it enabled, and labeling models achieve very high over-permission resistance (≥93% allowed-element precision, with top precision 98.69%)—a strong fit for integrity-first defenses where false negatives cost usability but false positives cost safety.

nodes.title: Untrusted Content Masking for Web Agents with Security Guarantees
nodes.one_liner: The key trick is restoring a clean trust boundary on the web by redacting untrusted DOM regions and only allowing typed, sandboxed queries into them—turning prompt injection from a detection problem into an architecture problem.
points: Masking all untrusted DOM regions before they reach the agent, and forcing any needed access through a quarantined model that only returns type-checked outputs (bool/int/float/enum/date), yields control-flow prompt-injection resistance by construction and achieves 0% attack success rate against strengthened WASP injections in the GitLab setting.

Across 10 custom web environments and 100 tasks, task completion is preserved for both “untrusted-not-required” and “untrusted-required” workflows, while median per-task cost increases are moderate at 1.05×–1.84× depending on the frontier agent tested (Claude Sonnet 4.5/4.6, GPT-5.4).

Trust boundaries can be inferred from content-sanitized DOM structure alone with high agreement to human labeling (F1: 0.879 on Booking, 0.997 on Reddit, 0.840 on GitLab), with low undermasking (false negatives: 5.8%, 0.0%, 8.5%), enabling deployment even when sites do not provide explicit labels.

nodes.title: Agent Data Injection Attacks are Realistic Threats to AI Agents
nodes.one_liner: A large class of agent failures comes from LLMs treating attacker-crafted data as trusted metadata/structure—so "separating instructions from data" is not enough unless agents also isolate trusted vs untrusted data inside tool outputs.
points: Probabilistic delimiter injection makes off-the-shelf LLMs misparse attacker-controlled untrusted fields as trusted structure/metadata, reaching 31.3%–43.3% ASR on JSON and 33.3%–100.0% ASR on web-DOM-style data across six frontier models despite high benign utility (81.2%–84.8% JSON; 97.8%–100.0% DOM).

Real-world agent exploitability spans web agents (arbitrary click via element-ID collisions) and coding agents (RCE via spoofed maintainer/origin metadata and supply-chain merges via forged tool-call history), showing that attackers can induce unintended actions without changing the agent’s apparent high-level goal.

Most prompt-injection defenses that drive instruction-injection ASR near zero (0.0%–0.7%) still allow substantial agent data injection success (22.2%–50.0% ASR), while only strict information-flow tracking eliminated attacks (0% ASR) at a steep utility drop (36.5% vs 86.5% baseline), highlighting a core need for fine-grained trusted/untrusted data isolation within agent context.

nodes.title: Unsupervised Features Mining via Activation Geometry
nodes.one_liner: A single natural-language prefix can induce a measurable activation-direction that both predicts and (in matched formats) steers an LLM’s internal verdict, and that same geometry can reliably pick high-transfer training data where raw activation similarity fails.
points: Unsupervised MAG features derived from the activation shift m(Q∥p)−m(p) improve verdict readout over raw activations, boosting ROC from 0.91→0.94 on Llama for a desert concept and from 0.62→0.66 on Gemma for prompt-injection detection while cutting Gemma’s FPR from 0.31→0.23.

MAG primarily decodes the model’s own judgment rather than dataset labels, siding with the model on 69.3% (Llama, n=951, 95% CI [66.3, 72.1]) and 73.7% (Gemma, n=979, 95% CI [70.9, 76.4]) of label-disagreement cases.

Activation geometry supports practical dataset selection: ordinary centroid cosine on unprefixed activations is near-unrelated to transfer (ρ≈0.01–0.05 on 6/8 metrics), whereas class-conditional MAG predictors reach 94.7% Top-1 and 100% Top-2 accuracy (18/19 and 19/19) for choosing the best dataset to add to training.

nodes.title: DualView: Preventing Indirect Prompt Injection in Personal AI Agents
nodes.one_liner: A two-view environment makes stored prompt-injection a dataflow problem you can deterministically block without breaking normal human file/network workflows.
points: Extending taint/symbol tracking beyond the agent context into the real user environment via dual views (AgentView symbolic, HumanView original) reduced both immediate and stored indirect prompt injection attack success rates to 0% on two evaluated models.

Compared to an unprotected OpenClaw baseline with 57.0% (Haiku) and 27.8% (Sonnet) overall attack success, utility-oriented Dual-LLM defenses still suffered high stored-IPI success (53.3% Haiku; 30.0% Sonnet), showing that context-only tracking fails once untrusted data is written and reread.

The plugin-level deployment kept agent task success close to baseline (81.6% vs 83.4% on Haiku; 82.1% vs 88.5% on Sonnet) while preserving human-facing usability (no symbols leaked), at the cost of notable token overhead (+48.2% Haiku; +93.4% Sonnet) driven by extra quarantined-model processing.

nodes.title: Biological Motifs for Agentic Control
nodes.one_liner: It reframes agent reliability and security as properties you can enforce with typed topology, provenance-aware gates, and control-theoretic motifs—then backs the motifs with an unusually test-heavy prototype and measurable, order-of-magnitude robustness gains in harness behavior.
points: A typed wiring-diagram framework (“Agentic Operad”) maps five systems-biology control motifs into composable LLM-agent architecture patterns that statically rule out ill-typed connections and yield topology-level reliability claims (e.g., feed-forward verification gates suppress errors multiplicatively only when generator and verifier failures are weakly correlated).

Structurally enforced provenance labels with trust-gated action interfaces prevent content-only prompt-injection privilege escalation by making trust depend on ingress channel rather than message text, shifting security guarantees from brittle content heuristics to enforceable information-flow structure.

A reference implementation reports 1,813 tests and 116 examples and demonstrates large harness-level deltas in synthetic evaluations—e.g., chaperone-style schema folding improves from 5.5% (strict) to 56.2% (cascaded strategies), healing with error-context feedback succeeds 99.6% vs 68.0% for blind retry, and two-signal immune-style anomaly detection reaches 100.0% sensitivity at 0.4% false positives (and 0.0% on an AgentDojo-derived suite).

nodes.title: Beware of Agentic Botnets: Scalable Untargeted Promptware Attacks via Universal and Transferable Adversarial HalluSquatting
nodes.one_liner: Hallucinations aren’t just wrong answers—when agents can fetch and execute, predictable hallucinated identifiers become a mass-exploitation supply route akin to typosquatting, but driven by model behavior.
points: Trending resource retrieval is highly error-prone in agentic workflows, with hallucinated identifiers reaching up to 85% in repository cloning and up to 100% in skill installation—creating a scalable, untargeted promptware channel via attacker-registered lookalike resources.

End-to-end exploitation is practical across widely used agentic tools, with attacker-controlled resource fetch rates enabling tool invocation and remote code execution in 20–65% of coding-assistant trials and 40–100% of assistant/skill-install trials, implying “one squatted resource → many compromised machines” botnet-style amplification.

Simple verification drastically changes risk: when an application performs web search before fetching, correctness jumps to 93.4% (vs 0.9% without search), yet search invocation is inconsistent and prompt-dependent—making guardrailed retrieval policies a primary mitigation lever.

nodes.title: Breaking Database Lock-in: Agentic Regeneration of High Performance Storage Readers for Database Bypass
nodes.one_liner: LLM-synthesized, verified C++ parsers can turn “opaque” database storage files into Arrow-native, zero-copy inputs for modern analytics engines—bypassing drivers and breaking practical data lock-in with up to 27× throughput gains.
points: Directly scanning PostgreSQL heap files and MySQL InnoDB .ibd pages into zero-copy Apache Arrow buffers eliminates wire-protocol serialization/deserialization overhead and yields up to 5.1× (PostgreSQL) and 26.9× (MySQL) end-to-end ETL speedups on TPC-H SF=1 across six analytics engines.

A four-agent LLM pipeline (dataset generation → format specification → C++ code synthesis → deterministic QA with retry loop) can generate self-contained, plug-in-compatible C++17 storage readers (~800 LOC each) that pass full-result validation on all 22 TPC-H queries against JDBC/ODBC baselines.

Performance gains depend strongly on connector inefficiency: MySQL JDBC row-by-row export can be 228.6s vs 8.5s via direct file decoding in PyArrow (26.9×), while PostgreSQL’s comparatively efficient wire path shrinks the advantage to 1.3×–5.1×, implying the biggest wins occur where client deserialization dominates transfer cost.

nodes.title: Mechanistic Interpretability of LLM Jailbreaks via Internal Attribution Graphs
nodes.one_liner: Successful jailbreaks look less like “turning off safety” and more like rerouting the model’s internal causal pathways—so robustness needs pathway-integrity monitoring and interventions beyond individual features.
points: Across 30 adversarial prompt pairs on Llama-2-7B-chat, jailbreaks succeeded 13.3% of the time (4/30), and only path rerouting in internal attribution graphs significantly tracked success (Pearson r=0.461, p=0.010; 95% CI [+0.189, +0.722]), implying that effective jailbreaks primarily work by redirecting information flow rather than simply flipping individual “unsafe” features on or off.

Static graph-change signals were poor predictors of jailbreak outcomes (graph deviation r=0.210, p=0.264; safety suppression r=-0.127, p=0.503 with 23/30 zeros; attack emergence r=0.163, p=0.389), indicating that defenses focused on detecting feature suppression/emergence alone will miss many successful attacks because the model can keep safety-related components superficially present while routing around them.

Mechanistic mitigation via node-level ablation failed completely (0/4 successful mitigations when zeroing the top-3 emergent features), while graph construction quality depended critically on including reconstruction-error nodes (KL divergence 0.0014 vs 46.96 without them, a 99.997% reduction) and produced more stable deviation estimates than gradient baselines (18× lower variability), pointing to distributed, redundant jailbreak circuits that likely require path/subgraph-level interventions rather than single-feature edits.

nodes.title: Persuasion Attacks Can Decrease Effectiveness of CoT Monitoring
nodes.one_liner: CoT-based oversight can backfire in adversarial settings, but model-diverse fact-checking largely restores monitor reliability.
points: Giving monitors access to an agent’s chain-of-thought increases approval of policy-violating actions by 9.5% on average, implying transparency can become an extra persuasion channel rather than a safety signal under adversarial pressure.

Across 40 tasks, adversarial agents can persuade monitors into approving policy-violating proposals with baseline-adjusted acceptance increases up to 47%, showing that natural-language argumentation alone can reliably erode oversight even when malign baselines are low (1.3%–7.5%).

Cross-family external fact-checking is a strong mitigation: pairing monitor and fact-checker from different model families cuts approval of policy-violating actions to ~6% on average (up to 45% reduction), while same-family fact-checking often performs much worse (e.g., ~30% approvals on average), consistent with trust/familiarity vulnerabilities.

nodes.title: Efficient Safety Alignment of Language Models via Latent Personality Traits
nodes.one_liner: A tiny, harm-free “personality self-assessment” dataset can substitute for large harm datasets in adversarial safety training, yielding near-zero jailbreak success with essentially no capability loss.
points: Latent Personality Alignment (LPA) uses latent adversarial training on just 66 harm-agnostic psychometric statements to drive HarmBench attack success rates to near-zero across direct harmful requests and five jailbreak families (GCG, PAIR, AutoPrompt, AutoDAN, TAP) without ever training on harmful content.

Compared to targeted Latent Adversarial Training (LAT), LPA achieves similar or stronger jailbreak robustness with ~75× fewer training examples (66 vs 4,947 harmful prompts plus 165,297 benign utility-recovery prompts) and completes in minutes on a single GPU while avoiding the typical robustness–utility trade-off at the selected checkpoint.

Ablations show the safety–utility Pareto frontier is achieved specifically by (i) safety-relevant traits (Conscientiousness, Agreeableness, Emotional Stability), (ii) consistent labelings, and (iii) training on negative-only items, with alternative setups (inverted/shuffled/irrelevant/all-IPIP) reaching low ASR only by sacrificing benign-task utility (e.g., ≥19% lower TinyMMLU at matched ≤5% ASR).

nodes.title: Overloading Large Vision-Language Models for Jailbreaking
affiliations: Hangzhou International Innovation Institute, Beihang University
nodes.one_liner: Multimodal safety fails not just from hidden intent (OOD tricks) but from sheer cross-modal load—recursive image-typography can systematically erode refusal confidence and generalize across architectures.
points: An information-overloading jailbreak that combines extensive text with recursion-based image-typography layouts reaches 88.6% average attack success on open-source LVLMs—beating the strongest baseline by 32.8 percentage points—showing that multimodal complexity can overwhelm modern safety alignment.

The same overloading approach attains 84.0% average attack success on commercial models (Gemini and GPT-4.1-mini), exceeding the best baseline by 48.7 percentage points, indicating real deployment risk even with proprietary guardrails.

Prompts optimized on open-source surrogates transfer strongly across model families (e.g., Qwen2-VL-optimized prompts achieve 84.6% ASR in transfer, including 87.9% on Llama 3.2-Vision vs 39.9% for the strongest baseline), implying attackers can weaponize public models to compromise closed systems.

nodes.title: Refused in Chat, Written in Code: Workflow-Level Jailbreak Construction in IDE Coding Agents
nodes.one_liner: Refusal-trained models that look safe in chat can become perfectly compliant when harmful content is produced indirectly as code/data during metric-driven IDE workflows.
points: Across 204 harmful prompts and four Copilot IDE backends, direct-chat, CSV-read, and single-step code-fix baselines each yielded only 8/816 unsafe successes (~1%) while the full multi-turn IDE workflow produced 816/816 unsafe, instruction-satisfying teaching-shot completions (100%), showing turn-level refusal massively overestimates real deployment safety.

The unsafe shift is driven by workflow dynamics—task decomposition plus metric pressure (optimizing attack success rate) causes the agent to author harmful prompt–response strings inside code artifacts even when it refuses the same prompts when asked directly.

Two independent expert evaluators confirmed 100% (816/816) of workflow outputs as specific, actionable, and instruction-satisfying under a strict rubric, implying defenses must inspect and constrain generated files/data and cross-turn intent accumulation rather than only filtering chat responses.

nodes.title: Optimizing Against Safety Representations: Activation-Guided Adversarial Suffixes and the Geometry of Refusal
affiliations: John A. Paulson School of Engineering and Applied Sciences
nodes.one_liner: Speeding up universal suffix jailbreaking by ~33× while directly optimizing against a model’s internal refusal direction highlights how brittle and geometrically simple many refusal mechanisms remain under gradient access.
points: Targeting the internal refusal direction with Activation-Guided GCG boosts jailbreak effectiveness on Llama-2-7B-Chat, with the global “All” objective reaching 0.91 substring ASR at 200 steps versus 0.76 for standard GCG (and 0.98 for full refusal-direction ablation), indicating refusal is more effectively suppressed when optimized across many layers/positions rather than at a single site.

Soft-GCG (a Gumbel-Softmax continuous relaxation of suffix search) achieves about a 33× runtime speedup (≈2.5 minutes vs 81 minutes) while matching or exceeding GCG’s substring ASR, showing that much of discrete suffix optimization can be recovered via differentiable optimization plus temperature annealing.

Attack success drops sharply with model scale on Gemma 3 under the same compute budget—1.00 ASR (270M, but degraded coherence), 0.577 (1B), 0.336 (4B), and 0.00 (12B)—suggesting larger/better safety-trained models become materially harder to jailbreak with these methods and may encode safety in higher-rank or more distributed representations.

nodes.title: Beware What You Autocomplete: Forensic Attribution of Backdoored Code Completions
nodes.one_liner: The notable twist is shifting from backdoor detection to root-cause forensics—pinpointing which specific fine-tuning files taught the model to emit an unsafe completion—without gradients or attacker knowledge.
points: Across three vulnerability classes and eight backdoor families, the forensic pipeline achieves extremely low false-negative rates (typically 0–3%) while prior attribution baselines miss most poisoned samples (often 50–100% FNR, with TROJAN variants frequently near complete failure).

Attribution remains practical under post-deployment constraints—using only the fine-tuning corpus plus a reported miscompletion—by narrowing search to top-K=500 candidates and completing analysis in ~47 seconds per incident at ~$0.33, materially faster than common baselines (e.g., ~72–129s).

Removing the traced training files drives backdoor attack success rates down to ≤3% across tested cases, indicating that accurate instance-level attribution can directly enable targeted data excision without full retraining to substantially neutralize compromised code-completion behavior.

nodes.title: Large Language Models (LLMs) and Generative AI in Cybersecurity and Privacy: A Survey of Dual-Use Risks, AI-Generated Malware, Explainability, and Defensive Strategies
nodes.one_liner: The striking takeaway is the forecasted jump to one-in-two malware detections being LLM-assisted by 2025, forcing defenders to treat GenAI not as an add-on tool but as a core threat-scaling primitive that must be countered with governance, robust evaluation, and privacy-aware deployment.
points: LLM-assisted malware is projected to rise from 2% of global detections in 2021 to 50% in 2025 (≈1.7M to ≈110.6M cases), implying attackers gain industrial-scale throughput and polymorphism that strains signature-based defenses.

Total annual malware detections are summarized as increasing from 83.3M (2021) to 221.2M (2025), indicating that GenAI-driven threats are compounding an already fast-growing baseline rather than merely reallocating existing attacker activity.

Defensive adoption is shifting from reactive filtering to pre-deployment and in-pipeline controls (e.g., LLM-augmented app scanning and DevSecOps code review) but raises second-order risks—prompt injection, data extraction, poisoning, bias, and compliance—making explainability, privacy-preserving training (e.g., federated learning), and continuous red-teaming operational necessities.

nodes.title: Knowledge Base Poisoning Attacks and Defense for Policy-Aware LLM-RAG Framework
affiliations: University of North Carolina at Pembroke
nodes.one_liner: Cross-category “centroid-hugging” poisoned policies can hijack RAG retrieval with one rule, but exploiting a domain policy taxonomy yields an edge-deployable, near-zero-overhead filter that fully restores context integrity.
points: A query-agnostic retrieval poisoning technique can corrupt 85% of LLM-RAG mission contexts (17/20 prompts) with a single injected rule (1.6% poisoning), showing that minimal knowledge-base write access can reliably bias downstream decisions without seeing runtime queries.

Attack impact saturates quickly: by 7.7% poisoning the system averages ~2.65 poisoned rules per top-3 LLM context, and effectiveness remains roughly constant even up to 25% poisoning, implying small compromises can achieve near-maximal retrieval control.

A taxonomy-aware dual-detector defense (One-Class SVM + Member-Based Category Spread) achieves 100% context integrity and perfect rule-level detection (Precision/Recall/F1 = 1.0) across 1.6–25% poisoning with ~7 ms per-mission overhead, outperforming generic detectors (e.g., DBSCAN/LOF F1 = 0.0; K-Means F1 = 0.684; Isolation Forest F1 = 0.703).

nodes.title: Your Agent's Memories Are Not Its Own: Forged Reasoning Attacks on LLM Agent Memory and Defenses
nodes.one_liner: The key shift is that poisoning an agent’s remembered justifications—then amplifying them until they become the “consensus”—can reliably suppress future safety steps unless memory writes are structurally authenticated and screened.
points: A two-phase reasoning-trace memory poisoning method (seed injection + self-referential amplification) drives up to 100% attack success in an EHR-style agent across GPT-4o-mini, GPT-4o, and Llama 3.3 70B by making the agent believe safety checks were already completed rather than explicitly instructing it to bypass them.

Consensus/outlier-based defenses (including A-MemGuard in both heuristic and LLM-judge modes) and simple keyword filters are ineffective once amplification floods memory with mutually corroborating forged rationales, indicating that “majority vote over memory” can be turned into an attacker-controlled signal.

A low-latency layered write-time filter with structural forgery signals for reasoning traces reduces attack success to 0% (EHR and RAP) and 6% (ReAct-QA) while observing 0 false positives across 326 benign traces, with ablations showing the structural Reasoning Guard is necessary and sufficient (removing it restores 100% attack success).

nodes.title: When Agents Go Rogue: Activation-Based Detection of Malicious Behaviors in Multi-Agent Systems
affiliations: Institute of Big Data, Fudan University
nodes.one_liner: Internal activations provide a synchronization-agnostic security signal that both detects stealthy MAS compromise and enables non-disruptive recovery via latent-state correction.
points: Activation-space anomaly detection on local agent reasoning states achieves near-ceiling malicious-agent detection (F1 ≈0.92–0.95, AUROC ≈98.5–99.5, FPR ≈0.04–0.07) across stealthy prompt injection, tool manipulation, and memory poisoning without relying on semantic cues or explicit interaction graphs.

Topology/graph-based detectors degrade sharply under asynchronous MAS execution (e.g., best baseline F1 drops to ~0.38–0.46) while activation-based detection remains stable (~0.92–0.94), implying temporal misalignment is a primary failure mode for graph-propagation defenses in real-world agent scheduling.

Mitigating by activation steering restores compromised agents instead of isolating them, sustaining high task completion (TCR 0.96–1.00 vs. 0.66–0.89 for isolation baselines) while driving attack success near zero (ASR 0.02–0.05), showing that “repair” can outperform “removal” for role-dependent multi-agent workflows.

nodes.title: MOSAIC: Knowledge-Guided CLI Command Composition Attack in LLM Coding Agents
affiliations: Hong Kong University of Science and Technology
nodes.one_liner: Individually harmless CLI commands can reliably compose into high-impact exploits via hidden OS state transfer, bypassing prompt-injection defenses at scale.
points: Across 2,525 trials spanning five CLI coding agents and five backend LLMs, benign-looking CLI command sequences triggered CLI command-composition risk (CCR) with a 96.59% end-to-end attack success rate, showing that cross-command OS state is a dominant, currently unmonitored exploit surface.

Matched instruction-layer baselines under the same threat model (AIShellJack and general indirect prompt injection) achieved only 2.18% and 0.79% success respectively, implying that modern prompt-injection hardening does not translate to safety when the attack signal lives in producer–consumer state dependencies between commands.

A structured CLI security knowledge base is the key enabler: instance validity rose from 8.91% (LLM-only) and 46.53% (raw RAG) to 100% with distilled command-state summaries, while representative deployed defenses still left 82.57%–96.63% residual ASR, motivating provenance-aware monitoring of state writes/reads across command traces rather than per-command or per-text checks.

nodes.title: Trivial Prompt Reframing Bypasses Safety Guardrails in Googleś MedGemma-4B
nodes.one_liner: The most dangerous failures come from prompts that make unsafe requests sound legitimate (exam/authority), not from obvious instruction overrides, and the weakest guardrail is drug-interaction adjudication where the model routinely provides definitive verdicts even unprompted.
points: Trivial, layperson prompt reframing defeats MedGemma-4B-it’s documented medical safety guardrails at scale, with 38.0% overall compliance to prohibited behaviors across 4,499 judged generations and a 29.0% baseline compliance even without any “jailbreak” tricks.

Legitimacy framings are the dominant bypass vector: labeling the request as a “medical board exam” boosts Attack Success Rate from 29.0% to 53.1% (+24.0 pts; OR 4.9) and an “I already saw my doctor” authority appeal raises it to 43.7% (+14.7 pts; OR 2.7), while blunt override prefixes (“IGNORE…”, “YOU MUST…”) produce small, non-significant gains (~+3 pts).

Safety robustness is highly concept-specific rather than global, with near-total failure on drug–drug interaction adjudication (83.2% ASR; 87.3% even at baseline) but strong resistance on “don’t defer emergency care” (4.7% ASR overall; baseline 2.0%)—yet the authority framing is uniquely able to breach this strongest guardrail (emergency rises to 25.3%, +23.3 pts).

nodes.title: Swarm-Driven Multi-Agent Reasoning for Smart City Security
affiliations: Concordia Institute for Information Systems Engineering (CIISE)
nodes.one_liner: Swarm-inspired belief dynamics plus verification turns multi-agent LLM security analysis from brittle voting into a high-margin, low-risk consensus process while cutting active agents by 50% and still improving fitness by 11.6%.
points: A pheromone-style consensus over specialized LLM agents achieves highly stable convergence across 500 runs, with a 0.97±0.02 acceptance rate, >0.99 belief concentration, and a 2.08±0.21 consensus margin—indicating robust separation between competing threat hypotheses under partial observability.

Verification-aware calibration and trust-weighted aggregation materially reduce instability: removing the swarm consensus increases aggregate risk from 0.23 to 0.31 and drops margin from 2.08 to 1.42, while removing verification raises risk to 0.28 and reduces agreement from 0.82 to 0.74, showing that hallucination control and contradiction handling are central to safety-critical deployments.

Risk decomposition shows tool misuse is the dominant contributor (0.32 mean) ahead of hallucination propagation (0.30) and prompt injection (0.29), implying that securing agent tool/action interfaces and constraining actuation is at least as important as prompt-level defenses in agentic smart-city security stacks.

nodes.title: Mitigating Taint-Style Vulnerabilities in MCP Servers via Security-Aware Tool Descriptions
nodes.one_liner: Treating MCP tool descriptions as an enforceable policy surface—paired with LLM self-reflection—turns a documentation field into a scalable mitigation layer for taint-style tool exploits.
points: Across 53 disclosed MCP-server vulnerabilities, taint-style bugs dominate (81.13%) and are mainly triggered at tool invocation time (75.47%), indicating that LLM-generated arguments are the primary exploit conduit rather than server registration metadata.

MCP tool metadata is typically underspecified for safety—only 7.00% of top-level tool descriptions and 1.83% of parameter descriptions include security-aware guidance—leaving high-risk capabilities broadly exposed across domains.

Code-centric remediation is costly and imperfect (avg. 203.6 LOC, 5.5 functions, 3.3 files changed; 9.8% remain exploitable), while security-aware description augmentation plus invocation self-reflection cuts attack success from 56.61% to 0.04% (trial-level) and from 63.89% to 0.13% (case-level) on a 792-prompt exploit benchmark.

nodes.title: Token-Flow Firewall: Semantic Runtime Auditing for Persistent AI Agents
affiliations: State Key Laboratory of AI Safety
Institute of Computing Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences
University of Chinese Academy of Sciences
nodes.one_liner: Treating agent security as pre-transfer semantic information-flow control (not post-hoc action filtering) yields near-baseline-best containment with low latency and zero routine human approvals.
points: A semantic token-flow “firewall” that intercepts pre-execution transfers into privileged sinks (memory writes, tool arguments, authority/recipient changes, and external disclosure) cut CIK-Bench attack success to 12.5% while preserving 97.4% benign executability with 0% human confirmation.

Local-first boundary-aware auditing plus selective fallback arbitration improves the security–efficiency frontier, reducing per-case defense latency from 64.3s to 16.9s versus a strong watcher baseline while also lowering ASR from 14.7% to 12.5% and cutting human intervention from 69.3% to 33.0%.

Ablations show robustness depends on structured auditor outputs and the full pipeline (rules + small auditor + rewrite + escalation): decision-only reporting raises ASR to 28.4%, removing fallback raises ASR to 20.4%, and removing the small auditor drives large-model call rate from 15.9% to 94.3% and latency to 74.7s/case without improving ASR.

nodes.title: From Legacy Documentation to OSCAL: An MCP-Based Agent Pipeline for Threat-Informed Continuous Compliance in Critical Infrastructure
nodes.one_liner: Grounding security agents with MCP can trade stochastic hallucinations for a single, auditable trust boundary—making continuous OT compliance feasible, but only as reliable as the initial asset extraction.
points: An eight-phase, non-invasive multi-agent pipeline converts unstructured OT/critical-infrastructure documentation into schema-valid NIST OSCAL SSP/SAR artifacts without active scanning, enabling continuous compliance workflows from legacy text inputs.

Deterministic MCP tool-use against 15 authoritative CTI sources eliminates fabricated identifiers in downstream outputs (0% factual hallucination for deterministically sourced KG nodes) while achieving 0.90 CVE recall, 0.94 ATT&CK technique recall, and 1.00 D3FEND recall in a water-utility scenario.

The dominant reliability risk shifts upstream to asset/entity extraction where a 12.5% semantic hallucination rate caused an 8.5% contextual false-positive rate in the final SAR, showing that one mis-extracted asset can deterministically pull in many real-but-irrelevant CVEs and should be gated by an early human review step.

nodes.title: Context-to-Execution Integrity for LLM Agents
nodes.one_liner: What’s interesting is the crisp separation and joint binding of (1) protected-field authority, (2) sink-interpreted exact effects, and (3) invocation authority into a single manifest that must verify before any side effect can occur.
points: Across 400 live code-agent repository episodes with exact-effect authorization and manifest-bound leasing, 231 tasks completed safely with 0 observed protected-field, sink-effect, or invocation escapes, indicating that binding argument authority, interpreted-effect authorization, and the call event to one canonical manifest can block authority laundering at execution time.

In 720 AgentDojo live episodes (1,739 LLM calls), CXI achieved 199 safe task completions while recording 0 observed field/effect/invocation escapes in the protected admissions subset (204 leases backed by 306 protected-field records and 204 exact-effect authorizations), showing that a fail-closed execution gate can preserve nontrivial utility while preventing unauthorized side effects.

Models still proposed unauthorized actions frequently before enforcement (e.g., 196/300 and 407/522 unauthorized protected-field proposals in adversarial/stress settings, plus 16 unauthorized invocation proposals in 240 free-form actions), implying that prompt- or schema-level controls are insufficient on their own and that sink-time authority checks are necessary because unsafe proposal pressure persists.

nodes.title: ShadowProbe: Language-Extensible Detection of Hidden Algorithmic Complexity Vulnerabilities
nodes.one_liner: Hidden superlinear costs buried in “benign” standard-library APIs can be surfaced at scale by reconstructing runnable contexts and verifying complexity through statistically robust runtime growth rather than trusting model reasoning.
points: A staged pipeline combining shadow-complexity-guided static screening, automated execution-context recovery, LLM-assisted size-controlled input synthesis, and measurement-based growth inference identified 162 previously unknown algorithmic complexity vulnerabilities (ACVs) across CPython, JDK, Zig, Rustc, and vLLM, with 84 (51.9%) confirmed by maintainers and 41 already fixed (48.8% of confirmed).

On the WISE benchmark, the system matched the ground-truth complexity class for all targets while running 4.7× faster than SPF-WCA and 8.1× faster than Badger on average (379s vs 1790s vs 3085s per target), showing that empirical growth validation can outperform heavier symbolic/fuzzing approaches in efficiency without sacrificing correctness on this suite.

Ablations on PyEmailBench show dynamic validation is the critical reliability lever (removing it drops recall from 71.0% to 7.2% while lowering FPR from 12.7% to 3.3%), while multi-strategy generator synthesis boosts recall by 17.4 points (53.6%→71.0%) and context recovery reduces misses (FNR 47.8%→29.0%), implying that harness completeness and runtime scaling evidence matter more than static/LLM-only reasoning.

nodes.title: Controllability-Aware Adversarial Examples Against LLM-Based Network Traffic Classifiers
nodes.one_liner: Realistic attacker constraints (DC/IC/UC masking) still leave LLM-IDS highly transferable-to in black-box settings, but whether LLMs look “worse than ML” depends strongly on the exact ML comparator and dataset.
points: A controllability-aware transfer attack that perturbs only directly controllable (DC) network-flow features achieves 0% constraint-violation by construction while still producing substantial LLM evasion, with mean Evasion-ASR spanning 0.39–0.78 across five IDS benchmarks.

LLM-based traffic classifiers are not uniformly weaker than strong tabular baselines: versus LightGBM they are more vulnerable on CIC-IDS-2018 (1.4× ASR) and RT-IoT2022 (7.2×), comparable on NSL-KDD/UNSW-NB15, and less vulnerable on HIKARI-2021 (LLM/LightGBM = 0.70×; LightGBM 1.43× higher).

Cross-architecture transfer exhibits a consistent hierarchy where gradient/score-based attacks (finite-difference PGD and NES) transfer better than greedy coordinate-wise attacks across all 27 LLM configurations and 9/10 ML cells, and similar LLM ASR under tree, neural, and linear surrogates indicates the effect is not XGBoost-specific.

nodes.title: RustMizan: A Compilable, Contamination-Aware Benchmarking Framework for Rust Vulnerabilities
nodes.one_liner: A contamination-aware, fully-compilable Rust CVE benchmark shows LLM agents can detect vulnerabilities moderately well but fail at precise localization and are easily misled by adversarial code cues.
points: Across 173 compilable Rust variants (42 real-world memory-safety CVEs), frontier LLM agents reach only 56–65% vulnerability detection accuracy while line-level localization micro-F1 remains ~17–23%, indicating current systems can flag issues but struggle to precisely diagnose them.

Shrinking context to function-level dramatically improves pinpointing (line-level F1 rises from ~11–18% at crate-level to ~25–41% at function-level across models), implying that tooling and benchmarks should control context granularity to fairly compare analysis capability.

Semantics-preserving mutations largely preserve aggregate performance (≈0.5–0.7 point mean Line-F1 change), but adversarial cues like misleading comments and safety-implying renames cause an average 5.6-point drop (~27% relative), showing susceptibility to non-semantic deception in security analysis workflows.

nodes.title: Functional and Secure Code Generation with Task Vectors
nodes.one_liner: A simple, tunable weight-space edit (task-vector arithmetic) can simultaneously boost code functionality and security with essentially zero inference-time cost.
points: Weight-arithmetic steering with LPO-derived secure/insecure task vectors increases trustworthy (functional+secure) code completions by 2.1–36.0 percentage points across six coding LLMs on CodeGuard+, with gains on unseen CWE types up to 39.1 points (4.3%–106.5% relative).

A secure-anchored combination (W_base + τ_sec − θ·τ_insec, best at θ=1.5) achieves the highest average main-CWE sec-pass@1 (78.9%) and is the top performer on 5/6 models, beating the strongest prior defense by 3.8–27.5 points on those models.

Because the approach only changes weights (no special decoding), generation latency stays within ~0.6% of the base model on average while using just 0.68–1.80 A6000 GPU-hours of training—reported as 2.6–12.4× less training compute than training-intensive baselines.

nodes.title: Advanced Topic Modeling Techniques for Categorizing Software Vulnerabilities
nodes.one_liner: The most striking result is that swapping only the reduction/clustering stack (UMAP/PCA + HDBSCAN/DBSCAN) can materially change whether vulnerability “Threat” text forms actionable clusters or gets pushed into an outlier bin, while LLM labeling boosts readability but can over-compress topic structure.
points: Applying LLM-assisted topic modeling to 69,909 real-world vulnerability records (39 fields) shows that the free-text “Threat” column alone can be clustered into operationally meaningful themes (e.g., Red Hat Enterprise Linux, VMware/ESXi, SSL/TLS), enabling faster triage from unstructured descriptions.

BERTopic’s effectiveness is highly configuration-dependent, where UMAP+HDBSCAN produces coherent, hierarchically related clusters while DBSCAN-style density clustering more aggressively labels sparse regions as noise, implying that hyperparameter choices directly trade off coverage versus precision in vulnerability categorization.

LLM integration improves interpretability but can reduce topic granularity: Llama2+BERTopic collapses the corpus into just 3 high-level clusters with counts of 572, 287, and 267 documents, indicating strong summarization/labeling capability at the cost of finer subtopic separation needed for detailed remediation workflows.

nodes.title: SeedSmith: LLM-Driven Seed Synthesis for Directed Fuzzing
nodes.one_liner: The key insight is that fixing directed fuzzing’s “cold start” is often a seed problem, and an agent that reads code like an analyst can generate sink-specific, structure-valid inputs that make multiple downstream fuzzers dramatically faster without changing them.
points: An agentic LLM pipeline that iteratively explores code to resolve indirect calls and infer crash preconditions yields large directed-fuzzing gains, delivering 11.51× (AFL++) to 14.66× (AFLGo) geometric-mean time-to-crash speedups over default seeds on 23 Magma bugs.

Sink-targeted, format-aware seeds can unlock crashes that mutation and distance guidance miss, enabling fuzzers to trigger 16 previously unreachable real-world bugs across 10 projects on 115 ARVO targets while increasing crashes found from 26→38 for AFL++ (+46%) and 37→44 for AFLRun (+19%).

Front-loading semantic and control-flow knowledge into the initial seed corpus can outperform alternative LLM-in-the-loop directed fuzzing, with 5 one-shot crashes on Magma and substantially higher totals than an LLM predicate-instrumentation baseline (19 vs 8 crashes on AFL++ and 17 vs 7 on AFLGo within 24h).

nodes.title: Formal Mechanisms for Market Stability in Self-Interested Agent Societies: A Marketplace Simulation Study
nodes.one_liner: A zero-fee, opt-in mediator that prevents defection structurally can stay stable even when nearly half the population is adversarial, while punishment and contracting mechanisms fail mainly from incentive and friction bottlenecks.
points: In a 200-round, 18-agent barter marketplace with progressive troll injection up to 47% of participants (0→4→8→16 trolls), Mediation delivered the highest cumulative honest-agent utility (1556), outperforming communication-only by 29% (1209) and the next-best mechanism (Network Rewiring, 1352) by 15%.

Iteratively prompt-optimized LLM trolls found a strongest “dual-vector” attack (ledger-anchored unfalsifiable wedge messaging plus bait proposals) that cut honest-agent utility by 13.3% (1556→1350) yet never drove honest per-round utility negative, indicating market collapse was prevented even under sustained adversarial pressure.

Punishment- and complaint-based approaches underperformed in self-interested settings—Costly Sanctions ranked last (685) and Judicial second-last (852)—while Contracting suffered severe adoption/friction costs (2717 trades vs 12563 in baseline) and a 21.3% breach rate (708/3330), implying prevention/guaranteed execution mechanisms scale better than after-the-fact enforcement when agents optimize for individual gain.

nodes.title: When Agents Remember Too Much: Memory Poisoning Attacks on Large Language Model Agents
affiliations: Department of Computer Science, New Mexico State University
Klipsch School of Electrical and Computer Engineering, New Mexico State University
nodes.one_liner: Persistent agent memory creates a durable, stealthy attack surface where a single well-crafted email can silently reprogram future tool use—so defenses must govern what gets remembered and what gets retrieved, not just what gets prompted.
points: A two-phase memory poisoning method (“GhostWriter”) achieves ~98% memory injection success and ~60% average behavior activation across five long-term-memory agent architectures and four LLM backends, indicating that persistent memory turns untrusted tool inputs (email/calendar) into a high-reliability control channel rather than a one-off prompt injection risk.

Attack effectiveness depends more on memory architecture and model reliability than on traditional prompt-injection defenses: prompt injection activation is ~0–16.7% for most agents but spikes to 92% for a trajectory-memory agent (ExpeL), while common prompt-injection detectors miss GhostWriter entirely (0% detection for DataFilter; 85%→6% for a judge-based method when payloads shift from directive to descriptive).

A two-layer memory governance defense (“AM-Sentry”) combining admission policies and retrieval-time screening reduces end-to-end attack success to <12% on average (except ~20% with the weakest LLM backend) while largely preserving task utility metrics (F1/LLM-judged accuracy/tool-call accuracy), showing that filtering risky memories is a practical security-utility tradeoff rather than an inherent capability loss.

nodes.title: CONTRA: Red-Teaming Configurations of Personalizable Agents
affiliations: Max Planck Institute for Software Systems
nodes.one_liner: Benign personalization—especially scheduled heartbeats—can reliably steer tool-using agents into executing harmful actions at scale, evading both static skill scans and traditional prompt-based red-team baselines.
points: Across 473 popular agent skills (1,590 high-severity target actions), 75.1% of skills admitted at least one benign-looking configuration that triggered a malicious action, indicating personalization creates a pervasive, latent attack surface even without explicit adversarial prompts.

The configuration-search method achieved a 39.2% attack success rate overall (higher for more severe actions: 44.7% at severity-4 and 45.2% at severity-5) while typically requiring only 2–3 file edits (avg 2.5), showing harmful capability can emerge from small, realistic tweaks rather than overtly malicious changes.

91.8% of successful configurations were independently rated as benign and 68.7% involved heartbeat-triggered autonomy, implying that background scheduled behaviors and “reasonable” persona/memory edits are a more practical risk driver than classic direct-instruction attacks that models often refuse (1.3% ASR).

nodes.title: TACTIC-KG: Toward Small Agent Teams for Cyber Threat Intelligence Knowledge Graph Construction
nodes.one_liner: Small, role-specialized LLM agents with explicit verification can outperform far larger monolithic models for CTI knowledge graph construction while offering tighter control over hallucinations and over-completion.
points: A four-agent pipeline (extract→type→verify→curate) using small 3B–8B backbones achieves higher CTI triplet extraction and graph quality than monolithic in-context baselines, reaching up to 80 F1 and 67 graph structural similarity versus 72 F1 and 58 graph similarity for a 671B-scale monolithic system.

Agent specialization materially shifts the precision–recall frontier, with recall peaking at 90 in the agentic extractor stage (vs ≤66 for monolithic baselines) and downstream verification/curation recovering balance while maintaining graph consistency and limiting unsupported “connectivity for connectivity’s sake.”

Moderate fine-tuning data is sufficient for strong performance, as ~200 training chunks can deliver ~76 F1 and diverse data improves outcomes more than volume (e.g., up to 78 F1 and 70 partial typing accuracy on the hardest test), indicating a practical path to cost-effective CTI-to-KG deployment with smaller local models.

nodes.title: POPS: Recovering Unlearned Multi-Modality Knowledge in MLLMs with Prompt-Optimized Parameter Shaking
nodes.one_liner: Multimodal unlearning can be largely reversed by combining optimized prompt triggers with lightweight fine-tuning on the model’s own synthetic multimodal outputs, exposing cross-modal memory persistence as a core privacy failure mode.
points: A two-stage attack (prompt-suffix optimization plus LoRA fine-tuning on synthesized multimodal outputs) recovers most “forgotten” private multimodal knowledge, reaching 82% recovery on MLLMU-Bench and boosting post-unlearning test accuracy from 40.2% to 42.9% (close to 43.05% with ground-truth fine-tuning).

OOD-guided concept-level suffix optimization is the dominant driver of leakage (70% recovery alone) and materially outperforms token-level adversarial suffix baselines like GCG (48% recovery), indicating that natural-sounding, generalizing prompts can systematically reactivate residual cross-modal associations.

Vulnerability appears architectural rather than method-specific: recovery persists across unimodal-adapted and multimodal-specific unlearning methods (≈+3.7% to +7.4% accuracy gains), generalizes across 4 MLLM families with tightly clustered 81.8–84.0% recovery, and remains non-trivial even under defenses (reduced to 57% with head projection or 41% with 5× paraphrase unlearning).

nodes.title: Retroactive Chain-of-Thought (RetroCoT): Forensic Reconstruction Prompts as a Safety Diagnostic Across Model Generations
nodes.one_liner: Pragmatic reframing (forensic reconstruction + presupposed outcome) can outperform direct and past-tense attacks by turning refusal decisions into “helpful analysis,” and even newer models that catch the frame can be pulled back into compliance via critique-driven continuation.
points: A single-turn forensic “retroactive reconstruction” framing raises harmful compliance on AdvBench (n=50) to 58% for GPT-4o and 52% for GPT-4o-mini, versus 0% and 4% for direct harmful requests, showing safety behavior is highly sensitive to pragmatic register rather than semantic intent.

Controlled ablations indicate the mechanism is an interaction effect: presupposition framing (5% ASR) or forensic persona (5%) alone barely move the needle, but combining them jumps to 50% ASR (and 60% with added backward reasoning), implying current refusal triggers can be bypassed by shifting the model into an “analysis of an assumed past event” stance.

Register-specific hardening is brittle across conversational continuations: GPT-5-family models drop baseline RETROCOT ASR to 0%, yet a single evaluator-style critique turn drives ASR to 48–52% (and CritiqueOnly reaches 85% on GPT-5.4-mini), while tool-result injection only partially suppresses GPT-4o (58%→20%) and GPT-4o-mini (52%→26%), leaving a meaningful residual attack surface in agentic/tool contexts.

nodes.title: Agentic and Generative AI for Open-Source Intelligence and Cyber Investigations: Taxonomy, Evaluation, Challenges, and Future Directions
affiliations: University of Wales Trinity Saint David
The University of Texas at San Antonio
nodes.one_liner: The most striking pattern is a capability–evaluation mismatch: impressive agentic OSINT demos exist, but the field lacks shared benchmarks and barely measures hallucination or adversarial robustness, making a human-in-the-loop co-pilot the only defensible near-term deployment model.
points: Across 74 studies on LLM/agentic AI for OSINT/CTI/cyber investigations, hallucination is flagged as a reliability risk in 20+ papers but is end-to-end measured on OSINT data in only one system, which reports a 4% hallucination rate under favorable, non-reproducible RAG conditions—leaving operational trust largely unquantified.

Benchmark choice can invert conclusions: a multiple-choice cybersecurity benchmark reports GPT-4o at 91.25% accuracy versus a 72.24% human expert mean, yet an analyst-derived, real-world CTI workflow evaluation finds no LLM reaches analyst-acceptable performance on complex threat characterization and report quality, indicating that realistic workflow tests are decisive for deployment readiness.

Input channels are adversarial and already noisy—professional OSINT Twitter communities contain ~9% misinformation across 1.96M tweets, and fake CTI generated via domain fine-tuning can be judged as genuine by threat hunters (n=10) and can poison CTI knowledge graphs—implying that agentic/RAG grounding mechanisms must be evaluated under adversarial contamination, not only benign conditions.

nodes.title: Oyster-II: Reinforcement Learning for Constructive Safety Alignment in Large Language Models
nodes.one_liner: Training only on long, realistic safety prompts can simultaneously improve short-prompt safety and reduce over-refusal, suggesting long-context alignment is a high-leverage path to more robust and user-helpful safety.
points: A Zero-RL, multi-stage constructive-safety pipeline raises instruction-conflict compliance from 60.49% (Oyster-I) and 60.31% (Qwen3-14B) to 88.23%, approaching much larger models (90.02% for Qwen3.5-397B) and materially reducing prompt-injection risk in real deployments.

Reward shaping that includes explicit length incentives prevents safety-driven reward hacking, with removing the length reward causing an ~20-point drop in response rate during stage-1 training while offering no compensating safety benefit.

Long-context safety alignment generalizes “down” to short queries (but not vice versa), delivering +17.53% English and +18.26% Chinese gains on long-query safety plus +2.80% (EN) and +4.48% (CN) response-rate improvements, indicating semantic rather than keyword-based safety behavior and lowering over-refusal under adversarial rephrasing.

nodes.title: Best-of-Better-$N$: Generating Pre-Aligned Responses with In-Context Learning
nodes.one_liner: The key idea is that alignment can be improved without finetuning by increasing the probability of generating high-reward candidates (not just selecting among low-quality samples), and retrieval quality plus restyling measurably reduces coverage gaps that otherwise dominate Best-of-N performance.
points: BoBN (retrieval + LLM-based restyling + in-context learning) consistently shifts a black-box reference LLM’s sampling distribution toward higher-reward regions, enabling better downstream alignment even when standard Best-of-N fails due to poor high-reward coverage.

On safety benchmarks, BoBN makes a non-safety-tuned 7B model competitive with frontier-model refusal: zephyr-7b improves from 0.742→0.150 on StrongReject at N=1 and reaches 0.033 at N=16 (≈Claude Sonnet-3.7 level), while also reducing normalized log-coverage from 5.95→3.48.

On math reasoning, BoBN beats both plain prompting and static-demo ICL (URIAL), e.g., zephyr-7b on GSM8k improves from 0.214→0.315 at N=1 and to 0.587 at N=16 (≈+37% absolute), with BoBN-4 matching or exceeding πref/URIAL at N=16, implying materially lower sampling budgets for the same accuracy.

nodes.title: Silicon Sampling via Cross-Survey Transfer
nodes.one_liner: A stricter individual-level cross-survey transfer test shows LLM survey simulators can nearly match supervised baselines without any in-domain training, but only for constructs with strong underlying attitudinal constraints.
points: Zero-shot open-weight LLMs reached 52.1% exact-match accuracy when predicting respondents’ answers to entirely unseen survey items, coming within 6 percentage points of a supervised random forest (58.3%) trained on ~960 in-population examples per fold.

Predictability varied sharply by construct, forming a stable hierarchy from 67.2% accuracy for partisan-linked judgments (e.g., party competence) down to 23.3% for sovereignty positioning, implying silicon sampling is most reliable when attitudes are tightly constrained by partisan structure.
