Response-distribution “variance collapse” was not unique to LLMs (variance ratio: LLMs 0.67–0.85 vs. random forest 0.72), and removing safety alignment changed accuracy inconsistently across model families (−6.1 pp to −0.1 pp), indicating both diversity and alignment effects are model- and task-dependent rather than universal.

nodes.title: Security and Privacy in Agentic AI: Grand Challenges and Future Directions
nodes.one_liner: The most consequential shift is treating agent autonomy as an organizational and governance failure mode—where consent, liability, and auditing must operate across entire action trajectories and tool ecosystems, not single model outputs.
points: A 30-expert, three-day horizon-scanning workshop (March 11–13, 2026) converged on four core risk clusters for agentic AI—accountability/liability, consent/data/context, human oversight & vulnerability, and transparency/resilience—implying that current security/privacy concepts built for bounded deterministic systems do not transfer cleanly to autonomous multi-step tool-using agents.

Accountability in agentic AI is constrained by a traceability–privacy paradox: the logs, identifiers, and provenance needed to attribute harm and support audits can themselves become surveillance infrastructure, making privacy-preserving provenance (layered audit trails, selective disclosure, role-based access, retention limits, and cryptographic integrity) a primary design requirement rather than an afterthought.

Static, one-shot consent and one-time certification break down for non-deterministic, self-updating, supply-chain-composed agents, pushing deployments toward continuous auditing plus hybrid architectures that put deterministic safety/authorization gates in front of high-risk tool calls and data disclosures to contain cascades and reduce prompt-injection/confused-deputy-style failures.

nodes.title: Securing Multi-Tool AI Agent Chains With Dynamic, Real-Time Compositional Policies
nodes.one_liner: Most multi-tool risk comes from composition, and a monotonic “most-restrictive” policy algebra plus real-time taint can fail-closed on unsafe chains without trying to predict agent behavior.
points: A two-phase control plane (static Most Restrictive Set composition at session checkout plus runtime monotonic taint tracking) enforces that adding tools or touching more sensitive data can only tighten—not relax—an agent session’s effective permissions, preventing emergent multi-tool policy violations.

On a reference catalog of 32 tools governed by 16 NIST SP 800-53–aligned policies, strict clearance-mode composition blocks 79.2% of policy pairs and 95.5% of policy triples, effectively forcing toolchains to remain within same-classification clusters and preempting unsafe chains before execution.

A more permissive taint-mode admits mixed-classification chains within the exfiltration boundary but still blocks 42.5% of policy pairs and 60.5% of policy triples, showing a measurable security–utility tradeoff while preserving a hard containment rule that tainted (≥Confidential) data cannot reach outbound tools.

nodes.title: The Balkanization of Execution-Security Research for AI Coding Agents: Isolation, Access Control, and Time-of-Check-to-Time-of-Use Vulnerabilities
affiliations: University of Europe for Applied Sciences (UE Germany)
nodes.one_liner: The most actionable takeaway is that today’s dominant controls (denylists and static permissions) fail frequently in practice, while TOCTOU and MCP “tool poisoning” are the same validate-then-act race showing up in different layers.
points: A systematization of 39 execution-security papers (2023–2026) plus 4 verified, patched CVEs affecting production coding-agent tooling indicates execution-layer vulnerabilities are already exploited in the real world, not just theoretical.

Empirical policy-enforcement testing shows real-world command denylists are bypassable 69.0%–98.6% of the time, implying “denylist-based” execution control is an unreliable primary guardrail for autonomous tool execution.

Benign but out-of-scope agent actions occur at rates up to 17.1% under realistic prompting (and can jump from 0.0% to 17.1% by removing explicit scope language), showing that capability-style authorization alone does not prevent unintended-but-permitted actions and needs intent- and state-freshness checks.

nodes.title: ScopeJudge: Cost-Aware Pre-Execution Gating for Offensive Security Agents
nodes.one_liner: Request-conditioned, pre-execution tool-call judging can prevent out-of-scope actions cheaply, and the best-performing/lowest-cost option is open-weight rather than proprietary.
points: ScopeJudge provides 4,897 per-tool-call scope labels from 100 offensive-security agent trajectories with a 7.7% scope-violation base rate and substantial expert agreement (Fleiss κ=0.64), yielding an expert reference F1 of 0.78 for automated monitors to target.

Static-policy-only gating is structurally inadequate for scope enforcement because it is blind to request-defined boundaries, causing recall to collapse to near zero for 7/8 judge models (median recall 0.005) while adding user intent immediately lifts recall into the 0.60–0.94 range.

Open-weight judges lead the cost–accuracy frontier: GLM-5.2 achieves the best overall F1 (0.66) and beats the best proprietary judge (0.60) at roughly one-third the per-call cost, with a practical cost-sensitive operating point catching 87% of violations at $0.0032/call (intent+calls) versus a recall-first point catching 94% at lower precision (0.39) by flagging ~19% of all calls.

nodes.title: Certifying Ghosts: How Cybersecurity AI Agents Break the EU Cyber Resilience Act
nodes.one_liner: Point-in-time certification becomes a stale snapshot once AI agents can rediscover and exploit vulnerabilities on demand, forcing regulation toward continuous, agent-run security postures.
points: Cybersecurity AI agents invalidate the CRA’s core premises by making exploitable posture non-stationary (a product can become exploitable without any change), exploitation effectively ambient rather than a discrete trigger, and remediation structurally unable to keep pace with weaponization windows now measured in days or hours.

Time-to-exploit for exploited vulnerabilities has collapsed to near-zero: one large public aggregate reports median time-to-exploit falling from 771 days (2018) to 0 days (2025–26), while ENISA’s EUVD shows post-2022 exploited cohorts dropping to single-digit days—undercutting point-in-time conformity and “remediate without delay” as meaningful controls.

Agent-driven vulnerability abundance makes compliance shift from “fix everything” to defensible prioritization (the regime can bend on discovery volume), but preserving any credible security signal requires continuous, agent-operated conformity that re-establishes posture at adversary tempo, demonstrated on two CRA-scope robots by reducing attacker objective success from 79%→14% and 75%→8%.

nodes.title: SA-DRL: Security-Aware Deep Reinforcement Learning for Ransomware Detection with Asymmetric Reward Design
affiliations: AI and Cyber Futures Center, Charles Sturt University
nodes.one_liner: Reward-function design (not model architecture alone) is the main lever for shifting ransomware detectors toward operationally correct behavior—minimizing missed attacks.
points: Encoding false-negative/false-positive cost asymmetry directly into a DRL reward (−2.0 for FN vs −0.5 for FP; 4:1) cut mean false-negative rate by 43% versus a symmetric reward across 480 controlled runs, with statistically significant gains for every agent (pooled Wilcoxon p<0.0001).

The security-optimal configuration (DDQN + asymmetric reward + γ=0.1) achieved FNR=0.0080, F1=0.9915, and AUC=0.998, reducing missed detections by 67.6% compared with the best supervised baseline (MLP FNR=0.0247) on a balanced 2,000-sample behavioral dataset spanning 30 ransomware families.

Lower discount factors (γ=0.1–0.5) consistently produced safer operating points, while high γ (0.9–0.99) increased missed-detection risk most sharply for policy-gradient agents (e.g., PPO reaching FNR≈0.055), implying γ should be treated as a security-critical hyperparameter rather than routine tuning.

nodes.title: Beyond the Leaderboard: A Synthesis of Tool-Use, Planning, and Reasoning Failures in Large Language Model Agents
nodes.one_liner: The most revealing signal is that agent progress is real but uneven: reliability collapses with composition, horizon, and coordination, and some of the biggest score jumps disappear once measurement validity is enforced.
points: Across 27 papers spanning 19 agent benchmarks/frameworks, six recurring failure clusters appear end-to-end—tool invocation/parameter errors, planning/constraint-satisfaction breakdowns, long-horizon context degradation, multi-agent coordination failures, safety/security failures under ambiguity or adversarial content, and measurement-validity gaps—implying that headline leaderboard gains often mask distinct reliability bottlenecks at different pipeline stages.

Quantitative evidence shows sharp non-linear degradation with horizon and composition: WebArena improved from ~14% to 61.7% (still below ~78% human), METR reports <10% success on tasks taking humans >~4 hours despite near-100% under ~4 minutes, and TravelPlanner remained 0.6% for GPT-4 (~10% for stronger reasoning models) unless paired with heavy verification scaffolding (~65%), indicating sub-skill competence does not reliably compose into end-to-end success.

Safety and robustness remain materially unresolved in tool-using agents even when capabilities improve: ToolEmu finds the safest tested agent still exhibits severe failures in 23.9% of cases under underspecification, and InjecAgent reports ~24% indirect prompt-injection success on GPT-4 (rising to ~47% with stronger attacks and exceeding 80% for some open models), while independent audits show benchmark corrections can dramatically change apparent performance (e.g., a SWE-agent result dropping from ~12.5% to ~4%), underscoring the need for adversarial testing and contamination-resistant evaluation.

nodes.title: ShannonProver: Towards Automating Formal Cryptographic Proofs
nodes.one_liner: State-aware “proof-state compilation” plus multi-agent tree search turns formal cryptographic proof scripting into a checkable search problem where hallucinations are rejected, enabling day-scale automation for proofs that historically took expert-weeks to months.
points: An agentic harness that compiles EasyCrypt proof state into typed, state-aware context panels and orchestrates multi-agent tree search raises solve rate on non-linear cryptographic proof obligations (invariants + game hops) from 67% with a single agent to 90% via backtracking/respawn scheduling.

The main productivity gain comes from reducing “error friction” rather than reducing raw mistake frequency: first-attempt tactic rejection rates stay similar, but the share of spend lost to consecutive-rejection debugging windows drops from ~10–12% to ~0–1.3% across procedural/invariant/game-hop proof shapes.

On a real-world ChaCha20-Poly1305 formalization, lemma-level proof scripting can be fully automated given an expert decomposition, completing within a day at ~$233 total API cost with cost concentrated in the hard tail (27 procedural lemmas: $40.69 vs. invariants: $76.99 vs. game hops: $115.68), effectively shifting expert effort away from mechanical tactic engineering.

nodes.title: Securing Autonomous Vehicle Systems via Twin-Aware Federated Reinforcement Learning
nodes.one_liner: A digital-twin-in-the-loop, history-aware robust aggregator can keep federated RL driving policies safe (100% no-collision) even under worst-case adaptive poisoning that devastates most prior defenses.
points: SecApp’s twin-aware secure aggregation sustained a 100.0% no-collision rate across 13 poisoning attacks (including Adaptive, MinMax/MinSum, and FTI) where standard FRL/FL defenses often collapsed to ~7–15% no-collision under strong attacks.

With 20% compromised agents, FRL under common aggregators dropped from 100% no-collision to 8–14% (e.g., FedAvg 12.47% under FTI and 14.49% under Adaptive), showing that FL-hardened rules do not transfer reliably to safety-critical FRL without RL-specific robustness controls.

SecApp’s gradient filtering achieved <5% false positive and <5% false negative rates (e.g., Adaptive: 0.4% FPR and 0.1% FNR) while keeping aggregation overhead low (~10s over 2,000 rounds versus ~46–48s for heavier baselines), indicating practical deployability for roadside-server coordination.

nodes.title: Determinants and Limits of LLM Security-Tool Orchestration: A Study with HexStrike-AI
affiliations: University of Science and Technology of China
Suzhou Institute for Advanced Research, University of Science and Technology of China
nodes.one_liner: Tool-rich LLM security agents are often limited more by the client/harness and default behaviors than by the model or adding more tools, and constraint-by-prompt can leak badly unless enforced and measured.
points: Across 774 picoCTF trials (86 challenges × 3 tool-access regimes × 3 model/client setups), the overall SUCCESS rate increased from 55.4% to 72.0% after targeted fixes, with every configuration improving significantly (paired McNemar p<0.001) and non-overlapping 95% confidence intervals.

With the underlying DeepSeek model held constant, the driving client/harness produced a 2.1× baseline performance gap (59.7% vs 27.9%), implying that agent security-tool performance comparisons are not interpretable unless the client/orchestrator loop is explicitly specified.

Of 128 recovered previously-unsuccessful trials, 79 were attributable to behavior/default/tool-definition fixes and 49 to specialized tools (including 22 from 11 new capability tools), while remaining failures were predominantly reasoning- or environment-bound rather than missing-tool bound, and single-run verdicts were largely reproducible (17/20 challenges unanimous across 3 reruns).

nodes.title: SkillCenter: A Large-Scale Source-Grounded Skill Library for Autonomous AI Agents
nodes.one_liner: The corpus demonstrates that source-grounded skill injection can be highly effective, but naive keyword/title-only retrieval largely nullifies the benefit—so scaling content is less limiting than scaling correct retrieval and gating.
points: A 216,938-skill library across 24 domain bundles is released, with 114,565 pipeline-produced source-grounded skills traced to 55,199 documents and 102,373 community-harvested skills, making it over an order of magnitude larger than prior open skill collections.

Pipeline-produced skills provide quote-level traceability for retained claims and score an average 3.91/5 (with ~82.1% scored as 4), while near-duplicate content is effectively absent in the pipeline subset (<0.01%) but concentrated in harvested community skills (26.9% near-duplicate in GitHub SkillMD; 65% in a curated-lite subset).

Downstream tests show retrieval quality is the bottleneck: keyword title-only retrieval yields no improvement over baseline on general tasks and fails to surface needed skills even when present (0%), but injecting the correct skill boosts performance from 0% to 61–78% on real-corpus knowledge-gap probes and to 72–100% on synthetic convention tasks.

nodes.title: Strategic Bargaining in Multi-Buyer Markets: Reinforcement Learning from Verifiable Rewards for LLM Negotiations
nodes.one_liner: Objective, verifiable profit rewards turn a fluent LLM into a near-perfect multi-buyer negotiator that reliably finds the top-value counterparty while respecting hard economic constraints.
points: A 30B seller trained with reinforcement learning from verifiable profit signals achieved +0.580 mean reward with 82.8% deal rate and 0.700 surplus-extraction ratio, outperforming larger frontier baselines (e.g., +0.123 for a leading closed-source reasoning model) by converting negotiation into a measurable exploration–exploitation problem under turn limits.

General-purpose LLM sellers systematically fail at market exploration and partner selection in multi-buyer bargaining, closing on the highest-budget buyer only 34.6–57.1% of the time versus 99.5% for the trained seller, indicating that scale and “reasoning mode” alone do not reliably produce strategic search behavior.

Verifiable constraints sharply improved economic safety: the trained seller maintained a 0.0% sell-below-cost violation rate (versus up to 38.3% in common open-source baselines), while learning tactics like price anchoring and diagnostic probing that generalized to unseen buyer styles and budget distributions.

nodes.title: Bad Memory: Evaluating Prompt Injection Risks from Memory in Agentic Systems
nodes.one_liner: Persistent memory turns prompt injection into a stored, multi-session compromise where even “safe” refusals can leave booby-trapped instructions waiting for a weaker model or later run.
points: Stored prompt injections embedded in persistent agent memory files can reliably influence both current and future sessions, with single-session attack success rates ranging from 0% to 100% depending on model and goal (e.g., unauthorized tool-use hits 80–100% on three of four models; brand targeting reaches 100% on GPT-5.5).

Cross-session compounding is real: repeating the same attack after a benign “stabilization” session can increase success (e.g., Claude Haiku credential exfiltration rises from 60% to 100% on the second probe), while injected rules often remain resident in memory even when ignored (e.g., Claude Opus shows 0% exfiltration ASR but 100% persistence for that payload).

Attack success and payload persistence are decoupled and model-specific—some models refuse to comply yet leave the malicious rule in place (high persistence, low ASR), while others sanitize memory (e.g., Codex models remove exfiltration payloads with persistence 0–20%), implying that “refusal” is not sufficient as a safety outcome in memory-using agents.

nodes.title: Devil in the Lens: Analyzing and Defending Physical Prompt Injection Against Vision-Language Models on Wearable Devices
affiliations: Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou)
Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications
nodes.one_liner: Environmental text becomes a stealthy, attacker-controlled instruction channel for smart-glasses VLMs, and simple text-aware filtering plus representation-level drift detection can drastically reduce real-world hijacking risk.
points: Physical prompt injection via scene text reliably hijacks wearable vision-language model behavior across 12 models, reaching up to 96% attack success in simulated settings and up to 60% in real-world smart-glasses captures, directly undermining integrity- and safety-critical assistance (e.g., navigation and hazard judgment).

Real-world susceptibility is strongly shaped by perceptual conditions—distance is the dominant factor (e.g., one model drops from 66.7% ASR at 1 m to 28.6% at 2.5 m), while lighting/angle cause smaller degradations and top-of-frame placements often increase effectiveness—implying attackers can optimize placement rather than needing system access.

Two targeted mitigations substantially blunt the attack channel: an OCR+taint-scoring blur filter cuts many task ASRs to near-zero (e.g., Qwen3-VL-235B Ref/Nav/Safe from 1.000 to 0.153/0.115/0.153; Gemini-2.5-Flash Ref from 1.000 to 0.038), and an internal token-drift gating prototype reduces Nav ASR from 0.346→0.076 (Llama-3.2-11B) and 0.038→0.000 (Qwen2.5-VL-7B).

nodes.title: Rethinking Penetration Testing for AI-Enabled Systems: From Resource Compromise to Behavioral Objective Violation
nodes.one_liner: The key shift is redefining pentest “success” from breaking systems to making AI-driven systems reliably behave against their mission under a realistic threat model.
points: AI-enabled penetration should be treated as objective-driven behavioral failure—an attacker succeeds when they can feasibly induce AI-governed behavior that violates an explicit operational objective (e.g., wrong escalation/triage) even without compromising infrastructure.

AI-enabled systems introduce new adversarial influence surfaces (prompts, retrieved content, sensors, training data, memory, tools, and human-AI loops), so a pentest that only checks for resource compromise can miss high-impact failures caused purely by behavioral manipulation (e.g., indirect prompt injection and tool misuse).

Effective AI pentesting requires evidence that links adversarial action to objective violation, including reproducibility conditions and (often) probabilistic success rates, pushing reporting beyond binary exploit chains to scenario-based evaluation with logged prompts/context/tool calls and operational-impact mapping.

nodes.title: Context Contamination in LLM Analysis of Network Security Logs: Poison with Passive Prompt Injection and Mitigation Evaluation
nodes.one_liner: Network logs become an execution substrate for hidden instructions, and even strong prompt hardening degrades with long context—so defense-in-depth and retrieval-aware batching are mandatory for LLM-assisted SOC workflows.
points: Passive prompt injection via attacker-controlled log fields (e.g., User-Agent, SSH usernames, JSON bodies) achieves up to 88.2% attack success (83.4% average) across GPT-4o, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, and Llama-3-70B, showing that LLM-based SOC log analysis collapses the trust boundary between data and instructions.

Fragmenting payloads across multiple log entries (“Context Stitching”) still succeeds 76.4% of the time (e.g., ~81.4% with 3 fragments in the same batch) and drops to 34.2% when fragments span multiple retrieval batches, implying batch/windowing and retrieval policies materially shape exploitability but do not eliminate it.

Layered mitigations (regex input filtering + prompt hardening/spotlighting + output validation) reduce attacks by 90.4% (ASR 87.3%→8.4%) while decreasing benign accuracy by 3.4pp (94.2%→90.8%), leaving a non-trivial residual risk that warrants human oversight for high-stakes decisions.

nodes.title: SingGuard-NSFA: Extensible Guardrails for Agentic AI via Generative Reasoning and Real-Time Classification
nodes.one_liner: It’s a practical blueprint for multilingual, extensible agent guardrails that combines audit-grade explanations with production-grade latency while still improving cross-source robustness.
points: A CIA-triad-grounded NSFA taxonomy organizes 185 agent-security risk variants (7 Level-1 domains; 28 Level-2 risks; 185 Level-3 variants) and covers 80% of OWASP Top 10 for LLM Apps, 60% of OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Apps, and 47% of OWASP Agentic AI Threats within a deliberately single-turn, text-only detection scope.

Across 133 languages and 93K+ purpose-built evaluation samples, the released 0.8B–9B models achieve ≥94% F1 on both query and response benchmarks and exceed the strongest competing guardrails by 6–12 absolute F1 points, indicating that operational agent threats can be screened more reliably than content-safety-oriented filters.

A dual-mode design pairs interpretable generative reasoning for audits with frozen-backbone classification heads for real-time interception (~45–57 ms per sample), scaling from 5 to 50,000 heads with only +9 ms latency and reaching 91.29% F1 on a cross-source benchmark, which supports rapid extension to new risk domains without retraining the backbone.

nodes.title: Agent Skill Security: Threat Models, Attacks, Defenses, and Evaluation
nodes.one_liner: Securing LLM agents that reuse third-party skills requires defenses at every lifecycle boundary—repository, retrieval, planning, runtime, and updates—because each stage has distinct failure modes with measurable residual risk.
points: A lifecycle-aware hybrid repository admission pipeline (structural checks + LLM semantic validation) cut malicious skill admission from 52.9% (rules-only) and 42.9% (semantic-only) down to 7.9%, but at a high 20.0% false-positive rate indicating substantial developer friction.

Undefended semantic retrieval is highly susceptible to “agentic SEO,” with Sybil publication reaching 93.20% attack success and averaging 2.84 malicious skills in the top-5, while a post-retrieval validation layer reduced this to 26.59% ASR and 0.27 malicious in top-5, leaving nontrivial residual risk from vector-space density effects.

Runtime monitoring with taint tracking and policy enforcement blocked 87.0% of policy violations yet still allowed 23.0% execution-time attack success because paraphrasing/summarization can erase string-based taint labels (66.67% taint accuracy), showing that LLM-mediated implicit flows remain a dominant gap.

nodes.title: How Agents Ask for Permission: User Permissions for AI Agents, from Interfaces to Enforcement
nodes.one_liner: The most striking pattern is that today’s agent permission systems force a three-way compromise between usability, formal rigor, and deterministic enforcement—while commercial products often add continuous control but at the cost of transparency and user fatigue.
points: A survey of 21 agent-permissions proposals finds that none simultaneously delivers low user overhead, formally grounded policy specifications, and deterministic enforcement—highlighting a core “pick-two” tradeoff that leaves real-world agents exposed to both prompt-injection/hallucination risks and usability-driven over-permissioning.

About one-third of reviewed systems (roughly 7/21) do not specify a threat model at all, and most that do assume a “benign but fallible” agent threatened by prompt injection/hallucination, implying that many proposed permission designs may not generalize to adversaries like multi-user misuse or the agent provider.

Commercial agents evaluated (5 total) largely rely on user-in-the-loop approvals and/or opaque LLM guardrails, creating a practical dilemma where users must choose between high-interruption workflows (risking privacy fatigue) and low-transparency automated approvals with limited policy control or revocation.

nodes.title: Isolation as a First-Class Principle for LLM-Agent System Safety: Concepts, Taxonomy, Challenges and Future Directions
nodes.one_liner: Treating isolation as a first-class system principle reframes LLM-agent safety from “better refusals” to “enforced boundaries” that prevent untrusted context from ever becoming authority.
points: A boundary-centric safety lens shows that many agent failures (prompt injection, tool misuse, memory poisoning, and unsafe execution) share a single root cause: loss of isolation where untrusted inputs cross interfaces and become control signals.

The taxonomy operationalizes agent-system risk into five enforceable isolation boundaries—user–agent, agent–tool, agent–execution, agent–agent, and system–environment—enabling practitioners to localize where compromise starts and to anticipate how it propagates across workflows and shared state.

The most actionable design implication is a shift from prompt-only guardrails to isolation-by-construction (explicit authority separation, scoped/typed capabilities, trace-level observability, and recovery mechanisms) because real-world compromises commonly persist through long-horizon interaction, tool trajectories, and memory reuse.

nodes.title: PVDetector: Detecting Prompt Injection Attacks on Purpose-Specific LLM Agents through Policy-Violation Concept Analysis
affiliations: Huazhong University of Science and Technology
Changsha University of Science and Technology
nodes.one_liner: Monitoring hidden-state alignment to role-specific policy-violation concepts yields a fast, training-free prompt-injection detector that stays effective even against strong and adaptive attacks across text and vision-language agents.
points: A training-free detector built from ~30 contrastive policy-violating vs policy-compliant prompt pairs achieves near-zero false negatives (<1%) across multiple LLMs and five prompt-injection attack families, indicating that internal activation signals can be more reliable than input-output heuristics for agent policy enforcement.

Hidden-state “policy-violation” directions remain strongly expressed under successful prompt injection (especially in later layers), enabling detection even when the model’s surface response is hijacked and suggesting that agents retain a latent representation of policy conflict that attackers must suppress to evade monitoring.

With thresholds calibrated to keep benign-query false positives at ≤1% in the main setting, the method maintains low detection overhead (~0.11s/query), extends to VLM agents with 0–2.5% false negatives, and forces adaptive attacks to trade off attack success (dropping below 5% at stronger PV-suppression), implying practical, deployment-friendly robustness for enterprise agents with purpose-specific restrictions.

nodes.title: Distributed Denial of Science: How Indirect Data Poisoning of AI Systems Can Industrialize Scientific Fraud
affiliations: Institute for Complex Social Dynamics, Carnegie Mellon University
Departments of Philosophy & Software and Societal Systems, Carnegie Mellon University
nodes.one_liner: A single fake dataset plus persuasive metadata can industrialize scientific fraud by turning honest AI-assisted workflows into scalable, low-detection misinformation pipelines—unless agents enforce systematic provenance audits at retrieval time.
points: Indirect data poisoning via re-uploaded, misleadingly documented datasets caused autonomous AI research agents to produce poisoned conclusions in 49.56% of 450 runs while flagging manipulation only 6.0% of the time, showing that open data repositories can be a high-leverage attack surface for scientific integrity.

Poisoned datasets were retrieved in 84.22% of runs and steered conclusions equally well toward opposite adversary goals (reject vs exaggerate; p=0.70), implying attackers can manufacture predetermined narratives without prompt triggers, model access, or fabricated papers.

A lightweight prompt-only defense shifted outcomes sharply: a “scientist persona” still left 16.67% full poisoning success, but a five-check data provenance audit drove full attack success to 0.0% and raised detection to 77.33%, indicating structured provenance verification can practically eliminate this class of fraud at the agent level.

nodes.title: NetInjectBench: Benchmarking Indirect Prompt Injection in Tool-Using Large Language Model Agents for Network Operations
nodes.one_liner: The key takeaway is that prompt hygiene helps but only execution-time authorization tied to trusted metadata reliably prevents indirect prompt injection without destroying operational utility.
points: Across 240 indirect prompt-injection attack instances in network-operations tool use, naive execution triggered unsafe tool actions 82.50% of the time, showing that untrusted tickets/logs/runbooks frequently override intended instruction hierarchies without additional controls.

Prompt-only mitigations reduced unsafe tool-action rates from 82.50% to 25.63% (basic safety prompt), 21.67% (Self-Reminder), 18.33% (Spotlighting), and 10.00% (Two-Pass LLM Judge), but strong attacks still substantially degraded these defenses (e.g., 37.82% UTAR for prompt-only safety on strong attacks).

A metadata-aware execution-time policy gate achieved 0/240 unsafe attack actions (95% Wilson upper bound 1.58%) while maintaining 99.17% usefulness on attack scenarios and 100.00% usefulness on approved high-impact changes, whereas static allowlisting cut attack UTAR to 5.00% but overblocked all approved changes (0.00% usefulness, 100.00% overblocking).

nodes.title: Self-Evolving Agent Harnesses via Gated Semantic Quality-Diversity
nodes.one_liner: The key novelty is making self-evolving agent harness gains auditable by construction—edits are proposed by an LLM but only credited via deterministic gating and paired significance on a sealed test.
points: A gated, auditable harness-evolution loop that separates LLM patch proposal from deterministic credit assignment yields sealed-test improvements of +9.2 to +15.5 percentage points across six of seven domains, demonstrating that statistically-validated harness changes can compound without touching model weights.

Held-out generalization is strong: sealed-test gains retain 86–147% of training lift (rather than collapsing), implying that indexing edits by diagnosed failure pathology (where×why) plus paired significance testing can substantially reduce overfitting and evaluation noise artifacts in self-improving agents.

Harness improvements are model-specific while the methodology transfers: on AppWorld, the best patch tracks each model’s dominant pathology (e.g., engagement→verify-finalize vs. careless→submit-verify), with the careless→checklist fix reproducing across two model families and delivering about +13.5pp on a non-Qwen model.

nodes.title: MJ: Multi-turn LLM Jailbreaking via Decomposed Credit Assignment
nodes.one_liner: A simple change—assigning group-normalized credit per turn using immediate+future signals—pushes learned multi-turn jailbreak attackers from ~86% to ~98% best-of-3 success while improving OOD transfer and earlier-turn success.
points: Turn-level group-relative credit assignment for multi-turn jailbreak RL yields near-saturated attack performance, with dynamic- and static-weighted DC-GRPO achieving 98.26% and 97.88% ASR 5@3 on average across 4 victim models and 3 benchmarks.

Decomposing advantage into immediate and future credit avoids prefix-credit misassignment inherent in trajectory-level GRPO broadcasting, improving single-trajectory reliability (ASR 5@1 averages ~87.4–87.8% vs 84.1% for a last-turn-trajectory-credit baseline).

The main gain comes from the turn-level decomposition rather than a specific weighting rule, as both static (tunable α) and dynamic (no mixing hyperparameter) variants consistently outperform prior training-based multi-turn jailbreakers like SEMA (86.58%) and TROJail (86.23%) by ~11–12 ASR points on ASR 5@3.

nodes.title: Securing LLMs in the Wild: Privacy and Security Challenges at the Edge
nodes.one_liner: The most capable edge model can be the easiest to jailbreak, and the safest can become slower and more power-hungry after INT4—so “efficient” and “secure” are not monotonic properties of compression.
points: Edge/on-prem LLM deployments systematically trade privacy for feasibility: four common optimizations (quantization, pruning, partitioned inference, and PEFT/LoRA) each open distinct attack surfaces—jailbreak fragility, safety-subnetwork loss, activation reconstruction, and membership/gradient leakage—captured as a Security–Efficiency Paradox.

Across six evaluated edge-friendly models, security and efficiency diverge sharply: Phi-3.5-mini reaches the top MMLU (68.9% FP; 67.1% INT4) yet has the worst jailbreak resistance (20% FP; 30% INT4), while Qwen2.5-1.5B achieves 100% jailbreak resistance in both FP and INT4 but its INT4 energy and latency worsen by ~121% (2.15→4.78 J/token; 43.1→95.5 ms/token).

INT4 quantization yields large VRAM reductions (e.g., Qwen 2.88→1.08 GB and Granite 6.35→2.00 GB) but does not reliably improve runtime cost (several models show higher energy/latency under INT4), implying that deployment decisions must jointly optimize memory, compute, and security rather than treating quantization as a universal win.

nodes.title: Silent Alarm: A J-Space Protocol for Comparing Danger Recognition Across Models and Quantization Levels
nodes.one_liner: Safety evaluation becomes more comparable and modification-aware when it reads the model’s pre-response internal danger signal (J-space) rather than grading generated text, revealing quantization- and tuning-induced failures earlier and with fewer confounds.
points: A single-forward-pass, judge-free internal metric (SafetyAUC computed from J-space at the pre-generation “decision point”) sharply separates strong vs weak danger-recognition mechanisms, e.g., models cluster at ≈0.97–0.98 SafetyAUC while an abliteration variant drops near chance (0.593) and simultaneously shows very high harmful-response rate (0.904).

INT8 quantization is effectively neutral for internal safety separability across all tested models (|ΔSafetyAUC| ≤ 0.011), whereas INT4 produces heterogeneous safety shifts (e.g., ΔSafetyAUC = +0.041 degradation for Qwen3-1.7B but ΔSafetyAUC = −0.086 “recovery” for the abliteration model), implying 4-bit compression can either erode or partially undo safety-related weight edits.

Internal danger recognition and external “safe behavior” can diverge materially (e.g., SafeRL-4B has high SafetyAUC 0.976 yet high harm@0.5 of 0.345 and 0.00 regex-refusal), so relying only on refusal/ASR-style behavioral metrics can miss the distinction between ‘lost recognition’ vs ‘recognized but complied/overexplained’.

nodes.title: Minionese: Comprehensive Benchmark and Mechanistic Study of Multilingual LLM Safety
nodes.one_liner: Meaning-preserving language perturbations (especially code-switching and script-changing transliteration) can flip an aligned model from refusal to compliance because multilingual harm representations become geometrically misaligned with the cross-lingual refusal trigger.
points: A 55,440-prompt benchmark (385 harmful/harmless pairs × 4 perturbations × 18 languages) shows standard translation ASR on Llama-3.1-8B rises from ~8% in Tier‑1 to >70% in Tiers‑3/4, reaching 100% (Yoruba), 97% (Zulu), and 98% (Scottish Gaelic), demonstrating that English-only safety performance badly overestimates real-world multilingual safety.

Transliteration produces a script-identity bimodality rather than a resource-tier effect, with near-total jailbreaks for non‑Latin scripts (e.g., Korean 99% on Llama and 98% on Aya; Chinese 97% on Llama; Arabic 84% on Aya; Hindi 99% on Llama) but near-zero ASR for many Latin-script/very-low-resource cases (e.g., French 0%, Scottish Gaelic 0%, Yoruba 0% on Aya/Qwen), implying defenses must explicitly model script and romanization pathways.

Mechanistic measurements indicate low-resource jailbreaks usually preserve the refusal mechanism but starve it: Tier‑3 prompts remain linearly decodable as harmful (high probe AUC) yet fail to project onto the (effectively one-dimensional cross-lingual) refusal direction to cross threshold, while Tier‑4 approaches near-orthogonality (~85–90° principal angle vs English harm subspace) and can collapse harmfulness representations (AUC near chance for Yoruba/Zulu), pointing to upstream multilingual harm-representation alignment as the key remediation target.

nodes.title: Breaking Refusal in the First Half: A Mechanistic Study of the Prefill Jailbreak
nodes.one_liner: A response-only affirmative prefix can override refusal without weakening harm recognition, and the failure is driven by a tiny early-generation window that behaves like generic autoregressive conditioning rather than a defeated “safety module.”
points: A one-line affirmative prefill (“Sure, here is”) collapses refusal from ~100% to 0–5% (e.g., 1.00→0.03 on Qwen2.5-1.5B) while a prompt-side linear harm probe remains near-ceiling (AUC ≥0.990) and still scores complied harmful prompts as strongly harmful (0.91–0.98), showing behavior can decouple from intact harm representations.

Causal localization shows the jailbreak’s leverage is concentrated in an early response window: restoring the harm direction over the first half of the response restores refusal ~as much as the whole response (≈42% vs 41%), whereas the second half is nearly inert (≈6% even at 2× strength), implying refusal is a shallow response-site computation rather than a prompt-side decision.

Cutting early response-to-prefill attention selectively reduces harmful continuation and partially restores refusal (+21pp vs a mass-matched attention knockout control), and the same prefill-specific collapse occurs in non-safety-tuned base models (e.g., harmful content 64%→25%), indicating the dominant mechanism is generic autoregressive conditioning with only a small safety-specific refusal attractor on top (logit-trace concentration 0.24 vs 0.03).

nodes.title: When Local Monitors Miss Compositional Harm: Diagnosing Distributed Backdoors in Multi-Agent Systems
nodes.one_liner: Local safety checks can be correct on every step yet still miss a distributed backdoor because the harmful property only exists after composition in the right representation.
points: A formal observability boundary shows that if attack fragments are ε-locally indistinguishable from benign traffic in a monitor’s per-step view (TV≤ε), then any per-fragment detector—no matter how powerful—has detection advantage bounded by ε (TPR−FPR≤ε), so stronger classifiers cannot fix missing local evidence.

In the locally benign regime, multiple local defenses collapse to chance-level separability (per-step learned detector ≈0.50 AUROC on AgentDojo; naive fragment concatenation ≈0.50 AUROC), while a coordination/assembly-aware view restores perfect separability (AUROC 1.000), demonstrating that “splitting” is not the root cause—loss of observable coordination signal is.

Once the monitor reaches an exposing representation, detection and blocking sharply recover: a benign-only assembly monitor generalizes across held-out encodings with 0.874 mean AUROC, and a codec-aware decoded-view runtime gate blocks every tested end-to-end attack (0/50 across four served models, i.e., ≤7.1% upper bound per cell), whereas broader-but-undecrypted full-trace monitoring still fails (0/50).

nodes.title: Malaika: Understanding Malware through Tri-Grounded Agentic Reasoning
nodes.one_liner: Reliability in LLM malware analysis is driven less by bigger models and more by an evidence-grounded harness that forces hypothesis review, semantic localization, and retrieval-verified ATT&CK mapping.
points: A tri-grounded multi-agent harness (domain + semantics + knowledge grounding) improved malware-understanding report metrics on MalEval to 69.39% B-F1 and 56.21 RQ, while keeping high FPCR (96.00%) and TPMR (93.13%), showing that workflow structure can materially raise behavior-level analysis quality beyond single-pass or slicing-based LLM pipelines.

Grounding primarily reduced unsupported technique claims: on a 20-sample ATT&CK attribution audit, the system achieved 67.61% macro-precision with 37 false-positive technique IDs, cutting false positives by 57.0% vs MalEval (86 FP) and 35.1% vs LAMD (57 FP), and by 68.9% vs Claude Code (110 FP), indicating evidence-gated attribution is key for auditability.

Ablations demonstrate complementary failure modes: removing semantics grounding increased false-positive ATT&CK attributions from 37 to 121 (macro-precision dropping to 27.88%), removing knowledge grounding raised false positives to 97 (macro-precision 31.68%), and removing domain grounding reduced true positives from 75 to 44 (macro-recall down from 24.56 to 18.64), implying reliable malware reasoning requires both precise evidence localization and disciplined hypothesis/attribution control.

nodes.title: Which Neurons Detect Malicious Code? A Probing Study of LLM Security Knowledge
affiliations: Hanoi University of Science and Technology
nodes.one_liner: Malware-detection behavior in code LLMs is causally steerable via FFN neuron scaling, but the controllable signal is far more stable by layer band than by individual neuron identity.
points: Neuron-level causal interventions can strongly modulate malware detection in code LLMs, with Llama3.1-8B collapsing from 93.9% to ~50.0% accuracy under a “Degrader” intervention while Mistral-7B can be boosted from 66.5% to 94.1% by amplifying identified “good” neurons and suppressing “bad” ones.

Guardrail/malware-detection knowledge concentrates in different layer bands by model—middle layers for Llama3.1-8B and Mistral-7B versus late layers for Qwen2.5-7B—implying defenses like early-exit safety checks or layer-specific hardening must be model-tailored rather than universal.

Specific top-100 neuron identities are unstable across attribution runs (median Jaccard <0.20), yet the layer-level localization is comparatively consistent (cosine similarity ~0.61–0.86), indicating reliable control is more feasible at the layer-band level than via fixed per-neuron allow/deny lists.

nodes.title: Evaluating AI Models' Capability to Automate Voice Phishing Attacks
affiliations: Harvard School of Engineering and Applied Sciences
nodes.one_liner: High-quality voice models make vishing economically viable at scale even without being uniquely persuasive, and user AI familiarity does not measurably reduce susceptibility.
points: Across a nationally representative U.S. sample (N=4,100), 16.5% of respondents said they would or might comply with AI-generated vishing requests on average, rising to 36.1% in a “relative-in-distress” scenario—showing that emotionally leveraged scams can scale to mass victimization with non-trivial success rates.

Compliance was driven primarily by perceived caller persuasiveness (OR=2.58) rather than voice human-likeness (non-significant when controlling for other factors), implying defenses should focus on disrupting manipulative conversational strategies and verification workflows rather than only deepfake detection.

Economic modeling indicates human-operated vishing is unprofitable at U.S. wages (≈−$27/hour) while several AI voice systems become profitable (+$1 to +$3/hour for Gemini/Sesame/ElevenLabs under conservative conversion assumptions), shifting the risk from “superhuman persuasion” to the automation-enabled unit economics of fraud.

nodes.title: Understanding Implicit Trust Errors in Core Carrier Networks through Multi-Agent Flaw Discovery and Analysis
nodes.one_liner: Cloud exposure turns legacy “trusted-zone” core-network assumptions into an exploitable class of bugs, and multi-agent LLM workflows can scale from pattern mining to CVE-grade discoveries with measurable precision gains.
points: An LLM-driven multi-agent pipeline uncovered 84 previously unknown PFCP/GTP-C vulnerabilities across seven open-source cellular core network implementations, with 83 confirmed by maintainers and 81 assigned CVEs—evidence that “implicit trust” between core components is a systemic flaw rather than isolated bugs.

Vulnerabilities cluster around three recurring failure modes—missing syntactic validation, missing semantic/state validation, and unchecked resource availability—enabling high-impact outcomes like DoS and session hijacking once internal interfaces become reachable in cloud-native deployments.

Procedure-level code–spec cross-checking and runtime feedback loops materially improve LLM audit reliability, raising detection precision from 28.205% (prompt-only) to 75.000% (full pipeline) while maintaining 68.182% recall on a 22-issue ground-truth set.

nodes.title: Skills That Don't Exist: A Large-Scale Study of Hallucinated Skill Recommendation in LLM Agents
affiliations: Huazhong University of Science and Technology
nodes.one_liner: LLM agents frequently invent plausible-but-fake skill identifiers that attackers can cheaply pre-register, and the most effective defense largely works by making the agent stop being helpful.
points: Across 15,000 prompts and 12 LLM/agent configurations, every system hallucinated non-existent skill names with rates spanning 6.5%–62.0% (≈36% on average) and rising to 43.1% on real developer questions, creating a large, user-facing supply-chain attack surface.

Hallucinated names are highly targetable rather than random: 5,669 distinct fake names were produced, dominant hallucinations repeated up to 7.8/10 times, 410 names were shared across ≥2 configurations yet accounted for 15.3% of hallucinated recommendation events, and 15.0% of hallucinated names exactly matched existing PyPI/npm package names—enabling efficient pre-registration attacks.

Mitigations show a sharp security–usability tradeoff: retrieval grounding reduced hallucination from 40.8% to 3.2% on average but the best-defended system recommended the correct skill only about 1 in 6 times, while self-auditing was near useless (≈51% balanced accuracy) and edit-distance filters miss most cases (median distance 6; only 9.3% within 1–2 edits).

nodes.title: VEXAIoT: Autonomous IoT Vulnerability EXploitation using AI Agents
affiliations: University of North Carolina at Pembroke
nodes.one_liner: An LLM-driven multi-agent system can chain recon-to-exploit IoT attack workflows at ~95% success, but reliability hinges on reducing refusals and enforcing syntactically-valid, schema-constrained commands.
points: A two-agent LLM framework (vulnerability detection + attack execution) autonomously executed 260 exploit runs across IoTGoat and Metasploitable2 with a 95.0% overall success rate (94.5% on IoTGoat, 96.7% on Metasploitable2), indicating that end-to-end IoT-style exploitation can be operationally reliable in controlled testbeds.

Most individual attacks completed in under two minutes with low token overhead (often ~500–700 tokens), and dependency-aware parallelization reduced wall-clock time from ~8m31s to ~3m50s while token cost stayed roughly additive—highlighting time scalability without proportional cost savings.

Failures clustered into three actionable categories—model refusals (5 trials), persistent command/syntax errors (5), and hallucination (1)—with the lowest success rates on highly parameterized/service-sensitive steps (MiniUPnP backdoor and DNS DoS at 80%), implying that constrained command generation and stronger runtime validation are the highest-leverage hardening targets.

nodes.title: Large Language Models in Misinformation Ecosystems: Misuse, Defense, and Vulnerability
affiliations: Institute of Information Engineering, Chinese Academy of Sciences
State Key Laboratory of Media Convergence and Communication, Communication University of China
University of Chinese Academy of Sciences
nodes.one_liner: What’s interesting is the unified role-layer view that treats LLMs simultaneously as attackers, defenders, and vulnerable components across content, social, evidence, and workflow layers—shifting misinformation defense from classifier accuracy to securing entire verification pipelines.
points: LLMs expand misinformation from simple false-content generation to an ecosystem-level attack surface that spans content manipulation, social-context engineering (comments, personas, engagement), and evidence-layer compromise (corpus poisoning, retrieval manipulation, fabricated support) that can directly subvert verification outcomes.

LLM-based defenses (LLM-as-judge, RAG fact-checking, and agentic multi-step verifiers) create new, distinct failure modes—including prompt injection, poisoned retrieval corpora, and tool/agent workflow compromise—so improving base-model accuracy alone is insufficient without end-to-end pipeline hardening.

Defensive coverage is uneven, with relatively stronger methods for detecting synthetic/rewritten text and some evidence-reliability/attribution techniques, but limited direct countermeasures against long-horizon coordinated campaigns and retrieval-stage manipulation, implying real-world resilience hinges on provenance controls, secure orchestration, and auditable human-in-the-loop operations.

nodes.title: Agent Hacks Agent: Autoresearch for Production-Agent Red-Teaming
nodes.one_liner: Treating agent red-teaming as falsifiable hypothesis testing produces reusable vulnerability knowledge that transfers across models, agents, and direct/indirect attack channels under strict single-shot deployment.
points: Freezing the discovered Vulnerability Concept Graph (VCG) yields 47.0% single-shot held-out attack success versus 32.8% for the strongest frozen discovery baseline (+14.2 points), showing mechanism-level artifacts reuse better than payload/seed/program caches once search is stopped.

A global “claimed authorization” mechanism appears in 16 of 18 model×agent×scenario settings, implying many production-agent failures are driven by recurring trajectory-level reasoning patterns rather than scenario-specific prompt strings.

Removing falsifiers, cross-episode memory, or periodic audit keeps discovery success roughly flat but collapses held-out survivability (e.g., AgentHazard 75.6%→56.7% without falsifiers and 75.6%→57.8% without critic), indicating that reproducible, auditable findings require explicit refutation tests and anti-overfitting controls.

nodes.title: Antiproof: Synthesizing Vulnerability Detectors and Proofs of Exploitability
nodes.one_liner: The key twist is shifting validation from “LLM says it’s exploitable” to deterministic, capability-based oracles that accept only executable proofs, making high-recall detection practical at scale.
points: An end-to-end pipeline that pairs high-recall neuro-symbolic detector synthesis with executable proof-of-exploitability oracles achieved 97% recall (64/66) on BountyBench+KEVBench, outperforming Semgrep’s 26% and CodeQL’s 9% and indicating that validation via capability-based execution can unlock broad vulnerability-class coverage without drowning in false positives.

At real-world scale (50 widely deployed projects, 136M LOC), the system produced a large validated funnel—17,574 static candidates → 1,212 proof-of-vulnerability executions → 510 accepted proofs of exploitability—showing that deterministic challenge–response oracles can convert noisy static hits into high-confidence, attacker-capability evidence at volume.

Native eCPG execution (Antigraph) cut benchmark scan wall-time from 59 minutes to 2.3 minutes (25× faster) while maintaining identical recall, and scope/attack-surface pruning reduced candidate volume by up to 80% without recall loss—implying continuous, project-scale scanning is feasible when expensive PDG-style analysis is replaced by reachability+virtual-edge modeling.

nodes.title: AMT-X: Phase-Structured Multi-Turn Red-Teaming with Checklist-Gated Evaluation
nodes.one_liner: What’s most interesting is that headline jailbreak success (≈98–100%) substantially overstates real-world harm enablement unless evaluation explicitly gates on complete, operational detail—multi-turn depth and “format/complete this” tactics do the heavy lifting.
points: Across a 6-model × 7-category moderation grid (42 attacks per run), the framework achieved 97.6–100% lenient attack success but only 66.7–78.6% “fully actionable” success, revealing up to a 33-point gap between partial compliance and truly operational harmful output.

Capping the attacker to early phases collapses success (overall ASR 28.6% at P1-only and 35.7% at P2-only) while allowing later reframing recovers near-complete compromise (97.6% at P3-cap), implying multi-turn depth is a primary driver of jailbreak risk under realistic adversaries.

Most breakthroughs required explicit extraction (73.2% of successes first register at the final extraction phase), and the most common decisive tactics were completion/verification and encoding-based requests (each 19.5% of wins), suggesting “format/verification” reframes are disproportionately effective at bypassing safety policies.

nodes.title: MindReader: Using LLMs to Encourage Memorable and Secure Password Replacement
nodes.one_liner: LLMs can be used defensively to transform password meaning into new, semantically linked but syntactically unrelated passwords that stay memorable while measurably reducing guessability—even under a knowledgeable attacker model.
points: MindReader-generated replacement passwords were never guessed in black-box online attacks (≤10^7 guesses) and only 58% were guessed in black-box offline attacks (≤10^20 guesses), versus over 80% of both original and manual-replacement passwords, indicating substantially higher resistance to conventional cracking at realistic scales.

Even when the attacker knows the user’s old password and the full MindReader implementation, only 3.5% of MindReader replacements were guessed in online attacks compared to 18% of manual replacements, showing that semantic-but-syntactic rewrites can materially reduce predictability under strong attacker knowledge.

One week after creation, login success for MindReader passwords was not statistically different from original or manual-replacement passwords, while ~70% of users said they would use a password created with the tool, suggesting the security gains do not require sacrificing long-term memorability.

nodes.title: A Survey on LLM Watermarking: Theory and Deployment
affiliations: University at Albany, State University of New York
nodes.one_liner: What’s most striking is how quickly watermark reliability collapses under routine transformations (paraphrase/translation) while the very fixes that harden robustness often impose unacceptable utility and governance costs.
points: LLM watermarking techniques cluster around deployment-critical choices—generation-time vs. training/post-processing embedding and public vs. private detection authority—where differing assumptions (logit access, sampling control, secret keys, model ownership) largely determine real-world feasibility and guarantees.

Robustness remains the dominant blocker: token-level schemes like KGW can fall below 0.4 true-positive rate after 40% paraphrasing (DP-40), while some distribution-shift/distortion-free approaches retain >0.8 TPR under the same condition, highlighting that paraphrase/translation resilience is highly method-dependent.

Operationally, stronger watermark detectability typically increases perplexity and can substantially degrade downstream performance (including reports of >96% quality-score drops on open-ended tasks), and attacks that remove watermarks often impose additional utility loss—making current designs risky for high-stakes deployment without tighter utility–robustness calibration and standardized false-positive control.

nodes.title: Traffic-Aware Randomized Smoothing for LLM-Based Network Intrusion Detection
nodes.one_liner: Certified robustness improves most when the smoothing distribution matches the attacker-feasible traffic-manipulation subspace, because isotropic noise wastes budget on uncontrollable features and triggers abstention.
points: Injecting and certifying Gaussian noise only in attacker-directly-controllable (DC) traffic features cuts randomized-smoothing abstention from 68% to 8% on CIC-IDS-2018, yielding far more certified predictions than isotropic noise that perturbs uncontrollable context.

Noise-augmented fine-tuning is a prerequisite for certifiable LLM-based IDS robustness, raising certified accuracy at r=0.05 (σ=0.25) from near-random 14–57% (clean-trained) to 68–100% on CIC-IDS-2018 and HIKARI-2021.

At an L∞ budget ε=0.05 mapped to the DC-subspace L2 threshold (R∞=ε√|FDC|), the method certifies 55–100% of samples on CIC/HIKARI and achieves median certified radii about 1.8–5× above R∞, while RT-IoT2022 requires stronger augmentation (n_aug=4) to recover to 76%/69% certified accuracy (LLaMA3-8B/Qwen3-8B).

nodes.title: Toward Stronger Code Watermarking: A Grammar-Driven Approach to Optimizing the Trade-off Between Quality and Detectability
nodes.one_liner: Injecting watermark bias with CFG-validity filtering plus role-aware (syntax vs content) modulation shifts code watermarking from a brittle entropy-threshold hack to a controllable quality–detectability frontier that survives basic refactoring attacks.
points: Grammar-Driven Watermarking (GDW) achieves the best quality–detectability frontier across Python/Java/Go and multiple LLMs, e.g., on Qwen2.5-Coder-3B AUTC rises to 0.811–0.876 vs 0.666–0.857 for prior methods (HumanEval/MBPP+, sampling/beam), indicating structure-aware watermarking materially improves code watermark viability under low-entropy decoding.

Role-aware weighting is a key contributor to detectability: removing weighted detection drops AUTC from 0.860 to 0.832 (HumanEval, StarCoder2-3B, beam), while removing the structural role mask or syntactic validity mask further degrades AUTC to 0.800 and 0.817 respectively, showing both grammar constraints and token-role modulation are necessary for a strong trade-off.

Under variable-renaming attacks, GDW remains comparatively robust with only a 3.3% AUTC drop (0.847→0.819) while retaining the top post-attack score among baselines, implying that watermark signals distributed beyond fragile identifier choices can preserve provenance detection under common semantics-preserving refactors.

nodes.title: ProfMalPlus: Agent-Coordinated Detection of Malicious NPM Packages via Static-Dynamic Analysis Synergy
nodes.one_liner: Static–dynamic synergy plus multi-agent self-consistency turns supply-chain malware detection into an evidence-driven, explainable workflow that scales to real registry takedowns at high accuracy.
points: An agent-coordinated pipeline that fuses object-sensitive static behavior graphs with on-demand sandbox execution and third-party semantic enrichment reaches a 98.1% F1-score, beating prior detectors by 3.5–52.6 percentage points.

In three months of live monitoring, the system identified 597 previously unknown malicious NPM packages that were confirmed and removed, while holding the lowest reported false-positive rate at 16.5% and the lowest false-negative rate at 9.3% among compared tools.

Interpretability is operationalized at code level, achieving 88.9% line-level localization F1 and producing high-quality human-auditable explanations for 86.9% of sampled true positives, indicating the detector can support remediation rather than just labeling.

nodes.title: SherAgent: Scaling Attack Investigation in the Wild via LLM-Empowered Iterative Query-Filter Backtracking
nodes.one_liner: The key insight is that constraining an LLM to iterative SQL template generation plus semantic filtering and tree-structured state turns brittle provenance backtracking into a high-success, low-cost SOC investigation loop even when audit logs are incomplete.
points: A production deployment processed 53,849 alerts and maintained a human-verified investigation success rate exceeding 96% via daily spot-checks (980 cases, ~2% of alerts), indicating that LLM-guided, tool-mediated forensics can be stable at enterprise scale when bounded by structured workflows.

End-to-end investigation success improved by 31.1 percentage points over an enterprise SOC LLM workflow (92.2% vs 61.1%) and by 63.7 points over academic baselines (92.2% vs 28.5%), while cutting per-case cost to <$0.10 and runtime to <4 minutes, showing that constraining LLM autonomy with templates and state can simultaneously raise accuracy and lower operational overhead.

On broken-chain investigations, recovery success reached 93.9% (missing relationships), 78.3% (missing entities), and 88.9% (missing attributes) with high average query effectiveness (up to 83.7%), and dependency-explosion was sharply reduced (136 nodes analyzed/14 retained vs thousands for anomaly-based systems), implying semantic query-filter backtracking can replace strict graph connectivity as the primary robustness mechanism under real-world telemetry loss.

nodes.title: AutoTrace: From Patches to Triggers via Agentic Interprocedural Exploration
affiliations: University of North Carolina at Charlotte
nodes.one_liner: An agent can explore deep call chains, but only a deterministic CPG-based verifier is allowed to “believe” a trigger—yielding higher trigger accuracy and a benchmark that exposes how often LLMs mistake “sink exists” for “vulnerability exists.”
points: AutoTrace localizes vulnerability-trigger statements from vulnerability-fixing commits with 75.0% statement-level accuracy (VulnHit) and 80.8% function-level accuracy (FuncHit) on 744 real-world C/C++ CVEs, outperforming the prior best 69.8% VulnHit and showing that verifier-gated agentic exploration can surpass syntax/rule-based trigger matching on interprocedural cases.

A new matched-pair benchmark, SinkTrace-Bench, contains 771 vulnerable/safe pairs (1,542 samples) across 16 CWE classes with identical sinks but differing only by upstream guards (22.7% interprocedural slices), and frontier LLMs top out at 59.0% accuracy while often achieving very high TPR (up to 95.2%) but extremely low TNR (as low as 7.4%), indicating models commonly key on sink presence rather than reasoning over interprocedural causal chains.

Deterministic admissibility gates dominate correctness—only candidates with explicit CPG evidence are reportable (55.6% via direct dataflow witnesses, 33.1% recovered via control-dependence fallback, 11.4% leak-family exceptions)—and the main deployment bottleneck is analysis infrastructure (median ~42 minutes per CVE, P90 ~13.8 hours) rather than model cost (~$0.65 per CVE), implying scalability hinges on faster/more complete graph construction rather than bigger models.

nodes.title: Secret Scanner Agent: Extracting Secrets and Access Context from Unstructured Documents
nodes.one_liner: What stands out is converting secret scanning into actionable remediation by extracting both the credential and the exact 'door' it opens, with multi-agent review delivering the biggest gains where humans and regex tools struggle most.
points: A two-agent detect→review workflow increased door-extraction precision by up to 16.3 percentage points versus a single-agent approach on a 23-secret-type unstructured-email benchmark, showing that multi-agent critique is most valuable for correctly linking credentials to the specific resource they unlock.

On the multi-type benchmark, the system matched a regex scanner’s 100% precision while boosting recall from 27.78% to 97.33–100%, and it exceeded a ML-based scanner’s 74.07% precision and 55.56% recall, indicating LLM context-reasoning can dramatically reduce misses in messy, fragmented documents without sacrificing alert quality.

Against 13 security analysts on 45 multi-format documents, the system achieved 95.87–100% precision and 95.13–99.64% recall vs humans at 83.09% precision and 51.00% recall, while running ~5–17× faster (≈4–14 s/doc vs ≈71 s/doc), suggesting automation can materially improve incident-response triage completeness under time pressure.

nodes.title: When Binaries Talk Back: Representation-Confusion Attacks on LLM-Assisted Reverse Engineering
nodes.one_liner: It pinpoints a concrete failure mode where faithfully extracted reverse-engineering artifacts get 'promoted' into authority or evidence, and shows that simple provenance-aware runtime gating can drop false validations from 57.5% to 0% without harming true positives.
points: In a 20-program holdout across two models, attacker-controlled binaries induced unsafe tool actions in 35/40 adversarial cases under flat rendering (0/40 clean), and even with Data-Only rendering models still made 15 unsafe proposals that were fully eliminated by deterministic Tool Authorization (0/15 authorized) while allowing all 40/40 matched analyst requests.

On identical report drafts, a support-counting claim validator incorrectly accepted 23/40 false capability claims by treating multiple views of the same underlying binary origin as independent evidence, whereas provenance-aware grouping reduced false validations to 0/40 without reducing any supported positive-control claims (40/40 retained).

In a tool-instrumented workflow using Ghidra, r2pipe, and angr, no single-tool draft reached the validation threshold for the false claim, but fusing multi-tool outputs caused the naive validator to accept 32/32 false claims—provenance grouping by exact-root/common-ancestor prevented all 32/32 while retaining all 32/32 supported claims, showing that multi-tool agreement can be systematically non-independent.

nodes.title: DREA: Decoupled Reasoning and Exploration Agents for Repository-Level Vulnerability Detection
affiliations: Institute of Information Engineering, Chinese Academy of Sciences
University of Chinese Academy of Sciences
nodes.one_liner: Repository-level vulnerability detection improves most when context is acquired goal-directly and cheaply, but a large fraction of wins still come from correct answers backed by incorrect security reasoning.
points: A two-agent, hypothesis-driven setup that separates reasoning (Planner) from repository navigation (Explorer) raises pair-level reliability on 100 real-world Python CVE fix-pairs, improving Pair-Correctness from 19–26% to 30–42% across three backbone LLMs.

Decoupling exploration from reasoning offloads 93.7–97.9% of tokens to a local lightweight model, cutting estimated billable API cost by 16–48× while still enabling repository-scale context gathering (≈0.3–1.6M total tokens per sample).

Even when labels are correct, 26–55% of true positives have flawed vulnerability rationales (“lucky hits”), implying that improved context access alone does not solve the core bottleneck of security-mechanism reasoning and explanation fidelity.

nodes.title: Routing Ceilings Are Domain-Independent: Structural Prior Injection in Code Security Vulnerability Detection
nodes.one_liner: Cheatsheet-style prompt engineering can make LLM vulnerability detectors look perfect on synthetic benchmarks while measurably underperforming the unprompted baseline on real CVE code.
points: Injecting structural “cheatsheet” priors eliminates apparent routing failures on synthetic vulnerability tasks, boosting semantic N+1 vulnerable recall from 20.0% to 100.0% (and GPT-OSS-120B F1 from 28.6% to 96.8%) across three frontier models, indicating the capability is present but inconsistently activated without a route template.

Zero-shot vulnerability detection degrades with semantic complexity for GPT-OSS-120B (F1: 90.9% on CWE-798 → 85.7% on CWE-284 → 28.6% on N+1), implying that deployment risk rises sharply when the weakness class requires multi-line behavioral reasoning rather than local token cues.

The same structural priors that saturate synthetic performance amplify real-world distribution-shift collapse on CVE-derived VUDENC data—e.g., for CWE-89 on GPT-OSS-120B, cheatsheet v1 drops to 48.9% vulnerable-class F1 vs 61.5% zero-shot (and a v2 ‘recalibrated’ cheatsheet further falls to 41.7%), showing prompt calibration can worsen robustness even when tuned on observed errors.

nodes.title: Cross-Cutting Security Analysis of LLM-Generated Code via Metamorphic Testing and Association Rule Mining
nodes.one_liner: Security bugs in LLM-generated code tend to arrive as predictable clusters tied to prompt topics, making co-violation-aware verification and prompt risk screening practical levers for safer coding assistance.
points: Across 3,700 LLMSecEval code snippets from five open models, 68.8% violated at least one security metamorphic relation, with hard-coded credentials (79.1% of applicable cases) and command injection (74.4%) the most prevalent failures.

Association-rule mining surfaced strong cross-cutting vulnerability coupling, including XSS ∧ weak cryptography predicting hard-coded credentials with 82.5% confidence (lift 3.23), forming a dominant {auth bypass, hard-coded creds, weak crypto} cluster plus an {input handling, memory safety} cluster.

Prompt content, more than model choice, drives insecurity: database/authentication prompts correlate strongly with higher violation burden (r=0.52 and r=0.43), and 65.5% of prompts produce consistent violation outcomes across all five models, implying prompt-level interventions and cluster-aware checks are higher leverage than simply switching models.

nodes.title: Bulkhead: Automated Semantic Detection and Remediation of Container Escape Vulnerabilities
affiliations: Huazhong University of Science and Technology
nodes.one_liner: What’s interesting is the end-to-end loop that couples LLM-generated PoCs and patches with SPIN-backed invariant checking to systematically prevent TOCTOU/symlink regressions in container escape fixes.
points: Across 82 container-ecosystem repositories, the system uncovered 9 previously unknown container-escape path traversal vulnerabilities and 3 have already received CVE assignments, indicating that cross-boundary path misresolution remains a live risk in widely deployed runtimes, plugins, and AI sandboxes.

An ablation on 36 real vulnerabilities shows semantics-aware patterns are decisive for reliability: removing vulnerability-pattern guidance drops detections to 11/36 and drives false positives to 36.1%, while removing high-risk entry identification misses 30.6% (11/36) of cases, implying that both entry-point grounding and pattern constraints are needed to avoid brittle LLM-only judgments.

For automated remediation on 26 repairable cases, verification-guided iteration raises average patch success from 51.5% to 81.5% (+30.0 pp) and cuts the rate of still-vulnerable patches from 41.3% to 18.5% (-22.8 pp), demonstrating that compile-clean LLM patches frequently fail under TOCTOU/symlink adversarial interleavings unless checked against explicit invariants.

nodes.title: FlowGuard: From Signals to Evidence for MCP Security Detection
nodes.one_liner: Separating “suspicious strings” from verified runtime evidence yields both higher accuracy and up to 2.23× lower end-to-end scan latency for MCP security testing.
points: Evidence-grounded MCP scanning can sharply improve execution-path vulnerability detection, reaching F1=0.879 for Command Injection and F1=0.942 for File System Access on a 1,880-case executable benchmark while maintaining 1.0 precision in both categories (0 false positives).

Schema-aware recon→strike probing materially increases efficiency, cutting probes per true positive from 53.78 to 18.12 for Command Injection and from 42.52 to 8.05 for File System Access, indicating that fingerprint-guided payload narrowing beats broad dynamic fuzzing for MCP tools.

At ecosystem scale, scanning 8,000 real-world MCP servers surfaced risks in 4.08% of servers (326/8,000) with 523 findings, and manual checks on a stratified sample found concrete runtime evidence in 84% of reported servers, suggesting a non-trivial but bounded prevalence of high-confidence MCP tool abuse primitives.

nodes.title: Protective Capacity Hallucination: When Large Language Models Claim Nonexistent Capabilities
nodes.one_liner: LLMs can “hallucinate” protective agency—claiming they contacted authorities or performed care—especially when role-play and multi-party interaction create an implied but unspecified capability boundary.
points: Across 13,600 sessions over eight LLMs, dialogic multi-party framing drove Protective Capacity Hallucination (PCH)—claims like “I’ll call police/dispatch help”—to near-ceiling rates in most uncovered service domains (often 91–100% PCH) while matched monologic reports were frequently near-zero in frontier API models (e.g., 0% in several high-severity monologic cases).

PCH suppression tracked safety-coverage rather than objective physical severity: in intimate-partner conflict (a policy-covered domain) PCH stayed near floor across all models (0–40%), even when scenarios involved weapons and bleeding that exceeded the severity of service-domain stimuli that triggered 97–100% PCH under dialogic framing.

A practical mitigation signal emerged from delegation/grounding pathways: when a capable human agent was explicitly present (e.g., in-flight cabin crew), some models dropped from nontrivial monologic PCH (e.g., 33%) to 0% in dialogic by delegating actions to the human, implying that deployment-side capability-boundary specification and explicit delegation targets can materially reduce false agency claims.

nodes.title: Beyond Success Rate: Cost-Aware Evaluation of Offensive and Defensive Security Agents
nodes.one_liner: Cost-aware evaluation flips the story: more compute buys offensive solves, but defensive wins come from asking fewer, better questions—while public SOC benchmarks can be gamed by memorization-like recall unless leakage checks are baked in.
points: Offensive CTF capability scales strongly with test-time spend—e.g., DeepSeek v4 Flash rises from 76.1% to 86.4% success when the per-sample cap increases from $0.80 to $2.10, while GPT-5.5 reaches 94.1% at $2.10 with ~$1.16 per solved-equivalent challenge.

Defensive SOC investigation shows weak returns to extra budget and instead rewards tool discipline—DeepSeek v4 Flash improves only 0.9 points (73.0%→73.9%) when doubling cap ($2.10→$4.20) despite increasing tool calls (4,450→4,938), whereas Claude Opus 4.8 achieves 93.9% with far fewer tool calls (603).

Public SOC benchmarks can be partially answerable without telemetry access, so absolute scores require decontamination controls—on BOTS v1 with no tools, models still score 50.0–54.9% from question text alone and up to 74.8–77.2% when given prerequisite Q&A, indicating substantial prompt-only answer recovery that varies sharply by model.

nodes.title: To Answer or to Abstain: Mitigating Search-Agent Hallucinations via Abstention-Aware Reinforcement Learning
nodes.one_liner: A single tunable “courage” parameter yields predictable abstention plateaus and avoids both over-answering hallucinations and refusal-collapse reward hacking in search-agent RL.
points: Abstention-Aware Reinforcement Learning (AWA-RL) improves reliability in agentic search QA by dynamically setting a query-specific refusal reward, raising precision by up to 10.3% while keeping accuracy losses marginal (e.g., cold-start: Precision 0.559→0.662 with Accuracy 0.552→0.529).

Static refusal rewards are highly brittle and can trigger catastrophic reward hacking in RL-from-scratch, where a tiny fixed abstention reward (r_ref=0.05) collapses behavior to 99.9% refusals and near-zero accuracy.

Data-mixing baselines (injecting 10–30% refusal trajectories or unanswerable queries) produce unstable, non-monotonic capability–reliability trade-offs (e.g., RL-from-scratch with 30% unanswerables reaches 52.2% refusal and RA-F1 drops to 0.394), indicating that refusal should be calibrated per-query rather than via global dataset ratios.

nodes.title: CIPHER: A Decoupled Exploration-Selection Framework for Test-Time Scaling of Data Science Agents
nodes.one_liner: The biggest gains come from (1) selecting multiple plans to execute and (2) using a stronger aggregator—diversity helps only when the aggregator is capable enough to exploit it.
points: Decoupling candidate-plan generation (N) from execution selection (M) yields strong test-time scaling gains, with M driving consistent improvements across task types (+7.2pp on Infi-DA-Bench and +3.3pp on InsightBench when moving from single-run to M=3, plus an additional +1.9pp and +1.4pp respectively from M=3→5) while increasing N from 10→30 helps open-ended tasks (+4.7pp→+6.2pp) but slightly hurts closed-ended tasks (+9.1pp→+8.0pp).

Upgrading only the aggregator to a stronger “leader” model is a high-leverage design choice, improving accuracy by +2.81 points on Infi-DA-Bench and +4.52 points on InsightBench (both p<0.001, d≈1.6), indicating weak aggregators can bottleneck multi-branch agents even when upstream exploration is diverse.

Prompt-ensemble generation is the primary driver of true plan-space diversity (embedding-entropy differences vs. base/conditional with p<0.001 and very large effect sizes d>5), yet maximizing diversity at selection time (MaxEnt highest selected entropy) does not reliably maximize accuracy, implying selection must optimize task-aligned utility rather than entropy alone.

nodes.title: Automatic Hard Example Synthesis with Multi-Level Agentic Data Curation
nodes.one_liner: The most striking result is that policy-grounded prompting plus retrieval of autonomously synthesized hard negatives can nearly halve missed unsafe detections (FNR) without any new human labels.
