Completion behavior was largely neutralized by evidence steering, with 90.0% of 638 valid completion attempts grounded in decoy provenance (SubDefuse), showing that controlling the agent’s “belief state” can be as important as blocking individual exploits.

End-to-end impact was decisive: across 45 attacker–CVE pairs on CVE-Bench at pass@3, verified real-target exploitation dropped to 0/45 (vs. 18/45 under static defenses and 10–12/45 under prior honeypots), suggesting trajectory-level deception can fully suppress successful exploitation under realistic budgets.

nodes.title: Isolated but Exposed: Persistence-Based Memory Extraction Attack on LLM Agents
affiliations: State Key Laboratory of Cryptography and Digital Economy Security, Shandong University
Shandong Key Laboratory of Artificial Intelligence Security, Shandong University
nodes.one_liner: Tool interfaces—not shared memory—are the key privacy break: a single compromised tool can persistently steer an agent to leak isolated long-term memories and even tie them to user identities via OAuth.
points: Even with strict per-user long-term memory isolation, agents can leak private LTM records through tool-call parameters, enabling a malicious tool to exfiltrate data without ever crossing user-level access controls.

A persistence-based tool-side attack (SPORE) reaches 80.0% record extraction with frequent triggering and still extracts 47.0% of LTM using only 20 legitimate user tool invocations, showing that platform tool-call limits reduce but do not prevent high-throughput leakage.

In multi-user deployments, OAuth 2.1 identity claims allow attackers to associate extracted memories with specific users, turning bulk memory scraping into identity-linked profiling suitable for targeted surveillance and personalized attacks.

nodes.title: MemSecBench: Tracking Agent Memory Poisoning from Persistence to Consequence and Repair
affiliations: Institute of Cyberspace Security, Zhejiang University of Technology
Binjiang Institute of Artificial Intelligence, ZJUT
College of Information Engineering, Zhejiang University of Technology
nodes.one_liner: Interesting because it evaluates agent memory poisoning as an end-to-end lifecycle problem—persistence, delayed consequence, and selective repair—revealing that backend choice can swing attack success and recovery quality by double-digit percentage points without a universal “safest” option.
points: Across 24 agent–memory–LLM configurations and 310 lifecycle cases, malicious instructions persisted in long-term memory in 84.2% of cases and produced a fully externalized harmful outcome in 50.3%, indicating that current agent memory stacks often turn single-session exposure into cross-session compromise.

The largest drop in the attack chain occurs at the adoption step (E2), where success falls from 76.1% recall exposure to 53.7% adoption, implying that defenses that specifically prevent recalled memory from becoming decision policy are likely higher leverage than retrieval-only filtering.

Selective repair remains unreliable: while 86.3% of poisoned cases can remove or neutralize the malicious memory (F1), only 56.1% achieve repair without losing required benign memories (SRSR), showing that “delete the bad entry” approaches frequently cause collateral memory damage that undermines safe recovery.

nodes.title: IH-Benchmark: A Conflict-Centered Benchmark for Instruction-Hierarchy Robustness in LLM Applications
nodes.one_liner: Privilege separation in LLM apps breaks most often at the tool boundary, and the failures that slip through are frequently subtle integrity attacks (minor distortions and injected framing) rather than overtly malicious actions.
points: Across 37 evaluated LLM variants, instruction-hierarchy conflict compliance spans 98.2% to 20.5%, indicating that robust privilege separation across message/tool channels is still not a default capability even for widely deployed models.

Strong direct SYSTEM≻USER compliance is a weak predictor of resilience to tool-output injection (USER≻TOOL), with some models scoring ~97% on S≻U yet dropping to ~66% on U≻T, implying that agentic deployments require dedicated tool-surface evaluation rather than relying on classic prompt-hierarchy tests.

Tool-output attacks that induce subtle presentation or factual drift are disproportionately effective (hardest U≻T families near ~50%: content-lie 50.1% and format-disclaimer 50.4%) compared to overtly dangerous actions that models often resist (e.g., close 97.2%, purchase 88.1%), suggesting real-world risk concentrates in “quiet” integrity degradation rather than obvious policy violations.

nodes.title: HoF-Bench: Rediscovering Real AI-Discovered CVEs Without Frontier Models
nodes.one_liner: HoF-Bench shows that rediscovering real, disclosed CVEs is often a systems-and-repeatability problem—cheap models plus repeated runs and portfolio diversity can match or beat single stronger runs, but large C codebases remain the hard frontier.
points: A deliberately minimal LLM-based scanner, given a target-file oracle but no CVE metadata, strictly rediscovered up to 65 of 95 real AI-discovered CVEs (68%), while no frontier model was used for detection anywhere in the evaluation.

Reliability is the dominant lever: moving from one pass to four repeated passes increased rediscovery by roughly 12–20 CVEs per model, and 62% of successes appeared in only 1–3 of 4 identical runs—meaning single-run scores materially understate capability.

Difficulty is strongly language-structured: JavaScript CVEs were nearly fully recoverable (best model 24/24; none missed by all with context), PHP was moderate (24/26 found by any model), and C infrastructure code was the primary failure mode (only 36/45 found by any model; 9/11 universal misses were in C).

nodes.title: SecRespond: Benchmarking AI Agents for Real-World Post-Compromise Incident Response
affiliations: The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology
nodes.one_liner: What’s striking is that even top models can “see” alerted compromise artifacts yet still cannot reliably finish the job—persistence hunting and verified remediation remain the hard wall.
points: SECRESPOND introduces the first post-compromise incident-response benchmark grounded in real forensic disk snapshots and security-product outputs, spanning 10 cloud-host cyber ranges across 4 entry vectors, 5 operating systems, and 21 MITRE ATT&CK techniques with 280 rubric checkpoints mapped to 52 capability items.

Across 23 frontier models, detection consistently outperforms remediation planning (e.g., GPT-5.5: 70.7% detection vs 36.0% planning; a 34.7-point gap), and no model achieved complete detection plus remediation on any single range—indicating current agents can react to alerts but fail at end-to-end incident closure.

Capability breakdown shows strong entity finding but weak persistence and process quality (avg detection: 75.4% intrusion entities vs 58.8% persistence; avg planning peaks at 55.3% baseline risks but drops to 31.8% investigation/response quality), implying the dominant failures are proactive hunting for silent persistence and producing verified, comprehensive remediation steps.

nodes.title: Mask2Shield: Strengthening LLM Safety against Neuron-Pruning Attacks
affiliations: Guangdong University of Finance and Economics
nodes.one_liner: Training the model to refuse while its own “safety neurons” are functionally missing makes post-hoc neuron-pruning jailbreaks largely ineffective unless the attacker prunes so much that generation collapses.
points: Masked-forward safety alignment that zeroes selector-identified FFN “safety” channels during harmful training cuts recomputed pruning attack successes from 80–279/313 prompts in base models to 1–44/313 across 10 diverse LLM configurations, indicating refusal can be redistributed away from a small removable neuron set.

Under the iterative TwinBreak pruning pipeline (five rounds of 1% channel removals), defended models reduce endpoint attack success rates from ~94–99% (published baselines after iteration 5 on HarmBench/AdvBench/JailbreakBench) down to 0–15% depending on architecture, demonstrating cross-pipeline robustness rather than overfitting to one neuron selector.

Cumulative targeted deletion on a defended model keeps ASR ≤18/313 up to 5% removal while maintaining 68.05% output validity, but at 10% removal validity collapses to 0/313, implying attackers must choose between failing to bypass safety or breaking coherent generation as pruning becomes aggressive.

nodes.title: RAGuard: A Layered Defense Framework for Retrieval-Augmented Generation Systems Against Data Poisoning
nodes.one_liner: A self-referential, counterfactual “remove-one-document” test can zero out measured RAG poisoning success without poison labels or ground-truth answers, trading primarily for extra generator compute rather than accuracy.
points: A black-box, label-free leave-one-out filtering layer (ZKIP) reduced measured poisoning attack success rate (ASR) to 0.000 across all defended Natural Questions configurations tested (dense retrievers and BM25) at 10% and 30% corpus poison ratios by flagging documents whose removal sharply shifts the model’s answer and/or lowers output uncertainty.

Adversarial retriever fine-tuning on synthetic poison families (fabrication/contradiction/reasoning-trap) improved retrieval under poisoning (e.g., Recall@5 0.319 vs 0.259 at NQ 10%) but still left nontrivial residual ASR (0.072), implying retrieval hardening alone is insufficient and benefits most as a ranking-quality complement to inference-time filtering.

ZKIP preserved retrieval utility while blocking attacks—keeping Recall@5 within ~0.03 of the clean-corpus dense baseline (0.282) in defended runs—at the cost of k+1 generator passes per query (6× overhead at k=5), making batching/early-stopping/approximate probing key for deployment feasibility.

nodes.title: A Structured Cyber Threat Intelligence Dataset Using STIX 2.1 Entities and MITRE ATT&CK Mappings
nodes.one_liner: A rare report-level STIX+ATT&CK ground-truth dataset that preserves entity relationships and shows local open-source LLMs can reliably audit annotations at scale.
points: A manually curated dataset structures 150 public English CTI reports (2015–2026) into STIX 2.1 report-level graphs totaling 4,777 entities and 5,817 directed relationships, averaging 32 nodes and 39 edges per report.

Adversarial behaviors are normalized via 1,273 STIX attack-pattern mappings to 269 unique MITRE ATT&CK Enterprise techniques/sub-techniques spanning all 15 tactics, enabling cross-report comparison despite vendor-specific terminology.

On a rigorously adjudicated 25-report reference subset (~17% of the corpus), human agreement was substantial (quadratic-weighted κ=0.64 type, 0.67 ATT&CK mapping, 0.62 relationships) and the best local LLM judge (Qwen3.6:27B) reached κ up to 0.803 with >92% micro-F1 and <5% false positives, indicating LLMs can flag inconsistencies but not replace expert validation.

nodes.title: Dynamic Capability Scoping for Enterprise AI Agents: A Synthetic Dataset and Three-Source Permission Architecture
nodes.one_liner: Dynamic least-privilege is treated as prevention (credentials absent) rather than detection (misuse noticed), with observe-only mode turning denied-permission attempts into a measurable misalignment signal.
points: A three-source permission architecture—role-based ceilings, a task-context permission classifier, and deterministic policy-derived combination prohibitions—aims to reduce enterprise agent attack surface by ensuring high-risk credentials never exist in context unless strictly required.

A released synthetic dataset of 600 enterprise task prompts labeled over a deployable 15-permission taxonomy achieved strong label reliability on a 10% human-reviewed sample, with Cohen’s κ improving from 0.917 to 0.967 after adjudication and exact-match rising from 68.3% to 85.0%.

Co-evolving synthetic prompt generation with the org policy exposed and fixed authorization gaps, cutting department ceiling violations from 46 to 3 (a 93% reduction), implying synthetic workloads can materially improve least-privilege IAM design before production rollout.

nodes.title: ZKP Security Tools and Verification: Coverage, Effectiveness, Adoption, and Challenges
affiliations: Max Planck Institute for Security and Privacy (MPI-SP)
nodes.one_liner: The striking result is how quickly ZKP tool effectiveness collapses from toy/isolated circuits to real codebases, even as practitioners already lean on LLMs but still lack checkable, end-to-end guarantees.
points: Across 70 real-world Circom vulnerabilities, automated tools detected 45.7% in isolated targets but only 19.6% when run on full project codebases, indicating that scalability, tool errors, and timeouts currently erase most practical coverage in realistic settings.

Security tooling is heavily skewed toward Circom and underconstraint/nondeterminism bugs, while practitioners report the biggest unmet needs are semantic errors, Fiat–Shamir/proof-system issues, and system integration failures that are perceived as poorly covered (e.g., proof-system issues: 60% hard-to-detect vs 15% adequately covered).

ZKP workflows remain human-led despite widespread LLM use (85% of developers and 83% of auditors), and adoption hinges less on raw detection power than on clearer guarantees, higher-quality reports, and lower integration effort—especially for specification- or verification-driven tools.

nodes.title: Poster: Rethinking Security in LLM Code Generation through Real-World Risk Scenarios
nodes.one_liner: Realistic prompt-side risk conditions (ambiguity, missing context, and functionality-vs-security tension) drive LLM-generated code into vulnerable defaults, and simple prompting mitigations help but can introduce regressions when requirements conflict.
points: Across 2,700 test cases spanning 9 programming languages and three real-world prompt risk scenarios, all 8 evaluated LLMs produced insecure code more than 56% of the time, indicating weak security-by-default under realistic developer inputs.

Ambiguous requirements are the most failure-prone condition, with vulnerability rates reaching 66%, implying that omitting explicit security constraints systematically pushes models toward unsafe “fill in the blanks” implementations.

Security-aware prompting substantially reduces risk (up to a 45% vulnerability-rate reduction), but in security–functionality conflict cases it can backfire with regression rates up to 19% (net gain 0.12), highlighting that mitigation must be conflict-aware rather than purely adding generic safety guidance.

nodes.title: SecDrift: Measuring Sector-Conditioned Security Drift in AI-Generated Code
nodes.one_liner: Industry framing doesn’t reliably make AI-generated code safer or riskier, but the choice of model and the blind spots of static analyzers materially shape measured security outcomes.
points: Across 5,355 generations spanning 7 LLMs, 8 CISA sectors, and 9 CWE scenarios, sector-conditioned prompting produced no statistically significant change in static-analysis vulnerability rates (baseline 14.0% vs industry 11.4%, −2.7pp; Fisher’s exact p=0.24; Cohen’s h=−0.08).

All 8 critical-infrastructure sectors showed negligible, non-significant drift versus baseline (0/8 significant with or without Bonferroni correction; |h|<0.15), and a non-CISA placebo (e-commerce/online education) matched the CISA industry rate (10.5% vs 11.4%, p=0.63), implying any small pooled pattern is generic “industry specificity” rather than sector identity.

The apparent aggregate “protective” shift is a composition artifact dominated by CWE-502 and CWE-22 (excluding both flips the drift to +0.4pp with p=1.00), while model selection is the reliable lever with full-output models spanning 11.6%–16.1% vulnerability rates (DeepSeek R1 drops to 1.8% but is confounded by high abstention), and human review found static analysis missed vulnerabilities in 26.7% of zero-flag categories (especially XSS and weak crypto), so reported zero rates are lower bounds.

nodes.title: Mapping CVEs to MITRE ATT&CK Techniques: A Curated Gold-Set Classifier and the Limits of LLM-Assisted Label Expansion
nodes.one_liner: The most striking result is that scaling cheap LLM labels does not help—and can harm the long tail—while a small amount of truly curated labeling monotonically improves CVE→ATT&CK mapping quality.
points: A curated 1,207-CVE gold set (CTID expert mappings) enables a RoBERTa multi-label classifier that nearly doubles analyst-facing ranking quality versus a zero-shot embedding baseline, raising recall@5 from 0.322 to 0.686 (MRR 0.397→0.620).

Deterministic CWE→CAPEC→ATT&CK derivation is dominated by table-expansion artifacts: on 39,156 CVEs it labels 88.3% but assigns a median of 8 techniques per CVE (mean 13.3) and stamps specific techniques onto ~half of all CVEs (e.g., T1574.007 appears in 53%), making it unsuitable as a training target for behaviorally faithful mapping.

LLM-assisted label expansion fails at ~0.39 expert agreement: adding 100–984 LLM-labeled CVEs yields no reliable ranking gains and at ~1,000 added rows reduces rare-technique coverage (macro-F1 −0.04), indicating performance is label-quality-bound rather than data-bound and that evaluation protocols must avoid test-split checkpoint selection to prevent noise-driven false conclusions.

nodes.title: StealthBench: Measuring Operational Stealth in Autonomous Offensive-Security Agents
nodes.one_liner: Operational stealth is largely independent from exploit capability, and a cheap, high-agreement judge panel can quantify the “recklessness tax” where agents succeed but burn the engagement.
points: No evaluated agent exceeded a 54% safe success rate (task solved and judged stealth-clean), showing that operational tradecraft failures remain a first-order blocker for deploying autonomous offensive-security agents in realistic engagements.

Across 771 trajectories, 68.4% solved the task but only 43.8% were both solved and stealthy, meaning 24.5% of all runs were “reckless solves” that achieved objectives while still creating detectable or damaging OPSEC incidents.

A 3-model LLM judge panel (GPT-5.6 Sol, GLM 5.2, Kimi K3) produced near-human-style consistency for stealth classification with Fleiss’ κ=0.834, 87.9% unanimous verdicts, and only 12.1% split votes, indicating stealth can be monitored at scale with structured rubrics.

nodes.title: Gubernaut: A Deterministic Homeostatic Controller for Affect-Regulated LLM Agents, Validated Across Independent Model Families
nodes.one_liner: A token-free, deterministic meta-controller that only reads numeric telemetry shows cross-family reductions in multi-turn emotional escalation while remaining structurally insulated from text-based prompt injection into the controller itself.
points: A deterministic runtime control layer reduced judged conversational reactivity in 15/16 generator×judge pairings (13/16 at p<.05), with the lone failure being a small null effect (−0.04) rather than a reversal, implying consistent cross-model behavioral stabilization but bounded by host headroom.

Adding an independent judge family (xAI Grok 4.3) preserved the effect (the Grok judge column passes 4/4 cooks), strengthening the claim that the observed calm is not merely judge-lineage or shared-style bias in LLM-as-judge evaluations.

The controller exhibited a replicated homeostatic “recovery signature” across 4/4 model families—arousal integrates during sustained hostile-valence input and then decays after user de-escalation—suggesting closed-loop regulation dynamics that a stateless “stay calm” prompt cannot produce in principle.

nodes.title: Cyber-Capable AI Agents: Vulnerabilities, Evaluation Containment, and Defensive Response
nodes.one_liner: The core takeaway is that cyber-capable agent evaluations must treat containment, tool privileges, and responder access as first-class security properties rather than background setup.
points: Indirect prompt-injection and memory-poisoning attacks can redirect tool-using agents at rates spanning ~24% to ~98% depending on scaffold and defenses, implying that “prompt safety” is an unreliable boundary once agents can retrieve, store, and act on untrusted content.

End-to-end exploit synthesis remains scaffold- and information-dependent (e.g., 157/898 ExploitGym instances solved in the strongest configuration, while one-day exploitation jumps from 7% to 87% when a CVE description is provided), so capability scores alone do not translate to real-world risk without explicit containment and privilege assumptions.

Defensive response is constrained by dual-use filtering: one benchmark reports a 2.72× higher refusal rate for defensive than neutral requests (with 43.8% refusals for system hardening and 34.3% for malware analysis), indicating that artifact-only safety gates can block incident responders unless role-aware access controls are engineered and evaluated.

nodes.title: False Prophets: On the Security of World Models in Agentic Systems
nodes.one_liner: World models add a new attack surface where simulation errors—not just LLM jailbreaks—can reliably trick agents into executing dangerous real-world commands.
points: Text-based world models used to vet agent actions can be adversarially steered into harmful mispredictions—with induced failures reaching up to 95% in some categories—enabling unintended command execution, denial of service, wallet-draining token blowups, and sensitive data exposure in terminal agents.

On a 700-script security benchmark (AgentWorld-Robust), Qwen-AgentWorld achieved 86% exit-code accuracy but only 44% exact-output accuracy (CWM: 77% / 23%), implying that “looks safe” simulations frequently diverge from reality even when the agent would proceed based on a seemingly correct high-level outcome.

Runtime/resource estimation is a critical intrinsic weakness: both evaluated models underestimated runtime in 95% of cases (often by tens of minutes, sometimes predicting <1s for jobs that exceed 1h), creating a systematic optimism bias that can approve scripts that actually time out or exhaust resources.

nodes.title: Evaluation of Adversarial Robustness in Arabic Language Models
affiliations: Public Authority of Applied Education and Training, Kuwait
College of Business Studies, Public Authority of Applied Education and Training, Kuwait
nodes.one_liner: Arabic-specific orthographic and morphological perturbations (especially diacritics) can nearly nullify sentiment classifiers with minimal visible change, and adversarial training only partially closes this gap.
points: Character-level diacritics insertion is an especially potent black-box attack on Arabic BERT-style classifiers, dropping AraBERT’s accuracy from 94% to 2% (−92 percentage points) while keeping perturbations low (~15% Levenshtein), showing that morphologically meaningful “small” edits can catastrophically break performance.

Word-level conjunction manipulation preserves meaning unusually well (≈93–96% cosine similarity) yet still causes large failures (up to −58 points on AraBERT and −39 on XLM-T), indicating that models over-rely on shallow syntactic cues even when semantics remain largely unchanged.

Standard adversarial training improves robustness most for higher-level shifts (e.g., paraphrase robustness gains up to +48.4 points for MARBERT and +45.3 for CaMeLBERT) but remains weak against character noise (e.g., AraBERT still only 22.61% under diacritics and 20.87% under visual attacks) and increases training cost by ~25–40%, implying the need for character-aware defenses beyond vanilla augmentation.

nodes.title: TriShieldRAG: A Three-Ring Defense-in-Depth Framework Against Knowledge Corruption in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
nodes.one_liner: The most interesting aspect is the explicit, formally stated failure boundary (minority-poison + provenance-tag assumptions) showing exactly when multi-stage RAG defenses should work and when they should be expected to fail.
points: A three-layer RAG defense (ingest-time lexical/statistical screening, retrieval-time provenance+consistency trust re-ranking, and generation-time cross-model voting with one bounded re-retrieval) reduced knowledge-poisoning attack success from ~91% to ~13% on a 5,000-document Wikipedia KB with 10 targeted questions while preserving benign-query accuracy.

Layered defenses hinge on explicit preconditions: retrieval/generation aggregation is only expected to work when poisoned documents remain a minority of the retrieved top‑k (ρ<0.5), because once poison becomes the majority it can dominate both inter-document “consistency” signals and majority voting, yielding confident but wrong answers.

Provenance weighting can provide a hard safety floor for correctly tagged trusted sources (a clean document’s trust score is guaranteed ≥0.45, above the drop threshold ϑ2=0.35), but this protection collapses if attackers can spoof or obtain trusted provenance metadata, making provenance attestation and write-access controls a high-leverage deployment requirement.

nodes.title: Distributing Security Controls Through Harness Engineering
nodes.one_liner: Security controls for coding agents can be reliably scaled to distributed teams by shipping them as harness-level defaults (especially sandboxing + skill scanning), avoiding vendor lock-in while preserving efficacy.
points: A distributable security-hardened harness (SHarD) embedded OS sandboxing, skill scanning, and tool restriction behind a single install command and reached a 100% adjusted test score with no regressions versus the baseline harness across any test category.

On two commercial coding agents, adding off‑the‑shelf controls improved composite security from 60.9%→87.0% for Claude Code (+26.1 points) and from 45.7%→69.6% for Codex (+23.9 points), with skill scanning showing the largest gains (Claude 58.3%→100%, Codex 16.7%→75%).

Content-protection/guardrail tooling provided 0.0 percentage-point improvement on targeted tests for both agents (Claude 66.7%→66.7%, Codex 61.1%→61.1%) and introduced workflow-breaking control conflicts, implying today’s filtering-based defenses are brittle under multi-control deployments compared to boundary-enforced controls (e.g., kernel sandboxing).

nodes.title: Open Security Benchmark: Towards Autonomous Enterprise Cyber Defense
nodes.one_liner: A practical benchmark substrate that finally makes “can we trust an enterprise defense agent?” measurable via frozen multi-vendor posture state, grounded answers, and auditable tool traces.
points: OSB closes the enterprise “environment data gap” by benchmarking agentic posture-investigation end-to-end on a frozen, cross-vendor enterprise snapshot with closed-form ground truth, enabling reproducible trust assessments rather than anecdotal demos.

The framework evaluates the same tasks through two operationally realistic modalities—execution-grounded text-to-SQL over a 44-table relational snapshot and native vendor APIs over a served instance—so agent scores reflect both answer correctness and the evidence-generation path used in practice.

An initial release instantiates 127 identity-security tasks (77 single-platform visibility + 50 cross-vendor correlation) across three environment scales (~75/400/2,000 employees; ~1,600/8,300/36,000 rows), making robustness to organizational size a first-class measurement rather than a hidden confound.

nodes.title: Agent Harness Distillation: Inference-Time Harness Extraction and Exploitation in Autonomous Multi-Agent Systems
nodes.one_liner: Inference-time harnesses are extractable like model knowledge, turning agent workflow engineering into a stealable, transferable capability layer—and forcing AMAS builders to treat orchestration as a first-class security boundary.
points: Black-box “Agent Harness Distillation” can extract and transfer inference-time orchestration (topology, tools, memory/verification routines) from autonomous multi-agent systems, showing that harness behavior is a practical IP leakage surface even when internal logs are inaccessible or encrypted.

Pre-distilled harnesses measurably boost weaker backbones more than strong ones, with average accuracy rising from 33.57% to 39.87% (+6.30) on Hermes-harness transfer and from 33.57% to 41.17% (+7.60) on Claude Code-harness transfer across four recipient models, implying stolen harnesses can “upgrade” commodity models into more capable agents.

Post-distillation loop alignment can deliver large downstream capability jumps (e.g., on MMLU-Pro CS with Qwen3.6-Flash: 38.75% baseline → 41.25% pre-distill → 86.25% post-distill, a +45.00 point gain vs pre-distill), while deception-based responses can substantially degrade extraction metrics (CV/IF/CT/PP) yet largely preserve task accuracy, making misdirection a plausible near-term defense.

nodes.title: Change2Task: From Repository Changes to Executable Coding Agent Tasks and Environments
nodes.one_liner: Repository history can be “replayed” onto modern, runnable code to mass-produce realistic coding-agent tasks while keeping evaluation outcomes and cutting environment costs.
points: Change2Task converts merged PRs into executable, verifier-backed coding-agent tasks on healthy descendant commits, achieving 79.6% verified construction success (900/1,130) across five task families and recovering 29.2% more verified Bug Fix tasks than a matched PR-mirroring baseline (500 vs 387 on 621 candidates).

Most recoverable tasks require adaptation beyond simple patch reversal—only 10.6% succeed via direct reversal and 21.1% via code mapping, while 68.3% need agent reconstruction—yet the resulting tasks preserve source-change structure with 0.894 weighted “change-profile fidelity” on average (macro 0.887).

Paired evaluations show reconstructed modern tasks largely preserve benchmarking signal: across 3,600 matched agent-task runs, branch outcomes agree 89.7% of the time (κ=0.787) with up to 98.0% agreement in some matched settings, while reusing 388 modern bases for 900 tasks cuts setup time 58.4%, storage 71.2%, and overall pipeline spend 10.8% ($1,917→$1,710).

nodes.title: (EC)2: Event-Centric Explainability for Cybersecurity Through Multi-Agent LLM Investigations
nodes.one_liner: Shifting from feature attribution to event-centric, evidence-grounded investigations makes LLM agents not just explain alerts but measurably improve boundary-case intrusion detection decisions—at the cost of ~17 minutes per alert.
points: (EC)2’s hypothesis-driven multi-agent investigations produced substantially higher-quality alert explanations than a single-call LLM baseline, improving mean scores on Attack Type Identification (3.21 vs 1.49), Entity Identification (4.10 vs 3.22), and Explanation Completeness (3.04 vs 1.29) over 50 CSE-CIC-IDS2018 events.

External evidence retrieval is the dominant driver of explanation fidelity: removing database access collapsed mean scores to 1.83 (attack type), 2.46 (entities), and 1.63 (completeness), while using only traffic or only topology still significantly underperformed the full system (traffic-only: 2.89/3.95/2.76; topology-only: 2.31/2.65/2.18).

Using investigation outputs to reclassify the most uncertain 5% of AE-IDS decisions (1,000 stratified samples) improved recall from 0.54 to 0.72 and precision from 0.56 to 0.73 while reducing FPR from 0.43 to 0.26, with McNemar χ²=118.4 (p<0.001) showing systematic error correction (207 fixed vs 37 newly introduced).

nodes.title: The Missing Layer: Specification Infrastructure for AI Oversight
nodes.one_liner: The most interesting takeaway is that many “AI safety” failures reduce to missing, governed, machine-checkable specifications that can be compiled into enforcement, evaluation, and escalation—turning oversight into composable infrastructure rather than bespoke prompts and ad-hoc monitoring.
points: A five-layer oversight stack (Legibility, Specification, Mediation, Evaluation, Escalation) crossed with six persistent concerns (alignment, robustness, adversarial defense, security, governance, accountability) highlights that Layer 2 “Specification” is the key dependency that must drive enforcement, evaluation, and escalation but is currently the least mature component in deployed agent oversight.

Layer 2 fails four concrete maturity indicators—shared vocabulary, design principles, composability standards, and governance practices—implying most current deployments cannot reliably turn intent into machine-checkable constraints, cannot compose policies across teams, and cannot produce audit-ready, versioned oversight artifacts demanded by regimes like the EU AI Act and NIST AI RMF.

Six actionable design principles for specification infrastructure (elicitability, composability, conformity, adversary-awareness, traceability, governability) are presented alongside a reference architecture where a single versioned specification compiles into runtime mediation, evaluation criteria, and escalation triggers, enabling post-incident attribution to the exact spec version and authority rather than to opaque model behavior.

nodes.title: ReCon: A Resource-Constrained Benchmark for LLM-Based Cybersecurity Compliance Across Ingestion and Retrieval Pipelines
affiliations: International Institute of Information Technology Hyderabad
nodes.one_liner: It shows that practical, privacy-preserving compliance gap analysis can be done on commodity CPUs, but only if you pick the right small model and retrieval/prompting setup.
points: A CPU-only, on-prem RAG pipeline can automate ISO/IEC 27002:2022 policy documentary compliance checks at scale, covering 93 controls across 288 unique model+retrieval configurations for 26,784 control-level evaluations without requiring GPUs.

Among eight open-weight models, Granite4.1:8B achieved the strongest overall reliability (75.0% balanced accuracy, MCC 0.548, Cohen’s κ 0.528) and the highest mean agreement with auditor ground truth (80.65%), while several alternatives clustered below 60% balanced accuracy—indicating model choice dominates outcome quality under resource constraints.

Retrieval design materially shifts agreement, with the best-performing pipeline for Granite4.1:8B using all-MiniLM-L6-v2 embeddings plus ms-marco-MiniLM-L-12-v2 reranking (Case 2) reaching ~80.64% mean agreement, and prompt design can induce systematic errors (e.g., weaker models conflating standard requirement text with policy evidence and producing misleading confidence scores).

nodes.title: ContractHIL-HLS: Contract-Aligned Multi-Agent Workflow with Hardware-in-the-Loop Feedback for HLS Design
nodes.one_liner: A lightweight “contract as executable spec” plus hardware evidence gates turns LLM-assisted HLS from prompt-local code generation into an auditable workflow that can reach board-level closure and trigger major system-level speedups.
points: Encoding natural-language HLS requirements as a structured contract (explicit interfaces, constraints, checks, and rollback rules) increased the estimated single-sample HLS-Eval testbench pass rate from 64.0% to 70.2% across 94 locally executable tasks, showing that making design intent machine-checkable materially improves first-try correctness.

Adding the full contract→HTML artifact handoff plus an evidence-gated revision loop achieved 70.4% pass@1 and 76.6% pass@5 on the same 94 tasks, indicating most gains come from contract alignment while multi-agent HIL scaffolding primarily supports traceability and iteration control rather than large kernel-level accuracy jumps.

In a board-tested post-quantum secure-message accelerator, a contract-driven dual-bitstream organization cut average six-message runtime from 207.3 ms to 52.4 ms (≈4× faster) while keeping positive routed timing slack on both images and preserving decrypted-message verification, demonstrating that hardware-in-the-loop evidence can drive system-level architectural decisions with measurable performance impact.

nodes.title: Share No More Than the Request Requires: Federated Disclosure for Perspective-Aware AI
nodes.one_liner: It turns selective disclosure into a graph-minimization problem with provenance-first responses, aiming to operationalize “share no more than the request requires” across federated, agent-mediated identity queries.
points: Provenance Preserving Chronicles (PPC) enforces minimum-necessary disclosure by compiling each holder’s temporal, predicate-labeled identity graph into a compact, relationship- and purpose-authorized evidence subgraph, so peers can be queried without centralizing raw personal data.

The framework separates authorization from sufficiency by (i) evaluating a local authorization function over every node/edge and (ii) validating a candidate release via structural requirements—ontology-typed path coverage, predicate-type completeness, connectivity, and provenance completeness—before anything is returned to the requester.

A two-phase “text-first, artifacts-second” release flow reduces irreversible high-fidelity leakage by returning provenance-linked textual answers initially and requiring explicit holder approval for any raw artifact access, while explicitly modeling post-disclosure risks like downstream inference and prompt injection as remaining hazards.

nodes.title: Agents That Certify Their Own Exploits: Confidence-Scheduled Restricted Responses for Safe Opponent Exploitation
nodes.one_liner: It turns safe exploitation into a runtime-audited property of the exact strategy you actually deploy, breaking the usual coupling between opponent-model error and exploitability blow-ups.
points: The method enforces a per-deployment safety budget by computing an exact full-tree best-response certificate on the *played* strategy and only committing strategies whose certified reference-relative loss is ≤ ε_max, yielding 0 certificate violations across 36,000 audited hands even under adaptive opponents.

In Leduc hold’em at ε_max = 0.15, it delivers 6.2× higher steady-state gain than a money-verified binary release gate while keeping the worst deployed certificate at 0.1496 (i.e., always within budget).

Trajectory-level mixing with the same opponent estimator achieves similar gains but catastrophically overshoots safety (worst exploitability 2.04, or 14× the budget), showing that certifying the deployed strategy—not trusting the model or construction procedure—is what prevents unsafe exploitation when the opponent model is wrong.

nodes.title: MulRobBench: A Decision-Level Benchmark for Safe and Security-Policy-Compliant Multimodal UAV Agents
nodes.one_liner: The standout result is that models can often describe context yet still fail where it matters: stably converting degraded multimodal evidence plus explicit security rules into an auditable safe next action.
points: MulRobBench introduces an offline, protocol-conditioned decision benchmark that couples real UAV multimodal observations with security-policy constraints and action-level safety auditing across 3,024 strict samples, 17 task-taxonomy nodes, and 12 scoring dimensions.

Across 17 audited multimodal models, the highest semantic protocol-decision score is only 0.5141 and the best strict mean scoring-dimension accuracy is 0.1599, indicating that current VLA systems remain far from reliably producing executable, policy-compliant UAV decisions under realistic constraints.

A matched 20-anchor modality-removal study changes 4–15 of 20 actions per model, and analyses identify modality-trust selection, constraint extraction, strong glare, missing data, and high-entropy operator shorthand as dominant drivers of action instability and policy-violation risk.

nodes.title: Conformal Changepoint Localization and Root Cause Analysis with Corrupted Observations
affiliations: Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology
nodes.one_liner: Distribution-free changepoint and root-cause confidence sets stay valid under corruption, but become useful again once uncertainty is turned into conformal weights—often collapsing huge sets back toward oracle-level sharpness.
points: Weighted conformal changepoint localization and root-cause analysis (W-CONCH/W-CROC) preserve finite-sample, distribution-free coverage under Huber contamination while sharply shrinking confidence sets by downweighting likely-corrupted observations using classifier uncertainty.

On image changepoint benchmarks at heavy contamination (ε=0.7), unweighted CONCH confidence sets ballooned to 137.43 (DomainNet) and 345.27 (CIFAR-100), while uncertainty-weighted W-CONCH reduced them to 18.77–22.84 and 7.24–9.18, respectively, at similar ~95% empirical coverage.

Meta-learned weighting (MW-CONCH/MW-CROC) further improved informativeness without needing test-time ε, reaching set size 3.61 on DomainNet at ε=0.7 (vs 9.81 oracle and 137.43 unweighted) and cutting root-cause penalized set size on CIFAR-100 at ε=0.7 from 4.835 (CROC) to 1.915 (MW-CROC EDL-M) at ~99% coverage.

nodes.title: Hybrid Analysis for Secure MCP Tool Use in LLM Agents
nodes.one_liner: The key insight is that securing MCP tools requires tying protocol-level intent to OS-level side effects, because hijacked or malicious tools can look benign in metadata and returned text while behaving dangerously at runtime.
points: A lifecycle-aware hybrid guard that combines pre-execution parameter auditing with in-sandbox eBPF runtime monitoring and post-execution verification detects 48.3% of unsafe MCP tool calls (116/240) versus 8.3% for a static tool-call-governance baseline and 0% for tool-result text inspection, demonstrating that message-only defenses miss a large fraction of tool-abuse behaviors.

Runtime evidence is decisive for host-side tool-call hijacking: the approach detects 75.0% of unsafe host-side calls (48/64) while both baselines detect 0%, showing that comparing declared tool calls to observed process/file/network behavior can surface execution-layer substitution that is invisible in the original tool-call message.

The defense preserves usability with a 3.7% average false-positive rate and adds roughly ~12.4 seconds of LLM auditing latency per tool call (≈5.9s pre + ≈6.6s post), implying the security gains are deployable for safety-critical agents but may be too costly for ultra-low-latency workflows without caching or selective auditing.
